member.summary: Issue #1238: set transiently by the argument-binding loops just before eagerly binding a top-level conditional (if/else), ternary, or switch-expression argument that has no target type yet. member.summary: Issue #1632: memoizes per (sourceType, targetType, allowExplicit). Overload resolution probes user-defined conversions for every candidate × argument pair that fails direct classification (IsConvertibilityApplicable in OverloadResolver), and each probe used to re-walk 's uncached GetMethods reflection scan on both the source and target declaring types. member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.Conversion.PlatformChecked
member.summary: ADR-0186 §3/§4: an implicit conversion of a platform value T! into a non-null reference destination. Implicit and operator-free in the source, but a runtime nil check is inserted at the coercion point. Deliberately not , for two independent reasons an implementer will otherwise hit in sequence. ConversionClassifier.BindConversion returns the source expression untouched on an identity classification, so an identity T! → T would silently reach no materialisation arm and §4's check would never be emitted anywhere. And the overload ranker prefers identity over implicit, so an identity T! → T? beside an implicit T! → T would invert §3's tie-break, which states the opposite (T wins). Both platform rows are therefore plain implicit conversions, distinguished by this flag, and §3's tie-break is stated once, in the ranker, rather than falling out of a classification accident.

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.LambdaBinder.localFunctionCapturedVariables
member.summary: Issue #4221: every function literal's captured-variable set, keyed by its own , as of the most recent time it was (re)computed. A generic local function is called directly through its rather than through a delegate value, so a sibling calling it (BoundCallExpression) carries no reference to its the way a physically nested literal does. consults this map to fold a callee's already-known captures into its caller's own set — the same transitive folding already does for a literal nested directly in the body being walked. Consecutive generic local-function declarations bind their bodies in source order (see ), so a callee declared earlier in the same group is already present here when its caller's body binds; re-converges the whole group afterward to cover a callee declared later (forward reference) or a call cycle.

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.OverloadResolution.ClrOverloadResolution.DefaultLiteralArgumentType
member.summary: Issue #1391: sentinel argument type representing the untyped default literal whose concrete type is supplied by the chosen parameter. The bare default is implicitly convertible to any type (its value is the zero/null of whatever parameter type it lands on), so during overload resolution against an imported (CLR) method it must classify as applicable to every (non-by-ref) parameter — mirroring the user-defined generic method path, which already accepts default. Using a dedicated marker keeps the literal neutral during betterness ranking (always an identity conversion) while the concrete-typed default is materialized by BindClrParameterConversions against the resolved parameter type.

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.OverloadResolution.ClrOverloadResolution.ForwardedBoundChainLimit

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.OverloadResolution.ClrOverloadResolution.InlineOutVarArgumentType
member.summary: ADR-0060 / issue #977: sentinel argument type representing an inline out var/out let/out _ declaration whose local type is not yet known. Such an argument is applicable to — and only to — a by-ref (ref/out/in) parameter; its declared local type is inferred from the chosen overload's parameter after resolution succeeds. Using a dedicated marker keeps the out-var neutral during betterness ranking (it always classifies as an identity conversion against a by-ref parameter) while still rejecting non-by-ref candidates.

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.OverloadResolution.ClrOverloadResolution.SymbolicByRefArgumentType
member.summary: Issue #3907: sentinel argument type representing a by-ref (ref/out/in) argument whose pointee is a same-compilation user REFERENCE type — a G# class, interface or named delegate the current compilation is still emitting, and which therefore has no CLR to match against.
member.remarks: By VALUE such an argument rides through the object boundary harmlessly (issue #658) — a class instance really is an object. By REFERENCE it does not: C# requires a ref argument to match its parameter EXACTLY, so ref Node is not a ref object. Erasing it made the non-generic Interlocked.Exchange(ref object, object) an exact IDENTITY match for Interlocked.Exchange(&nodeField, nil), so it beat the Exchange(ref T, T) where T : class the author meant and the call's type silently became object. csc never considers that overload at all. Like the inline out var sentinel, this one classifies as an identity conversion against any by-ref parameter and as inapplicable against everything else, so it stays neutral during betterness ranking. The candidate restriction — only a by-ref parameter that is GENERIC in the open definition can accept it, because no imported signature can name a type this compilation has not emitted yet — is applied before resolution by MemberLookup.ExcludeNonGenericByRefCandidates, since a candidate closed over the erasure no longer remembers which of its by-ref parameters were generic. The type argument is then recovered symbolically (MemberLookup.BuildSymbolicMethodTypeArgs → TryRecoverErasedTypeArguments), which is what makes the resulting call's type the user's own class rather than object.

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Compilation.Compilation._nullability
member.summary: Gets or sets how this compilation reads nullability-oblivious imported reference positions (ADR-0186, --nullability=). Defaults to since ADR-0186 step 3 — an oblivious imported reference position is the platform type T!. selects ADR-0136's older T? reading and stays available.
member.remarks: The default is read from NullabilityOptions.DefaultMode, which the GSHARP_NULLABILITY environment variable can set back to . That override exists so the full test suite can be run both ways from one tree, which is how the flip's before/after was measured. An embedder that sets this property always wins over it. The mode is installed as an ambient scope around binding and emit () because the metadata reader that consults it, ClrNullability, is a static leaf with no in reach. Note that the interning caches in the Symbols namespace are process-wide: two compilations that disagree about this mode in one process should not share a .

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Compilation.Compilation._platformNilChecks
member.summary: Gets or sets a value indicating whether ADR-0186 §4's runtime nil check is inserted wherever a platform value T! is coerced into a non-null reference destination. Defaults to true.
member.remarks: Only observable under — nothing constructs a PlatformTypeSymbol otherwise, so no such coercion exists to check. Turning it off (--platform-nil-checks=off) is a measurement and escape-hatch switch and is strictly weaker than either the old or the new model, not a supported mode: today many of the silenced sites are compile errors, and with checks off they are neither an error nor a check.

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Emit.TypeIdentityComparer.KeyCache
member.summary: Issue #1679: process-wide memoization of , keyed by the CLR instance. TypeRefs/TypeSpecs (see ) are keyed by this comparer, so every dictionary probe — including cache hits — used to rebuild the type's assembly-qualified name from scratch; for a constructed generic like Dictionary<string, List<Foo>> that string is built recursively and is invoked many times per emitted method body (casts, boxes, array creations, local signatures, member-ref parents). A keyed on the itself lets repeated probes for the same Type instance reuse the already-computed key without allocating a new string, while still comparing/hashing distinct Type instances that describe the same logical type by their (now-cached) AQN string. Being weakly keyed, entries are collected automatically once the owning 's Type instances become unreachable, so — unlike the process-wide caches added for #1622 — this table needs no explicit ClearCache/Dispose wiring to avoid pinning a disposed context.

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullabilityOptions.ChecksSuppressed
member.summary: ADR-0186 §4: whether the coercion check is inserted at each T! -> T boundary. Stored inverted — as "suppressed" — so that the unset 's false already means "checks on", which is the default the ADR specifies and the only supported mode.

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullabilityOptions.Current
member.summary: The mode installed for the current logical call, or null when nothing installed one. Nullable, not a bare enum, and that is load-bearing at step 3. Step 1 relied on being the enum's zero value so an unset already answered the default. The flip makes that reasoning silently wrong in the dangerous direction: every reader that never entered a scope — and there are some, because ClrNullability is a static leaf reachable from the importer — would keep reading ADR-0136's answer while the compilation around it reads ADR-0186's. "Two readers disagreeing about one declaration" is the #3705 family-2 defect this whole design is careful about. Storing "unset" distinctly and resolving it to makes the default a single fact.

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullabilityOptions._defaultMode
member.summary: Gets the mode a Compilation starts at when its embedder does not say. ADR-0186 step 3 flipped this to . GSHARP_NULLABILITY still selects, and its polarity is inverted with the default: it now recognises enabled and leaves platform-types as the no-op it names. That is not symmetry for its own sake — it is how the "before" half of a before/after measurement stays runnable on a branch that has already flipped, which is exactly the use the variable was introduced for in step 2. Step 5 adds oblivious (see ). An unrecognised value selects the default rather than failing, because this is a measurement affordance and not a supported product switch; /nullability: is the supported one and it rejects an unknown mode by name. The variable is read once, and only a compilation that never sets Nullability observes it — an explicit assignment always wins, so the differential fixtures that assert both columns keep asserting both columns under either setting.

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.PlatformTypeSymbol.Cache
member.summary: Reference-identity cache, mirroring 's. This is not an optimisation. SymbolEqualityComparer.Default is ReferenceEquals and G# symbols are reference-unique within a compilation, so two independently-constructed wrappers over the same underlying type would be two different types to every symbol set, dictionary and identity comparison in the binder. De-duplicating here is what makes T! a type rather than a family of indistinguishable look-alikes.

member.name: F:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.PropertySymbol._returnRefKind
member.summary: Gets or sets the by-reference mode of this property's (or indexer's) GETTER return value — issue #3879, the ADR-0060 amendment that extends the by-ref return from func to prop. means the property was declared prop P ref T: the PropertyDef signature and the get_P MethodDef signature both encode T&, so a CLR consumer can alias the storage (ref int slot = ref holder.P). Only , , and are valid here, mirroring . stays the POINTEE type T throughout, exactly as it does for a ref-returning function — the by-ref-ness is a separate bit, not a wrap.

The arguments are ordered outermost-first (CLR order), aligned 1:1 with the enclosing generic parameters the emitter reifies the nested type over (ECMA-335 §II.10.3.1), so a use-site reference / local / field slot encodes Box1+Tag1 rather than the open self-instantiation Box1+Tag1. Issue #2342: runs with set as 's ambient "current declaring package" (see ) for the duration of a single member-body bind, restoring the previous value afterwards. This lets an unqualified type-alias reference inside the body (e.g. a data-class object literal such as AnonymousType0{...}) prefer its OWN declaring package's same-simple-name type over an unrelated package's homonym — the ambiguity that arises when two packages each independently synthesize a type with the same simple name (the Oahu.Data EF-migration shape).
Issue #2456 (per-file import scoping / #2395 follow-up): ALSO sets as the ambient "current referencing syntax tree" (see ) for the same duration, so a same-simple-name collision encountered while binding this body (e.g. a struct-literal or bare-constructor-call reference — issue #2455) is only disambiguated by an import declared in THIS body's own file — never a sibling file's import.

member.summary: Issue #1506: resolves a dotted type clause that places type arguments on an OUTER segment and then dots into a nested type — List[int32].Enumerator, Dictionary[string, int32].Enumerator, A[T].B[U].C — to the nested CLR type closed over the constructed outer. A nested type of a generic outer is reflected as the outer's open nested type definition (e.g. List1+Enumerator), which inherits the outer's generic parameters. Resolution therefore (1) finds the longest viable outer prefix — whose trailing segment may be a generic type carrying the outer's arguments while every earlier prefix segment is a plain namespace component — keeping it OPEN, then (2) walks the remaining segments as nested types (each preferring its OWN arity-mangled name), and finally (3) constructs the deepest definition via (cref:Type.MakeGenericType(Type[])) over the cumulative argument vector (outer segment's arguments followed, in source order, by each nested segment's own arguments) — matching how reflection orders (cref:Type.GetGenericArguments).

member.summary: Issues #4089/#4090: asks both constraint questions of a G#-declared generic TYPE-CLAUSE construction — does an OPEN argument forward the declared bound (GS0580, #4067), and does a CLOSED argument satisfy it (GS0152, #4090) — deferring the ask until every same-compilation declaration's type-parameter constraints are resolved.
member.param: The symbolic arguments, in declaration order.
member.remarks: Why it cannot be asked here. A declaration's type-parameter constraints are resolved by ResolvePartialTypeParameterConstraints when that declaration's own body (a class) or members (an interface) are bound — #2519's aggregate-shell lifecycle, which exists so a constraint may name any same-compilation type and so CRTP works. A type clause in ANOTHER declaration may bind before that, and then the declared parameter still reads no constraints at all, which both checkers read as "nothing to violate" and accept. That is not a conservative default; it is a silent hole whose shape is source order. Both defects are that one hole. Interface members bind after every class body, so a G#-declared generic INTERFACE was NEVER checked (#4089). A class is ordered base-first (AddBaseFirst), so class Unf[T] : GsHandler[T] happened to work — but a FIELD type has no such ordering, and class Unf[T] { var f GsHandler[T] } was accepted whenever GsHandler was declared below it. Measured both ways. Deferral, not lifecycle surgery. The alternative — resolving interface type-parameter constraints before class bodies bind — is the #2519 CRTP shell lifecycle, and moving it is a far larger change than the rule needs. Queuing costs one list per compilation and answers with exactly the same code. Once has run, later constructions — member bodies, which BindProgram binds through a freshly derived scope chain, and any subsequent interactive submission — are answered in place. The deferred base and field initialisers bind BEFORE the flush and so ride the queue.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.Binder.EnumerateForwardedParameterChain(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeParameterSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #4067: and every type parameter its own bounds prove it to be an instance of — through a dependent bound ([U SchemeOptions, T U]) or through a type-parameter-valued class constraint. Cycle-safe and TOTAL: a cycle is already rejected at declaration by GS0581, and the visited set terminates the walk on a malformed symbol graph anyway.
member.param: The type parameter to walk from.
member.returns: The chain, argument first.
member.remarks: Issue #4084 made this internal: the IMPORTED twin of #4067's rule, ClrOverloadResolution.TypeParameterSatisfiesClrBound, asks the same "which parameters does this one stand for" question and had a second, narrower walk that read only ClassConstraint. This is a pure symbol walk with no Type dependency, so both sides can share it — and a dependent bound now forwards on both. Review finding (#4084): the 32-element cap is gone. It was belt-and-braces on top of the visited set, and it was LOSSY: a chain of 40 dependent bounds ending in a class or interface bound was truncated and the bound reported unforwarded. Measured on this branch's parent b4478875 and before this removal — a 40-link chain reported GS0159 at an imported generic method and GS0580 at an imported generic type, while the 5-link control bound. The cap was never needed: refuses a parameter already in the set, so the walk visits each DISTINCT parameter at most once and terminates on any graph, cyclic or not. The membership test is a on reference identity so removing the bound does not turn the walk quadratic.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.Binder.FindFirstSignificantStatement(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundStatement)
member.summary: ADR-0065 §2: recursively descends into a single-statement block to find the first effective top-level statement. Used by to allow trivial pre-pass wrapping (e.g. statements injected by lowering passes added at a later date) without giving up on the chaining check.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.Binder.FlushPendingUserGenericConstraintChecks(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope)
member.summary: Issues #4089/#4090: answers every queued G#-declared generic type-clause constraint check and latches the queue closed, so any later construction is answered at its own site.
member.param: Any scope in the compilation's chain.
member.remarks: Called from BindGlobalScope after ExpandStructInterfaceClosures. The BINDING constraint is the interface-members loop just above it: that is where an interface's own type-parameter constraints are resolved (#2519), and nothing before it can answer #4089's question at all. The later boundary is the conservative choice, and it was measured rather than argued. The obvious worry is 's interface arm: it answers through , which reads a class's own Interfaces list, so flushing before the closure expansion might reject a class that inherits its implementation. Traced by moving the call up to immediately after the interface-members loop, rebuilding, and compiling both shapes — an implementation inherited from a BASE CLASS and one reached through a BASE INTERFACE. Both stay green at either boundary, because walks BaseClass itself and asks SelfAndAllBaseInterfaces(), and both of those are populated by the time the interface loop ends. The later point is kept anyway — it is the first place at which every declaration-phase structure this predicate can read is final — and both shapes are pinned as green rows so moving either boundary is caught. The queue is DRAINED before the first check is answered, not cleared after the last. The deferral only works while the queue is a faithful record of what has yet to be asked, so it must be left empty on every path: were a check to throw, a clear-afterwards would strand the remaining items in the root scope and they would be answered later against whatever declaration happened to trigger the next flush. This is the error-path counterpart of the two speculative rollback sites in ResolvePartialTypeParameterConstraints.

member.remarks: The rule, and why it is not the #4032 check. #4032 asks "does this ARGUMENT satisfy the bound", which only a CLOSED instantiation can answer. Here there is no argument: T stands for every type its own bounds admit, so the instantiation is valid exactly when T's bounds are at least as strong as the definition's — C# §13.4.3, which csc reports as CS0314. Measured, not assumed: csc reports CS0314 (not CS0311, which is the CONCRETE-argument case G# already spells GS0152) at a base clause, a field type, a local type, an interface list entry and a return type alike, which is why this sits at the shared construction sites rather than in the base-clause binder. What is still not asked. Only a type argument that IS a type parameter. A composite open shape (Handler[List[T]]) has no forwarding question to ask and is skipped exactly as before, and so is a position whose declared bound MENTIONS another of the definition's own parameters (#4031's dependent-bound shape). The rule therefore only ever ADDS rejections it can prove.

member.summary: Issue #4067: reports GS0580 when an instantiation of a G#-declared constrained generic writes the enclosing declaration's own type parameter at a position whose bound that parameter does not forward — class Unf[T] : GsHandler[T] over open class GsHandler[TOptions SchemeOptions].
member.param: The bag the diagnostic is reported into.
The symbolic arguments, in declaration order.
member.returns: true when a diagnostic was reported.
member.remarks: Why #4037's checker cannot reach this. #4037 put the implication rule at , the one entry point every user-facing Type.MakeGenericType construction funnels through. A G#-declared generic base is never closed that way: the declaration binder resolves it by symbol substitution over StructSymbol / InterfaceSymbol / TypeParameterSymbol and never touches a CLR open definition, so it reaches no CLR checker at all. The RULE is identical (C# §13.4.3, which csc spells CS0314); only the substrate differs, so this is the symbolic twin of ClrOverloadResolution.TypeParameterForwardsDeclaredConstraints and reports the same diagnostic. Only a type argument that IS a type parameter. A composite open shape (GsHandler[List[T]]) has no forwarding question. A CLOSED argument is a DIFFERENT question that this checker deliberately does not ask; since #4090 it is asked immediately afterwards by , which reports GS0152. A declared bound that mentions another of the definition's own parameters is skipped, exactly as #4037 skips it: that is the #4031/#4041 dependent shape, where answering on an unsubstituted parameter is precisely what goes wrong. Never called at the construction site. #4067 wired this inline at the STRUCT/CLASS type clause, which made the answer a function of DECLARATION ORDER: a declaration's type-parameter constraints are resolved when its own body/members are bound, so a reference that binds earlier reads ClassConstraint == null and is silently accepted. Measured three ways — a generic INTERFACE is always accepted (#4089, because interface members bind after every class body, #2519), and even the class case flips on source order (class Unf[T] { var f GsHandler[T] } is accepted when GsHandler is declared BELOW it and rejected when it is declared above). #4089/#4090 therefore route every type-clause construction through , which queues the question until runs it with every same-compilation constraint resolved. The RULE is unchanged; only when it is asked moved.

member.remarks: Type.MakeGenericType checks constraints for a live runtime definition and does NOT for one loaded by a — which is where every /reference assembly lives. So Handler[string] over Handler where TOptions : SchemeOptions closed silently, the emitted extends row named a type the CLR refuses, and the program threw TypeLoadException: GenericArguments[0], 'System.String', … violates the constraint of type parameter 'TOptions' the first time it touched the type. The imported generic METHOD path has checked this explicitly since #750/ADR-0088 for exactly the same reason; this is that check one type parameter over. Only fully CLOSED instantiations are asked. A type argument that still mentions a type parameter is erased to the object placeholder in , and asking a constraint of a placeholder is how a projection breaks constraint satisfaction for a SIBLING parameter (the #4016/#4031 lesson). An open instantiation has no closed answer to give, so it is left alone — the CLR only loads the type once it is closed anyway. The same-compilation class case is NOT skipped, because ClrOverloadResolution.SatisfiesGenericTypeConstraints is handed the SYMBOLIC vector and walks a user class's own base chain (UserReferenceTypeErasedSymbolSatisfiesBaseConstraint) rather than reading the erased object. That is the whole reason class MyOptions : SchemeOptions stays green.

member.summary: Issue #4090: reports GS0152 when a CLOSED type argument at a G#-declared generic TYPE clause does not satisfy the bound the definition declares — class Bad : GsHandler[Unrelated] and var f GsHandler[Unrelated] over open class GsHandler[TOptions SchemeOptions].

The symbolic arguments, in declaration order.

member.remarks: The rule already exists; only this site did not ask it. The CONSTRUCTOR spelling GsHandler[Unrelated]() has always reported GS0152 — OverloadResolver.Constructors runs over the vector — and so has the struct-literal spelling (ExpressionBinder.Literals). The two TYPE-position construction sites (BindNonNullableTypeClause and BindAndConstructUserGenericSegment) called nothing, so the same violation written as a base clause or a field/variable type compiled and emitted IL that fails verification with UnsatisfiedMethodParentInst. This is C# §13.4.3's concrete half, which csc spells CS0311. Only fully CLOSED arguments are asked, which is the exact complement of : an argument that still mentions a type parameter stands for every type its own bounds admit and has no closed answer here, so it is the FORWARDING question (GS0580) or it is a composite open shape that neither checker asks. The two never both fire at one position. The whole vector builds the substitution before any position is checked. A dependent bound ([TBase, TDerived TBase], #4043) is only answerable once the BOUNDING parameter's own argument is known, and reads it out of that map. A per-position check without it would ACCEPT — the deliberate indeterminate direction — and silently lose the dependent shape.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.Binder.SymbolContainingType(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #526 / #1506: resolves a dotted-qualifier type clause (Outer.Inner, A.B.C, List[int32].Enumerator) to a wrapping a (possibly nested, possibly constructed) CLR type. Strategy: enumerate "split points" between an outer prefix that is a fully-qualified type name and the remaining segments that name nested types of that outer. The longest viable outer prefix wins, which lets callers write both Outer.Inner (with import Probe.CSharp providing the namespace prefix) and the fully-qualified Probe.CSharp.Outer.Inner. A single trailing type-argument list attaches to the deepest (last) segment so a nested generic such as Outer.Generic[int] resolves to the constructed Outer.Generic1 closed type. Per-segment type-argument syntax (e.g. Outer[T].Inner, List[int32].Enumerator, A[T].B[U].C) is now fully expressible: the parser records a type-argument list per qualifier segment (see ), and resolves the nested type against the constructed outer — the nested CLR type definition (which carries the outer's generic parameters) closed over the outer's type arguments plus each nested segment's own arguments — rather than the open definition. Issue #1069: returns the enclosing type of a (possibly nested) user type symbol — the value set via SetContainingType during declaration binding — or null for a top-level type or a non-aggregate symbol.

ADR-0146 / issue #2243: synthesizes a top-level class declaration backing a rich anonymous-object literal. This declaration is a stable predeclared shell: fields use their explicit type or an object placeholder, methods/events and the base/interface type clauses retain syntax identity, and literal-site binding later installs inferred field types, constructor parameters, base arguments, captures, and bound method bodies without relocating executable expressions.

Succeeds only when every leaf tail is an expression statement (or variable declaration) of one identical, capturable type: an if without an else, an empty block, mixed arm types, or a non-value tail on any path all decline the capture (no echo), exactly like the historical single-statement shapes declined non-capturable values.

member.summary: Issue #1069 / #1506: resolves a dotted type clause (Outer.Entry, Outer.Middle.Inner, Outer[int32].Inner) to a user-defined nested type declared in the current compilation, by walking the enclosing-type chain. Each segment after the first must name a type whose enclosing type is the symbol resolved for the preceding segment. Type arguments may appear on any segment (issue #1506): the deepest segment's arguments construct the returned closed generic, and every earlier (outer) generic segment's arguments are bound and validated against that segment's definition. member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.Binder.TypeParameterForwardsUserDeclaredConstraints(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeParameterSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeParameterSymbol,System.String@)

member.param: The type parameter written as the type argument.
The definition's type parameter at that position.
The unforwarded constraint's description, when the answer is no.

member.remarks: Two different walks, and the difference is load-bearing. A TYPE bound is implied by anything the argument is provably an instance of, so it is asked of the argument AND of every bound in its chain — that is what makes [T DisposableOptions] forward [TOptions IDisposable] when DisposableOptions implements it, the false rejection #4037's review caught in the imported twin. A SPECIAL constraint (struct / class / new() / unmanaged) is a property of the PARAMETER's own declaration and is asked only of the type parameters in the chain: a class bound with a public parameterless constructor does NOT give the parameter new(), and accepting it there would be a false accept the CLR then refuses. Indeterminate accepts. A bound that still mentions a type parameter has no closed answer here and is skipped, and so is a dependent bound (TypeParameterBound) — the #4031/#4041 shape. A wrong "no" is a GS0580 on a legal program, which is strictly worse than the defect being fixed.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BlittableDetector.IsBlittableValueStructPointee(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: ADR-0122 §4 / issue #1034. Returns true when is a legal unmanaged-pointer pointee that is a blittable user/value struct (e.g. *Point). A pointer to a struct is legal only when the struct is a value type (not a class) and every field is itself blittable — mirroring C#'s "unmanaged type" rule. Blittable formatted classes are deliberately excluded because a pointer-to-class would point at a managed reference, which is not a raw unmanaged pointer target.
member.returns: true when the type is a blittable value-type struct.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BlittableDetector.IsUnmanaged(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #1336. Returns true when is an unmanaged type — bit-for-bit representable with no GC-tracked references. This is a strict superset of : bool, char and decimal are unmanaged (they satisfy C#'s where T : unmanaged and are valid sizeof operands) even though they are not blittable for P/Invoke marshalling. Enums, pointers, and value structs whose fields are recursively unmanaged also qualify; managed reference types and structs containing a managed field do not.
member.param: The bound type symbol to classify.
member.returns: true when unmanaged.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundBinaryOperator.IsReferenceEqualityOperand(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #2188: true when participates in reference equality — a reference type (in nullable or non-nullable form) or a reference-constrained type parameter. A nullable wrapper is unwrapped first; the underlying is reference-comparable when it is an interface, a delegate / function / sequence reference, a user class, a reference-constrained type parameter ([T class …] or a class-base constraint), or any CLR-backed non-value, non-pointer type (e.g. object, string, imported classes/interfaces). Value types, unconstrained and struct-constrained type parameters (whose T? erases to Nullable<T>) are excluded.
member.returns: true when the type participates in reference equality.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundBinaryOperator.IsStringOrNullableString(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #1927: true when is string, string? or — ADR-0186 §6, issue #4324 — string!. The platform arm is not a new rule but the absence of a carve-out: §6 says T! participates in every existing construct, and the concatenation arm's whole justification ("a null operand is treated as an empty string by String.Concat") is a statement about the runtime value, which a string! shares with a string? by construction. Answering false here made string! + "x" report GS0129 in both operand orders, which is an oblivious value being treated as less capable than either string or string? — the one thing §6 rules out.
member.returns: Whether the operand is a string in any of the three states.

member.summary: Gets a field-initializer map's entries in order. The maps are identity-keyed ImmutableDictionary instances, so a pass that numbers temporaries while rewriting each initializer must walk this view instead of the map. member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.CollectExtensionFunctionMatchesFromOtherPackages(System.String,System.String,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #2414: collects every extension-function overload visible from this scope's Parent chain that is stored under a package-qualified key for OTHER than (the caller's own package-qualified key, already tried) and matches . A package-qualified bucket (storage key "{package}#{name}" — see ) is created only when two or more packages declare a same-simple-name extension (see ); before this fallback existed, a package that neither owned the plain bucket nor had its own qualified bucket for that name could never see any other package's colliding overloads, silently breaking the documented "extensions are broadly visible; packages are not import boundaries" contract (e.g. a same-named extension declared by a consuming project's own package shadowed every sibling package's extension of the same name for every OTHER caller).
member.param: The method name at the call site.
The caller's own package-qualified key, already probed by the caller; skipped here.

member.returns: The matching extension overloads from other packages' qualified buckets, or an empty array when none match.

member.summary: Gets the imports declared directly in this scope only — unlike , this does not walk . Used by ) to populate with only the current submission's own imports (issue #2101): that field is later re-seeded, one historical per chained REPL submission, into a fresh per-level by ). Using the walking/cumulative there previously made every submission re-import the ENTIRE flattened history of every prior submission into its own scope layer, which was then itself re-flattened on the next call — an I(k) = sum(I(0..k-1)) recurrence that doubles the import count (and binding time) on every single REPL submission.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.IsDeferringUserGenericConstraintChecks
member.summary: Issues #4089/#4090: whether a G#-declared generic type-clause constraint check must be QUEUED rather than answered where it is written, because same-compilation declarations may not have their type-parameter constraints resolved yet.
member.returns: true while the declaration phase is queuing.
member.remarks: Defaults to false — answer in place — and is set only for the DECLARATION phase's own scope chain, by BindGlobalScope. The default direction is load-bearing: BindProgram derives a FRESH scope chain (CreateParentScope) for member bodies, so a body binder never sees this flag, and a queue it could never flush would silently drop the check. Answering in place is exactly what those binders did before, and by then every constraint is resolved anyway.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.IsNestedDirectlyIn(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #1174: whether is a user aggregate nested directly inside .

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.IsSameDeclarationScope(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Issue #1080 / #2342: two type declarations share a declaration scope — and are therefore a genuine GS0102 duplicate on a simple-name clash — when both are nested directly in the SAME enclosing type, or both are top-level (no enclosing type) AND declared in the SAME package. Two top-level declarations of the same simple name in DIFFERENT packages no longer share a scope: package identity, not one flat compilation-wide table, decides top-level uniqueness. Package identity for the already-stored value prefers a registered alias-declaring-package override at (see ) over the best-effort inference from the value itself; package identity for the incoming prefers the caller- supplied the same way. This is what gives a plain type Name = Target alias a stable declaring-package identity independent of whatever package (if any) its target happens to belong to.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.MangleArity(System.String,System.Int32)
member.summary: Issue #1051: builds the storage key for a type alias keyed by (simple name, generic arity). Arity-0 types keep their plain simple name as the key (so existing simple-name lookups keep working), while generic definitions are suffixed with the CLR backtick-arity convention (e.g. Foo1), letting Foo and Foo[T] coexist.
member.returns: The composite storage key.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.PackageQualifiedName(System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Issue #2342: builds the package-qualified fallback storage-key segment for a top-level type — packageName + "#" + simpleName — used when two top-level declarations share a simple (arity-mangled) name but belong to different packages. '#' cannot appear in a gsharp identifier or in a package name (both are lexed from letter/digit/underscore identifier tokens — optionally dot-joined for a package name — see ), nor in the dotted containing-type-qualified key format produced by , so this key space never collides with either of those.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.Pop
member.summary: Returns the enclosing scope, for a pop that pairs with an earlier scope = new BoundScope(scope) push.
member.returns: The enclosing scope.
member.remarks: Binders push and pop scopes in matched pairs, so a scope being popped always has a parent -- only the root from has none, and nothing pops the root. Stating that once here replaces the twenty identical scope.Parent! suppressions the binders carried, and upgrades the failure mode from a null that propagates into an NRE somewhere later into a GS9998 naming the cause at the pop itself.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.QualifiedTypeName(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #1080: builds the containing-type-qualified dotted name of a type (e.g. Outer.Middle.Inner for a doubly-nested type, or the plain simple name for a top-level type) by walking the enclosing-type chain. Used as the fallback storage key for a nested type whose simple name is already taken by a differently-scoped type, so it remains a distinct stored value without colliding.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.ReceiverConvertibilitySpecificity(System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.FunctionSymbol}.Builder,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #1548: ranks the specificity of a convertible extension receiver among the same-named extension candidates declared in THIS scope. The score is the number of those candidates' declared receiver types that is implicitly convertible to (counting itself). A more-derived receiver converts to more of its siblings' base/interface receivers, so it scores higher and wins on the singular deterministic lookup path (e.g. string beats object for a string receiver).
member.param: The same-scope, same-name extension candidates to rank against.
member.returns: The specificity score (higher is more specific).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.ReceiverConvertible(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #1548: determines whether a CONCRETE declared extension receiver type is applicable for a call-site receiver that is not an exact (identity / same-CLR-type) match, by classifying the implicit convertibility of the call-site receiver TO the declared receiver.
member.param: The static type of the call receiver.
member.returns: true when the call receiver is implicitly convertible to the declared receiver.
member.remarks: Applicability requires an implicit conversion — identity, implicit reference (derived-to-base, class-to-implemented-interface, constructed-generic covariant reference), or boxing (value type to object / an implemented interface) — mirroring C#/Kotlin extension-method receiver semantics. Explicit (narrowing) conversions do NOT qualify, so a genuinely unrelated receiver still fails to bind. The exact/same-CLR fast path is checked by before this method, so this only needs the conversion classification.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.ReceiverMatches(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Determines whether an extension's declared receiver type matches the static type of the call receiver.
member.param: The static type of the call receiver.
member.returns: true when the receiver types match.
member.remarks: Package-owned user struct/class/interface receivers are interned, so reference equality matches them exactly (and must remain the primary check so two distinct user types never collide). Imported/BCL and primitive receivers, however, are not interned: the captured at the extension declaration and the receiver's type symbol at the call site can be distinct ImportedTypeSymbol instances (or symbols materialised through a ) that wrap the same logical CLR type (issue #1103). For those we fall back to an exact structural CLR-type identity comparison via — exact identity, never assignability, so genuinely different types do not match.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.ReceiverMentionsAnyTypeParameter(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeParameterSymbol})

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.SetCurrentDeclaringPackage(System.String)
member.summary: Issue #2342: sets the package name of the top-level (or nested) type or function declaration whose body/initializers are CURRENTLY being bound, so ) can prefer that package's own type over a same-simple-name homonym declared in a different package. Stored at the root of this scope's chain (mirroring ) since one shared instance is used for the whole compilation. Pass null to clear (no ambient package preference — the pre-#2342 behavior). Returns the PREVIOUS value so a caller can restore it once the body finishes binding (nesting-safe: a top-level declaration's nested types/functions always share its own package, so they never need their own inner set/restore).
member.param: The package name to make ambient for lookup, or null to clear it.
member.returns: The previous ambient package name.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundScope.SetCurrentReferencingSyntaxTree(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.SyntaxTree)
member.summary: Issue #2456 (per-file import scoping / #2395 follow-up): sets the syntax tree (file) of the declaration whose type clauses, or member whose body, is CURRENTLY being bound, so ) and all other import-dependent lookup to imports declared in THIS file only — never a sibling file's import. Stored at the root of this scope's chain, exactly like . The value is execution-context-local so concurrent binder operations sharing the same reconstructed scope cannot overwrite one another. Pass null to clear (falls back to the legacy order-dependent "first declared wins" behavior for that lookup, exactly as if this fix did not exist). Two imports whose targets resolve to the SAME are not a collision either — the choice does not matter.
An implicit import is also a FALLBACK for resolution, not a competitor: it contributes a type only when no explicitly written import resolves the name. A namespace the author never asked for must not shadow one they did. member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ChannelRuntimeBinder.HasAuthorWrittenCancellation(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundImportedCallExpression)
member.summary: ADR-0174 D4/D7: distinguishes a facade call the BINDER lowered from a channel operator (<-ch, ch <- v, a channel range, a select arm) from one the AUTHOR wrote by name.
member.param: A facade call, already matched by .
member.returns: true when the trailing cancellation argument was written by the author rather than supplied by the binder.
member.remarks:
Every lowered operation is bound with a cancellation the binder itself supplied — the uncancellable default token when no lexical scope encloses it, or that scope's Context when one does — precisely so the suspension pass can later park it on the ambient context via . A call written out as ChannelOps.Receive2(ch, token) has already chosen its cancellation, so there is nothing for that pass to retarget: it is an ordinary blocking call to a public library method.
That distinction is load-bearing for the COLORING. Marking the caller suspending prepends a hidden Context parameter and retypes the return as ValueTask — an ABI change — which is the point for a channel operator but is pure cost for a written facade call, whose body the pass leaves untouched. It also breaks callers that reflect over the signature: an xUnit [Fact] that drains a channel through the facade is rejected at discovery as "not allowed to have parameters" (#3501, migrated test/Extensions.Tests).

member.summary: Resolves a goto/conditional-goto's target label to the basic block that declares it, or when the label is not declared anywhere in the region this graph was built over.
member.param: The label-to-block map for this region.
member.returns: The declaring block, or if the label escapes the region.
member.remarks: Issue #2360: several analyses (, ) build a fresh, narrowly scoped over just one nested compound statement's body — a try/catch/finally block, a select case, a scope, or a fixed body — because the outer graph treats those as single opaque statements (issue #1642). A goto lexically inside such a region can legitimately target a label declared outside it: the async lowering pipeline's generalized try/finally-with-return funnel ('s RewriteReturnStatement/WrapWithMethodExitEpilogue) rewrites a return inside a protected region into exactly this shape — a goto to a synthesized exit label placed after the whole enclosing statement, i.e. outside the try body's own region. The same applies to a user break/continue lowered to a goto past a loop that encloses (but is not entirely inside) the region. Such a label is, from the narrow region's point of view, indistinguishable from any other exit out of the region — exactly like a return or throw, which already connect straight to (see the switch above). Routing an unresolved label to keeps every synthesized branch target meaningful to the analysis (the region-scoped liveness/assignment fixpoint folds in whatever is live/assigned past the region, via each analyzer's own liveOutOfRegion/isFunctionBody plumbing) instead of throwing and crashing the compiler (GS9998) the moment a by-ref-like local or an out parameter happens to make either analyzer examine the region.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ControlFlowGraph.StatementDefinitelyReturns(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundStatement)
member.summary: Structurally determines whether a bound statement definitely returns (or throws) on the fall-through path — without constructing a sub control-flow graph. This is deliberately conservative: escaping jumps such as continue/break/goto (which the lowerer emits as goto statements targeting labels outside the statement) are treated as NOT returning. Building an isolated CFG for such a statement would fail because those jump targets are not present in the isolated graph (issue #1596 follow-up: fixes a crash on continue/break inside a switch arm nested in a loop).
member.returns: Whether the statement definitely returns or throws.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ControlFlowGraph.SwitchAlwaysReturns(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundPatternSwitchStatement)

Such a switch never falls off its end and therefore acts as a control-flow terminator for definite-return analysis (issue #1596). A switch without a default arm can fall through (the discriminant may match no arm) and is never treated as definitely-returning.
member.returns: Whether the switch definitely returns on every path.

The CLR-backed side's generic arguments are normalized through so a BCL primitive (e.g. System.Int32) and the corresponding G# alias (e.g. int32) resolve to the SAME . Requires at least one side to be symbolic so genuinely CLR-backed comparisons keep flowing through the existing (variance-aware) rules.

A same-compilation user type used as a CLR generic argument has a null ClrType and erases to object on the closed shape, so a purely CLR-based comparison spuriously fails for otherwise identical instantiations (e.g. the declared variable type Channel[BufferEntry] vs. a factory method's return type).

member.summary: Issue #2354 follow-up: true when and denote the exact same (possibly self-referential, possibly open-generic) G# type, even though they may be two non-reference-equal instances. This normalizes the asymmetry between an OPEN generic definition (whose is empty by construction — e.g. the type used for a generic class's own this parameter) and the SAME type spelled out explicitly with its own type parameters as arguments (e.g. a member signature written Box[T] inside class Box[T], which binds through ). Both must share the same , and every type-argument slot (defaulting an open definition's missing arguments to its own ) must itself convert as identity — recursing through so a nested self-reference (e.g. Wrapper[Box[T]]) also unwinds correctly.

The governing rule is a single line — a check is inserted exactly when a platform value flows into a destination whose declared type is a non-null reference type — and every row below is its expansion. Stating it over the DESTINATION's nullability rather than over the literal type T is what makes the upcast rows (T! -> object, T! -> BaseClass, T! -> IFace) check rather than silently storing a nil into a slot the program may read back as non-null indefinitely.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.Conversion.DerivesFromConstructed(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.StructSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.StructSymbol)
member.summary:
Issue #1248: determines whether a (possibly constructed generic) class implicitly upcasts to a constructed generic base class by walking the inheritance chain while substituting type arguments at each level.
A base-type reference is declared in terms of the derived class's OWN type parameters (e.g. TransformBase[TIn, TOut] : FilterBase[TIn]), and a constructed instance keeps that base reference unsubstituted ( is the open definition's base). A naive reference-equality walk therefore compares FilterBase[TIn] against the target FilterBase[int32] and fails. This walk threads a substitution map mapping each class's declaration type parameters onto the concrete type arguments seen at the most-derived level, composing the map down every hop, so the base reference is fully substituted before the comparison. Handles multi-level chains (concrete leaf → generic mid → generic base), type-parameter renaming, and partial type-parameter flow (only some of the derived's parameters reaching the base). A wrong type argument or an unrelated definition still fails (GS0155).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.Conversion.IsCovariantArrayUpcast(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #3685: reports whether a one-dimensional array/slice pair forms a CLR-covariant reference UPCAST — the source element is a reference type that converts to the target element by an implicit reference conversion ([]DirectoryInfo → []FileSystemInfo).
member.returns: true for a covariant one-dimensional array upcast.
member.remarks: G# slices stay INVARIANT for IMPLICIT conversions (issue #2516): an unannounced covariant assignment is the classic hazard, and no implicit branch consults this predicate. But the runtime representation of []T is exactly a CLR T[] (ADR-0016), which the CLR already treats as a B[] for any base B of T, so the conversion cannot fail — it is a no-op reference upcast. Requiring it to be SPELLED (cast[[]FileSystemInfo](dirs)) keeps the hazard visible at the use site while giving migrated C# (whose array covariance is implicit) a faithful, identity-preserving target — the alternative, a projecting copy, would silently change reference identity.

member.remarks:
The sibling of , which recognises the concrete CLASS. Only the five interfaces Dictionary<K, V> actually implements over its OWN key and value participate, each matched element-wise by the same comparison the class arm uses. sequence[KeyValuePair[K, V]] is included because it is the alias spelling of IEnumerable<KeyValuePair<K, V>> (ADR-0040), not a separate rule.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.Conversion.TryClassifyPlatformTypeArgumentMismatch(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.Conversion@)
member.summary: ADR-0186 §3 rule 3: C[T!], C[T] and C[T?] are three distinct constructed types, and exactly one implicit conversion exists between them — C[T!] -> C[T?], recursively for nested arguments. Why a dedicated arm rather than a tweak to the equivalence helpers. Every existing comparison this pair would otherwise reach answers a question about RUNTIME shape, and for that question string! and string genuinely are one type: PlatformTypeSymbol relays its underlying's ClrType, AreRuntimeEquivalentIgnoringReferenceNullability strips the wrapper on purpose, and AreTypeArgumentsEquivalent compares CLR types by name. Teaching each of them about the wrapper would be wrong (they would then disagree with the emitter, which erases it) and is the per-site-predicate shape ADR-0186 removes. The conversion question is a different question, so it gets its own answer, once. Scope. This arm is inert unless a PlatformTypeSymbol appears somewhere in one of the two types, which — while --nullability=platform-types is off — is never. In particular it deliberately does not touch C[T] ↔ C[T?], which ADR-0186 §3 rule 4 leaves "unchanged by this ADR". (Measured on this baseline that pair converts freely in both directions, for imported and G#-declared generics alike, because the annotation strip at the top of discards inner nullability before any conversion rule runs. That is a real pre-existing aliasing hole of exactly the shape ADR-0186 §3 describes — and the ADR's assertion that "plain invariance has always and correctly rejected" it does not hold for this compiler — but closing it is a change to T?'s own semantics, which this ADR puts explicitly out of scope.)
member.param: The source type, before the annotation strip.
The target type, before the annotation strip.
The decided conversion when this arm owns the pair.
member.returns: true when this arm decides the pair.

The array arms deliberately go through rather than reconstructing the element from the CLR type, because that accessor is the same one an element READ uses. It is what makes obliviousArray()[0] come back as string!, and this comparison has to agree with it: the whole question rule 3 asks is whether a read through the destination view would produce an unchecked non-null element, so the two must not derive the element type by different routes. (GetTypeArgumentSymbol is the GENERIC accessor and answers TypeSymbol.Error for an array — using it here is how the first attempt at this arm silently compared nothing.)

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.Conversion.TryGetImportedGenericShape(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,System.String@,System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol}@)

member.remarks: The same two-step recovery performs: prefer the retained symbolic TypeArguments (the only place an open K survives — the is the ADR-0004 type-ERASED shape), and fall back to reading the closed CLR arguments when a metadata-recovered symbol carries none.

member.summary: The corresponding argument positions of two types, when the two are the same constructed shape, with their reference nullability intact. Both sides are taken together on purpose. The question ADR-0186 §3 rule 3 asks is not "what are this type's arguments" but "are these two the same container, and if so which positions correspond" — and answering it one type at a time is what made the first version of this arm miss every magic collection. A slice, a fixed array, a rectangular array and a map are containers with element positions exactly as a constructed generic is, but none of them carries or , so the per-type helper declined for all four and the pair fell through to an equivalence arm that answered identity. The measured consequence: an oblivious string[] holding a null assigned into a bare []string compiled with no check at all — strictly worse than the status quo, where the same program is rejected outright. Requiring the same kind on both sides, not merely the same CLR type, is load-bearing: []T and [N]T are both backed by T[] (issue #3962), so a CLR comparison alone would treat [3]string! and []string as one container. A pair this cannot compare is declined, never rejected. That is the difference between the caller that decides a whole conversion — which must leave []string! -> object and []string! -> IEnumerable[string] to the ordinary upcast arms — and the nested walk, which has already established that the two types are the same shape before it recurses. Scope is deliberately the four invariant, mutable container kinds plus constructed generics. sequence[T], asyncSequence[T] and chan[T] are omitted: their element positions are read-only or direction-typed, so §3's write-direction soundness argument does not apply to them and applying it anyway would reject legitimate covariant conversions.
member.returns: true when the two are the same constructed shape.

The two per-argument predicates above assume their container has already been matched — asked about the containers themselves they have no shape guard, so an ordinary upcast such as []string! -> object, whose two sides have no corresponding argument positions to compare, comes back Illegal. This entry declines for such a pair, and for a function shape, a value-type container and a pair whose platform-ness already agrees; it answers only for rule 3's three illegal directions and rule 2's one permitted widening. (every reference type is nullable at the CLR level regardless of G#'s own annotation). member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ConversionClassifier.AcceptsNilAnnotatedArgument(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ParameterSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #3907: true when is annotated @AllowNull and is the nullable spelling of the parameter's own — i.e. the argument is precisely the nil-carrying input the annotation declares the parameter accepts.
member.param: The target parameter, or null when not binding a call argument.
member.returns: true when the argument is accepted as-is.
member.remarks: Two properties make this safe, and both are load-bearing. It is annotation-only. The parameter's own declared type is never widened. Widening it would make a value-type T emit a Nullable signature slot where T is expected — wrong IL that ILVerify does not catch, because the metadata is internally consistent and simply describes a different method. Keeping the slot at T also preserves the asymmetry the attribute exists for: reads of the parameter inside the body still see a non-nullable T and still need the author's !!. It never reshapes the emitted call. The relaxation is gated on being false, so the source nullable is one whose runtime representation is identical to its underlying (ADR-0001 §Phase 3.C.1: for a reference type or an unconstrained type parameter, T? relays T's ClrType and the IL value is the same reference either way). A value-type nullable — int32? into an @AllowNull int32 slot — really is Nullable on the stack, is rejected by C# too, and stays rejected here. The underlying must also be IDENTICAL to the target rather than merely convertible to it, so this admits exactly T? at a T slot and no other shape; the argument is returned unchanged, with no synthesized conversion node.

Issue #3932: the newobj analogue of and . A constructor has no receiver, so neither of those helpers can fire and a CLR ctor parameter declared as the declaring generic's own slot (ValueTask<T>(!0)) stayed at the type-erased closed shape — object — for the whole argument-conversion pass. The argument was then classified as a boxing conversion, so gsc emitted box !!T in front of a newobj whose parent TypeSpec is the correctly symbolic ValueTask1<!!T> — invalid IL that ILVerify reports as [found ref 'T'][expected value 'T']. The equivalent method call (List[T].Add(v)) has always emitted the raw T, so this is a ctor-only hole in machinery gsc already had.
Mapping the OPEN constructor's parameter type through the construction's symbolic type arguments recovers the real slot. Bare type parameters are accepted here (unlike the #765 receiver gate, which deliberately skips them and leaves that case to #1540's helper) because for a ctor there is no second pass to fall back to.

The condition is exactly "a same-compilation type appears somewhere in this type" — at the top level (where ClrType is already null and the symbolic path was always taken) or at any structural position inside a constructed generic, a slice, an array or a nilable, where the surrogate hides behind a perfectly real closed ClrType.

member.summary:
Issue #910 / ADR-0110 / issue #1069: binds the BODIES of the nested type declarations declared in a class or struct body, reusing the type-name shells declared earlier by (phase 1). Splitting shell declaration from body binding lets a sibling member signature (a field/property/parameter/return type, a generic argument, an array element type, …) forward-reference any nested type by simple name, for every nested kind (class/struct/data struct/ interface/enum). Nested enums are fully bound in the shell phase (their members reference no user types) and need no body pass here. Nested-in-nested declarations are handled recursively because the per-kind body binders bind their own nested types.
All nested kinds inside either encloser (class or struct) are emitted as real CLR nested types. The emitter materialises every enclosing TypeDef row before its nested rows (ECMA-335 §II.22.32) via a unified pre-order emission pass (ADR-0110), so no kind/encloser combination needs to be deferred.

Walking the chain closest-first lets a deeper base's type arguments (which are expressed in terms of a shallower base's type parameters) resolve transitively, so a multi-level chain such as Leaf : Mid[int32] : Base[T] maps Base.T -> int32. The resulting map is consumed by ) so an override whose concrete signature mentions the substituted types is matched against the base member's un-substituted (open) signature. member.summary: Issue #2362: builds the substitution map from a constructed generic interface's OWN type parameters (declared on iface.Definition) to 's type arguments, for comparing an interface property's declared (open) type against an implementer's concrete type via ). member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.DeclarationBinder.CanSerializeAttributeTypeOperand(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #4095: returns true when a typeof operand names a type the custom-attribute blob can describe, so an operand whose identity still depends on an in-scope type parameter is rejected as a non-constant argument (GS0202) rather than approximated.
member.returns: true when the operand can be serialized.
member.remarks:
Once the serializer writes the ENCLOSING argument vector of a nested type, an operand such as Outer[T].Inner inside a generic declaration would serialize the type parameter itself, and no such name resolves. Before #4095 the same operand silently took the CLR path and wrote the ERASED close, which is a different closed type from the one the source names — a wrong answer rather than a rejected one.
An UNBOUND generic DEFINITION stays legal and is admitted before the type-parameter test runs: typeof(Box[_]) and typeof(Outer[_].Inner) denote the open definition, which ECMA-335 II.23.3 describes and reflection reifies. Their type parameters are the definition's own, not an argument borrowed from an enclosing scope.
Nothing else is filtered here. Every shape the serializer already described before #4095 — a slice, an array, a nilable, a construction over a same-compilation type — keeps the path it had, which is what the Issue4073GenericAttributeTypeArgumentTests rows pin.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.DeclarationBinder.CheckPendingCovariantPropertyOverrides

A narrowing keeps its overridden-property link, from which the emitter gives the getter a new slot bound to the base getter by a MethodImpl (#4508); anything else has no CLR override form, loses the link, and reports GS0185.

member.returns: The enclosing type parameters, outermost-first.

Every other caller keeps the exact comparison. The scope is thread-static and counted, so it follows the recursion and nests safely.

member.returns: true when the signatures conform.

The function carries no body and is never emitted; its sole purpose is to expose as the enclosing type (via ) so that treats a private/protected member of the enclosing type reached through a type-qualified receiver (Type.Member) or a constructor call (Type()) as accessible — matching how a shared function body already behaves.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.DeclarationBinder.DeclareNestedTypeShells(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.StructDeclarationSyntax,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.PackageSymbol)
member.summary:
Issue #1069 (phase 1): declares the type-name shells of the nested types declared in and records the enclosing type on each via SetContainingType, BEFORE any member body of the enclosing type is bound. This makes every nested type resolvable by simple name from within the enclosing type (and as a CLR nested type by qualified name from outside) regardless of declaration order, mirroring the two-phase scheme used for top-level types (#973).
struct/class/data struct: a shell is declared (fields/base bound later) and its own nested
shells are declared recursively.
enum: fully bound now — enum members reference no user types, so there is nothing to defer.
interface: a shell is declared; its method signatures are bound later by
.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.DeclarationBinder.DeclareStructShell(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.StructDeclarationSyntax,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.PackageSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #973 (phase 1): declares the struct/class type-name shell and registers it in scope BEFORE any member body is bound, so that field, parameter, and base-clause types may forward-reference a user type declared later in the same compilation (e.g. a class whose field type is a struct declared further down). The returned shell has empty and ; those — along with the base clause and all members — are bound and installed later by .

Issue #4183: queues a parameter's default-value expression for deferred binding instead of calling immediately. Called from every site that used to bind a default value inline during the per-struct declaration-body pass (primary-constructor parameters, instance/static method parameters, explicit constructor parameters) — see for the full rationale and the ordering constraint the drain () must respect.
member.param: The parameter syntax carrying the default clause.
The bound parameter symbol to attach the default to.
The type declaring the parameter's owning member; supplies the accessibility context and enclosing/own type parameters the default-value expression may reference (e.g. default(T)).
The package the declaration belongs to.

The owning method's OWN generic type parameters (empty for a non-generic method, a primary constructor, or an explicit constructor), so a default value may reference them (e.g. func M[U](x U = default(U))).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.DeclarationBinder.DerivesFromSystemAttributeDuringDeclaration(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.StructSymbol,System.Collections.Generic.HashSet{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.StructSymbol})
member.summary: Issue #4143 code review: a side-effect-free stand-in for IsAttributeType, safe to call DURING declaration binding (from BindStructBaseAndInterfaces / BindConstructorDeclarations), where a same-compilation base may not have had its own body bound yet.
member.param: Cycle guard across the recursive walk.
member.returns: true when the symbol is or derives from .
member.remarks:
IsAttributeType falls back to bindTypeClause when a base's flags are not yet set — correct for its own USE-site caller, which runs once every declaration already exists. Calling THAT fallback during declaration binding re-resolves a base clause that is either still being bound or belongs to an unrelated, non-attribute class, and for a GENERIC base (an open type parameter in scope elsewhere, not yet visible from here) it reported a spurious "Type '...' doesn't exist" — measured: regressed Issue1244GenericAbstractOverrideBinderTests.
This walks the same shapes using only side-effect-free lookups: the already-computed flags first, then — only when a same-compilation base is a SIMPLE (non-generic, unqualified) name — the @Attribute sugar marker or a literal : Attribute / : System.Attribute spelling on the base's own declaration syntax, and ) (silent on a miss, unlike bindTypeClause) to recurse one level further when the base names another same-compilation type.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.DeclarationBinder.DetectClassInheritanceCycles(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.StructSymbol})
member.summary: Issue #973: detects transitive base-class inheritance cycles among the supplied class symbols and reports a diagnostic for each one. Before the two-phase declaration split (#973) a base clause could only resolve a type declared earlier in source, so a mutual cycle such as class B : C / class C : B was implicitly rejected because the forward reference failed to resolve. Now that all type-name shells are declared before any base clause is bound — which is exactly what makes legitimate forward references work — the cycle resolves cleanly and must be caught here, after every base class is installed via . Each has at most one user base class, so the base relation forms a functional graph; this walks every node's chain and, on finding a back-edge into the current path, reports the cycle and clears the offending base link so the later base-chain walks in and the emitter do not loop forever. Direct self-inheritance (class A : A) never reaches here because it is rejected — and its base left unset — in the base-clause loop.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.DeclarationBinder.ExpandStructInterfaceClosures
member.summary: Issue #1006: once interface base clauses have been bound, expand each implementer's interface set to include the transitive closure of base interfaces. A class C : B where interface B : A must implement (and metadata-declare) both B and A, matching C#. Base CLR interfaces of user interfaces are folded into the implementer's CLR interface set so dispatch through them works too.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.DeclarationBinder.InferAnonymousClassLiteralReturnType(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.FunctionDeclarationSyntax,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.Accessibility)
member.summary:
ADR-0146 (Kotlin visibility narrowing follow-up, issue #2243): when a function/method's return-type clause is omitted and its (parser-desugared) body is exactly return <anonymous-class-literal> — the func F() -> object { ... } shape recognized by Parser.IsAnonymousClassLiteralStartAfterArrow — the return type must be inferred from the literal instead of defaulting to void:
Local/private/internal declarations retain the actual synthesized anonymous type (full
custom-member access), mirroring a let/var binding of the same literal.
Public/protected declarations — a public API boundary — narrow the exposed type to the literal's
declared supertype (object : Type { ... }) or, absent one, to the universal top type object (), exactly like Kotlin's anonymous-object visibility rule. Every other omitted-return-type declaration (any shape other than a bare arrow-returned anonymous-class literal) is left untouched and still resolves to void.

Constructed generic types are not interned ( and can yield fresh instances), so a raw reference comparison wrongly rejects, for example, the class method func Iter() IEnumerator[T] against the interface requirement ISeq[T].Iter() IEnumerator[T] once the interface's type parameters have been substituted with the implementing type's arguments. Reference identity is honoured first (covering plain type parameters, primitives and cached imported types); constructed generics are then compared by definition and ordered type arguments, recursing through slice / array / nullable wrappers. Issue #3093 also projects sequence[T] and async sequence[T] onto their matching CLR enumerable interface shapes. The comparison stays strict — distinct type arguments (e.g. IEnumerator[int32] vs IEnumerator[T]) are not equated — so genuinely mismatched signatures are still rejected with GS0187.

ADR-0192: semantic half of the partial-method consistency check. PartialMethodMerger compares the two parts as source text and then keeps only the implementing part's signature, which is what gets bound (, , ). Identical text is not proof of an identical signature: each part binds against its own file's imports, so a name can be unresolved in the declaring file, or resolve to a different type there. This binds the declaring part's own type-parameter constraints, return type, parameter types, parameter attributes, and default values in the declaring file and compares them with the implementing part's, reporting GS0611 on the first difference (Copilot review rounds 7, 10 and 12).
Type clauses bind in their own file through bindTypeClause, which redirects import lookup to the clause's own tree ("Issue #3336"); attributes and deferred defaults do the same by their syntax's tree. Each comparison is skipped when binding the declaring side already reported an error — that error names the problem more precisely than a follow-on GS0611. The declaring side goes through the same post-processing as the implementing side (async return wrapping, variadic widening), or every async or variadic pair would compare unequal.

member.summary:
Issue #3879 (ADR-0060 amendment): validates the ref return modifier on a property or indexer declaration and yields the resulting ref-kind. This is the property-side counterpart of , and deliberately does NOT share its rule set — a property has no async/iterator form to reject, and it has two rules of its own.
The by-ref return is restricted to the COMPUTED, read-only forms:
the getter must have a body, because a by-ref return has to name the storage it aliases. An
auto-property's getter copies out of a compiler-synthesized backing field, so ref would alias the field — which is either a lie (the caller thinks it is writing to the property) or a hazard: #3878's GS0219 sweep found the auto-property backing-field path is exactly where by-ref problems concentrate. A bodiless { get } — an abstract slot or an interface requirement — is rejected for the same reason plus a second: nothing in this declaration says what is aliased.
there must be no set / init accessor, because the returned reference already IS the write
path. C# spells this same rule CS8147.
member.param: The bound property name, used in the diagnostics.
Whether a get accessor with a block body is present.
The set / init accessor, or null when the property is read-only.
member.returns: when the declaration is a well-formed by-ref property, otherwise .

Runs the forward "must be assigned" fixpoint over the CFG of (wrapping it in a synthetic block first if it isn't already one), seeded with . When is true, every path reaching the region's end is an actual function exit and is checked against (mirrors the original top-level check). Otherwise, internal returns are checked here because they leave the function from a point the outer CFG never sees (issue #1642), throw paths terminate without requiring assignment, and normal fall-through paths are merged and returned. Returns null when the region never completes normally. The region only reads its initial assignment set.
