Reporting happens only in the final diagnostics pass, once every declaration in the function has populated the tracked set.

The definitely-assigned sets after evaluates to true and to false, starting from . Mirrors C# §9.4.4: for A && B the right operand runs in the when-true state of the left, and the whole is false when either was (intersection); dually for ||; ! swaps.

The predecessor's exit state along : the polarity-specific set when the predecessor ends in a conditional goto (the CFG builder attaches the goto's own condition object to the true edge and a negation of it to the false edge), the plain exit otherwise.
The fixed body always runs (no branching), so its assignments flow through unconditionally once its synthetic pinned and pointer locals are seeded as assigned.

A pattern switch, unlike select, can complete having matched no arm at all when there's no exhaustive default — that "nothing matched" path must also be in the meet (it contributes the untouched incoming set).

try/catch/finally semantics (mirrors C# definite assignment):
Each catch clause is analyzed as if entered at the very top of the try statement — an exception
can occur before any try-body statement runs — so catch bodies never see try-body assignments.
An assignment made only in the try body (with no matching unconditional assignment in every catch)
is NOT guaranteed after the statement, because an exception could have skipped it.
An assignment in finally IS guaranteed, because finally always runs before control can
continue past the try statement.

Walks a basic block linearly, updating in place. When is non-null, reports GS0239/GS0238/GS0522 at every detected violation (including ones nested inside try/select/scope/fixed bodies). Returns the exit set.

Intentionally narrow — no aliasing through arithmetic, field access, or indirection chains — and not merged across CFG joins (best-effort, shared per function rather than tracked per-path); this only needs to catch the common straight-line var p = &v; *p = expr pattern.

Issue #3887: the single chokepoint every member access, method call, index and null-conditional step routes through. When the receiver's type is ALREADY , the lookup below cannot succeed and will report GS0158 Cannot find member / GS0159 Cannot find function naming a member that usually exists on the type the user actually meant. The receiver can only be error-typed downstream of an expression that was already diagnosed, so those two reports are provably redundant with that first diagnostic — and they dominate triage: one bad argument was measured producing sixteen of them, all naming reflection surface, on a wall with no reflection defect in it.
The suppression deliberately keys off the receiver's TYPE rather than its node kind. The binder already short-circuited on a node, but node identity is exactly what a binding loses: once the poison flows through a local (let loaded = broken()) the receiver is an ordinary variable reference that merely HAS the error type. Keying off the type makes the suppression survive inference.
The lookup still RUNS and the diagnostic is still ADDED to the bag — only its visibility changes. Suppression here must alter which diagnostics are emitted and never what binds; see for the two narrower-looking designs that violate that and the session tests that caught each of them.

member.summary:
Issue #503 follow-up: binds the right-hand side of an event subscription against the event's declared handler delegate type. This is the unified entry point for both user-event and CLR-event subscriptions, so method-group conversions (src.Changed += this.OnHit, src.Changed += OnHit) are resolved consistently against the event delegate's Invoke signature.
The helper first inspects the syntactic form of the handler:
A bare that names an instance
method on the implicit this is bound as an instance method group captured against this.
An whose left part
evaluates to a user-defined class and whose right part names an instance method on that class is bound as an instance method group captured against the bound receiver. If neither pattern matches, the handler is bound through BindExpression as usual.
Once bound, a method-group handler is routed through BindConversion with the event's declared delegate type so the resolved overload, target delegate, and (for instance groups) captured receiver are all known by the time the emitter runs.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.BindIfLetExpression(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.IfLetExpressionSyntax,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,System.Boolean)
member.summary: ADR-0151: binds if let a = e [, let b = e2]* [&& guard] { value } else { value }.
member.remarks:
The lowered shape for if let a = e0, let b = e1 && g { T } else { F } is shown below.({ let a = e0 } → a != nil ? ({ let b = e1 } → b != nil ? g : false) : false) ? T : F
Each initializer therefore sits inside the arm that is only reached once every earlier binding matched, which is what gives ADR-0151's left-to-right short-circuit both under the interpreter (a evaluates only the selected arm) and under IL emit (it branches). A && chain could NOT be used for the same purpose: Evaluator.EvaluateBinaryExpression evaluates both operands of a logical operator before combining them.
The then/else branches each appear exactly ONCE in the produced tree. Reusing a single bound-node instance in two positions would alias the emitter's identity-keyed slot dictionaries (see SlotDictionaryAliasingAssertionTests), so the nesting is put in the CONDITION rather than duplicating the arms per binding.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.BindNullCoalescingAssignmentExpression(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.NullCoalescingAssignmentExpressionSyntax)
member.summary:
Issue #4967: binds target ??= value in value position. The value is the target's final value: the value read when it was not nil, otherwise the stored value. The lowering is the compound-assignment shape, a of the receiver and index captures overread ?? { let <ncaVal> = value; write(<ncaVal>); <ncaVal> }
so the target is read once, the right-hand side runs only when that read is nil, and the ?? operator table types the result: T when the stored value is known non-nil, otherwise T?. A throwing right-hand side is the fallback itself (read ?? throw E).

The right-hand side is bound against the target's T?, so the author can write either an underlying-typed value (which lifts via the implicit T -> T? conversion) or another nullable value. Statement position () and value position () differ only in whether the lowering yields a value.

The lowered statement and its captures are anchored to the statement, a rebuilt target read to the target and the write to the ??= expression, so the semantic model resolves each syntax node.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.BindValuelessBlockExpression(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.BlockExpressionSyntax,System.Boolean)
member.summary:
Issue #4965 / #4966 (ADR-0202): binds a block expression that has no trailing value. Two cases need no value, and they are the only ones:
The block's end is unreachable — it ends in return, throw,
rethrow, break, continue or goto (see ). Its type is then the bottom type never, exactly like a throw expression's, so it unifies with any sibling branch, arm or target type. Its never-produced value is an unreachable throw nil trap after the exiting statement, which every later stage already understands as a throw expression.
The block is in a position whose value is discarded
(: an expression statement, a void arrow body, a lambda body), where it is a void block, as the equivalent block statement is.
Anything else still reports GS0277.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.BindWithPatternVariables(System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.LocalVariableSymbol},System.Func{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression})
member.summary: ADR-0166: binds with declared in a fresh child scope — the region in which those pattern variables are definitely assigned.

Issue #1547: builds a smart-cast-narrowed read from a bare (declared-type) read and its narrowed static type. For a nullable value type (e.g. int32? = System.Nullable) narrowed to its underlying type, the storage slot/field holds a Nullable while the narrowed static type is the bare T. A plain narrowed load would leave a Nullable on the stack where T is expected, which fails ilverify. Instead we wrap the bare read in a synthesized !! (), reusing the proven value-type unwrap emit path (spill → Nullable::get_Value). The nil-guard already proved the value non-nil, so the assertion can never throw at runtime. For a nullable reference type the narrowed type and its storage share the CLR representation, so narrowing is a metadata no-op and the bare narrowed read is produced unchanged (wrapping in !! would add a pointless runtime null-check).
member.param: A read of the declared (un-narrowed) type.
The narrowed static type, or null.
Factory building the narrowed read node for the reference-nullable (metadata no-op) case.
member.returns: The narrowed read (possibly a value-type unwrap).
member.remarks: Issue #4943: this is the single place that builds a narrowed read. Call binding (OverloadResolver.BuildCalleeLoad) uses it too, because a narrowed (unmanaged[CC] () -> R)? callee is a value-type Nullable<nint> whose storage must be unwrapped before calli; the emitter rejects a narrowed node that skips it.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.BuildObjectArgumentArray(System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression})
member.summary: Wraps the bound hole values in an object[] creation, boxing value types via an explicit conversion to object so the emitter produces verifiable IL (ADR-0055 — no Convert.ToString mis-typing).

Issue #1638: the shared post-overload-resolution CLR call-argument construction pipeline — RebindFormattableInterpolationArguments → ApplyInterpolatedStringHandlers → (delegate rebind) → BindClrParameterConversions — used by every resolved CLR call dispatch (ctor, static, instance, inherited-instance, extension). Centralising the sequence keeps a fix applied once (e.g. a step re-ordering or a missing step) from drifting out of sync across the five call sites.
argumentSyntax is the call's source argument syntax list, used to detect interpolated-string arguments; it does NOT include a slot for a synthesised receiver. delegateRebindMode selects which delegate-argument rebind step runs; see . receiverType is passed to the delegate-rebind step's symbolic-target lookup. Issue #1512/#1320: conversionReceiverType is the receiver type passed to instead — the instance-call path deliberately feeds the delegate rebind the enumerable-normalized receiver type while feeding the parameter-conversion pass the raw (un-normalized) receiver type, so this can differ from receiverType; defaults to it via hasConversionReceiverTypeOverride when not overridden. receiverArgCount is the number of leading argument/parameter slots reserved for a synthesised receiver (0 for plain calls, 1 for imported extension calls).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.CanAccessInternalsOf(System.Type)

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.CanBindClrInstanceMember(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression)
member.summary: Returns whether CLR instance lookup may continue through a receiver: the receiver has a loadable and its type is not a — that is, nobody has stated it T?. A receiver that IS stated nullable, whether a source-declared T?, an annotated-nullable imported member (e.InnerException) or a generic member substituted with a nullable type argument (Box[string?].Value), must be narrowed, asserted (!!) or read through ?. first. This predicate never sees a : both callers run PlatformCoercion.InsertCheck on the receiver first (the read path through CheckPlatformReceiver, the write path explicitly in BindMemberFieldAssignmentExpression), which inserts ADR-0186 §4's nil check and unwraps T! to its underlying T. That coercion, not this test, answers an oblivious receiver's safety question. Issue #4356. This test used to carry a second disjunct, || receiver is BoundClrPropertyAccessExpression, which let lookup continue through ANY nullable receiver that happened to be an imported field or property read. It was added (#2459) for oblivious members, which ADR-0136 imported as T?; ADR-0186's T! now handles those. But it tested the kind of bound node rather than where the nullability came from, so it also waved through stated-nullable chains with no narrowing and no nil check. ADR-0186 step 4 kept it only because cs2gs output depended on it; #4356 fixed cs2gs and deleted it, along with its twin in .

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.CheckPlatformReceiver(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation)
member.summary: ADR-0186 §4 and §5, in one move: replaces a platform-typed receiver with the checked, unwrapped value before member binding runs. §4. The ADR's revised §4 is explicit that instance-member receivers get the check like every other coercion. The earlier draft's receiver exemption — "the CLR checks a callvirt receiver anyway" — was falsified by enumerating the emitter's opcode selection: receiverIsClass is is StructSymbol {IsClass: true} and receiverIsInterface is is InterfaceSymbol, so a wrapped receiver type, string, Array, non-virtual event accessors and method-group capture all emit call — or ldftn, which does not dereference the receiver at all and lets the nil travel into a delegate's Target slot and arbitrarily far from the site that produced it. The exemption may be re-derived once #4312/#4313 unify that opcode selection onto a single "is this a reference at runtime" predicate; until then it would make the design's safety depend on an emit property four known paths violate. §5. Because the replacement expression's type is platform.UnderlyingType — the same symbol the reader built, not one re-minted from ClrType — member lookup, overload resolution and extension resolution run against T by construction. A receiver's platform-ness is therefore not an input to member selection and cannot select a different member (§5a), and the symbolic or generic-substituted projection the underlying carries survives intact, so the result type is the one a T receiver would get (§5b). That is the whole mechanism: nothing downstream needs a PlatformTypeSymbol arm, which is exactly the point — the closed switch in MemberLookup.GetImportedTypeSymbol would otherwise fall through to the erased answer at each of its call sites and turn Queue[Entry]!.Dequeue() from Entry into a CLR erasure. Guarded accesses are deliberately NOT routed here: ?. and ?[ unwrap their own receiver on the branch where it is already known non-nil, so no coercion to non-null occurs and §4 inserts nothing.
member.param: The bound receiver, possibly null for a static access.
The access site, for the check's message.
member.returns: The checked receiver, or the original when it is not platform-typed.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.ClassifyConditionalNarrowing(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression)
member.summary:
Issue #4964: computes the smart-cast narrowing frames that a conditional's condition implies for each branch. The if-expression (if c { a } else { b }) and the conditional operator (c ? a : b) are two spellings of one value form, and both bind their branches under these frames, so the two cannot narrow differently. The if let expression's guard shares these frames (ADR-0201).
Issue #2640 introduced the frames for the if-expression: a top-level nil guard (x != nil, x == nil, nullable value types included), merged with the type-test and short-circuit frames of ClassifyTypeTestNarrowing (x is T, !, &&, ||).
member.returns: The frame for the branch taken when the condition is true, and the frame for the branch taken when it is false. Either may be nil when that branch narrows nothing.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.ClassifySubmissionGlobalWriteReceiver(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression)
member.summary: Issue #3185: classifies a member-write receiver against the submission-global chain rules. Walks CLR member-access links from the receiver down to the chain root; only a chain that bottoms out at an addressable submission static field classifies as anything but . Crossing a reference-typed link makes the remaining chain heap-rooted (writable regardless of the root's read-only flag); crossing a computed (property) link makes an in-place write impossible. Issue #3252 / issue #3292: a value-typed ELEMENT link classifies by its storage — an array-backed element (ps[0] over an array or slice) has a real address (ldelema) and is , while a map/indexer element (m[k] — the getter returns a copy) is , matching the GS0499 rejection the identical same-cell shape reports.
member.returns: The chain classification.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.CollectBaseClrMethodCandidates(System.Type,System.String)
member.summary: Issue #1260: collects the candidate inherited CLR instance methods named that are reachable for a base.M(...) call against . Unlike the ordinary inherited-CLR lookup (public only), a base call may target a protected virtual member (e.g. System.IO.Stream.Dispose(bool)), so this includes non-public methods but excludes members a derived type cannot legally call via base (private, and other-assembly internal).

member.returns: The deduplicated candidate methods (most-derived signature wins).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.CollectDelegateTargetCandidateParameterLists(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ImportedClassSymbol,System.String)
member.summary: Issue #908: collects the parameter lists of the CLR methods a member-style call could resolve to — static methods of the accessed class, or instance methods on the receiver plus imported extension methods — so an arrow lambda argument can be target-typed from its matching delegate parameter before binding. Extension-method parameter lists have their leading this receiver parameter stripped so every returned list aligns at a zero parameter offset, matching the positional argument indices.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.CollectErasureSurrogates(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #4006: the CLR types 's own erased elements present as.
member.returns: The erasure surrogates, always including object.
member.remarks:
object is always in the set: it is what an in-scope type parameter and a same-compilation struct/interface/delegate erase to, and it is the only surrogate #3989 knew about. A same-compilation CLASS erases to its IMPORTED BASE instead (MemberLookup.TryProjectErasedClrType), which is how a map[string, Derived] reached a genuine Dictionary<string, ImportedBase> parameter by identity with no object in sight.
In practice the set is exactly { object } ∪ { the imported base of each same-compilation CLASS in the argument }: an in-scope type parameter, a same-compilation struct, interface or named delegate all erase to object, which is already present. A same-compilation ENUM is deliberately EXCLUDED: it erases to int, and treating every nested int position as suspect is both far too broad and unnecessary — a List[MyEnum] at a List<int> parameter is already refused by MemberLookup.ExcludeErasureOnlyEnumCandidates, which drops those candidates before applicability runs.
Deriving it from the ARGUMENT rather than from a fixed list is what keeps the suspicion as narrow as the erasure that caused it: a parameter mentioning an imported type this argument did not erase into is untouched.
Suspicion is not a verdict. A []Derived trips this test at an ImportedBase[] parameter just as a map[string, Derived] does at a Dictionary<string, ImportedBase> one — and keeps binding, because CLR arrays are COVARIANT and Conversion.Classify therefore finds a real conversion to emit. Invariance is what makes the map case unsound, not the erasure.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.ComputeBestCommonType(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol})
member.summary: Computes the best common type (least-upper-bound) across the supplied arm types. Candidates are enumerated from the most-derived "anchor" arm type — itself, then its base-class chain, then its implemented interfaces, then object — and the first candidate to which every arm is implicitly convertible is returned. Returns null when no common type can be found.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.ComputeClrCandidateWorstConversionRank(System.Reflection.MethodInfo,System.Type[])

Returns when the arities do not line up positionally (the candidate matched in an expanded / named / defaulted form this cheap check cannot reason about, so the tie-break is skipped and the instance method keeps winning).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.ComputeConditionalCommonType(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary:
ADR-0062: chooses a common result type for two conditional branches using the following ordered rules (mirroring the ADR §2 common-type procedure):
Identity (Tx == Ty).
One-way implicit conversion (Tx → Ty but not Ty → Tx, or vice versa).
Both convertible implicitly — pick the wider via the numeric tie-break rule (ADR-0037) when both
are numeric; otherwise no common type.
nil compatibility — when one arm is the nil/null sentinel and the other is reference- or
nullable-compatible, use the other arm's type. Returns null when no common type exists.
member.returns: The chosen common type, or null.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.ComputeConditionalResultType(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary:
Issue #1158: computes the conditional/if-expression result type using the same target-typing + best-common-type machinery as switch-expressions, in the following priority order (first non-null wins):
Target-typing — when an explicit, valid target type is supplied and BOTH arms implicitly convert
to it (C# 9+ target-typed conditional).
The existing pairwise (identity, never/null lift, one-way
implicit, ADR-0037 numeric tie-break).
Best-common-type (least-upper-bound) across the two arms — unifies sibling subtypes to their
shared base/interface. Returns null only when none of the three yield a type, so the caller reports GS0263.
member.param: The optional target type (C#-style target-typing), or null.
member.returns: The chosen result type, or null.

member.summary: ADR-0055 Tier 4 (#369): builds the per-argument flags consumed by , marking each positional argument whose syntax is an interpolated-string literal. These arguments may convert to an IFormattable/FormattableString parameter in addition to their natural string type. Returns null when no argument qualifies so callers pay nothing on the common path.

member.summary: Issue #1112: computes the switch-expression result type. When a target type is available (C#-style target-typing from an enclosing typed local, function return type, or argument context) and every arm is implicitly convertible to it, the target type is used. Otherwise the best common type (least-upper-bound) across the arm types is computed by walking the base-class chain and implemented interfaces, falling back to object. member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.FilterCandidatesByDeferredLambdaShape(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Reflection.MethodInfo},System.Int32,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.CallExpressionSyntax,System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Int32})
member.summary:
Issue #3659: narrows a deferred arrow-lambda probe's candidate set to the overloads whose deferred-lambda parameters can actually receive a lambda, i.e. are delegate-shaped (or Expression<TDelegate>-wrapped) with exactly the lambda's parameter count. Without this, an overload set whose other members take a non-delegate in the same slot (e.g. List[T].Sort(IComparer[T]) alongside List[T].Sort(Comparison[T])) probes as ambiguous — the deferred slot is passed as null, which is applicable to everything — so the lambda never receives a target type and binds untargeted (GS0304), which in turn fails the whole call (GS0159).
This is only a narrowing of the best-effort target-type probe; the call is re-resolved for real once every argument is bound. The filter declines (returning unchanged) whenever a candidate's slot shape cannot be determined — a bare generic-parameter slot, a non-lambda deferred argument, or a metadata load failure — so no existing overload-resolution behaviour is loosened.
member.returns: The narrowed candidates, or when no narrowing applies.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.HasOnlyClrFaithfulSymbolicArguments(System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol})
member.summary:
Issue #4024 (review finding 4): returns true when every retained symbolic type argument nonetheless has a FAITHFUL closed CLR type, so MakeGenericType over the projected arguments yields the real constructed type and members bound off it are correct.
Retention has two quite different causes, and only one of them invalidates the closed CLR shape. An argument with no CLR type of its own — an in-scope type parameter, or a same-compilation user type still being built — is projected onto the object SURROGATE, so a literal bound off Box<object> would read every member as object; those must still bail. An argument that is merely NON-INJECTIVE — a slice or fixed array (both backed by the one SZ-array T[], #3962/#4024) or a named tuple (backed by the unnamed ValueTuple, ADR-0172) — has a real closed CLR type; the symbolic vector records identity the CLR cannot express, beside a shape that is perfectly usable.
member.returns: true when every argument has a faithful closed CLR type.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.IsApplicableIgnoringReferenceNullability(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #3992: whether would be applicable at the imported parameter once the deliberate CLR-boundary leniency about a REFERENCE annotation is applied — i.e. whether the argument's non-nullable form is applicable.
member.returns: true when only a reference annotation stood in the way.
member.remarks:
Applicability ALREADY ignores the annotation on the CLR path: NullableTypeSymbol.ClrType relays its underlying, so a chan[int32]? argument is presented to ClrOverloadResolution as Chan<int> and reaches a Channel[int32] parameter by ordinary CLR assignability, exactly as a string? reaches a string parameter. Only the ADR-0148 SYMBOLIC fallback — the callback above, which exists because CLR surrogates cannot see a G# argument's structural shape — re-asked the question on the still-annotated symbol, and so re-introduced an annotation the rest of the boundary had already dropped.
That mattered only where no CLR relation links the two shapes, which is precisely the ADR-0174 D2 channel view: no base class or interface links Chan<T> to ChannelWriter<T>, so a NON-GENERIC Plain.W(ChannelWriter[int32]) was ranked only here. The annotation-dropping conversion the boundary then applies is classified EXPLICIT on purpose (that is what keeps a G#-DECLARED chan[int32] parameter reporting GS0154), and this callback asked for an IMPLICIT one — so the candidate was dropped before the conversion was ever reached, and Plain.W(c) reported GS0159 for a chan[int32]? while binding for a chan[int32]. The generic half of the same asymmetry was fixed by #3995's ChannelViewAppliesAtErasedGenericSlot, which never sees the annotation because it works on erased CLR shapes — which is why #3992 was narrowed to the non-generic parameter rather than closed.
Scope is deliberately narrow. Only a REFERENCE nullable is peeled, so a value-type Nullable<T> keeps its own lifted rules (#3673); StructuralProjectionPlanner.CanProject is NOT re-asked; and nothing becomes applicable whose non-nullable form was not already applicable. BindClrParameterConversions passes allowExplicit: true for CLR arguments, so the conversion this admits is one that call path was always willing to perform, and the leniency stays confined to CLR boundaries.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.IsNamespacePrefixSegment(System.String,System.Boolean)
member.summary:
Whether is a pure namespace/package prefix component. Import aliases prevent peeling unless they target source packages. Leading segments also exclude values, predefined type aliases, and type parameters. Check import aliases before canonical lookup because namespace targets do not name types. Later components use the complete prefix through . A simple name from another package must not stop the qualified lookup. Namespace aliases use source lookup to avoid recursive namespace resolution. Source ambiguity does not exclude an independently resolved CLR receiver. Exact lookup retains the complete prefix when binding the source type.
The in-scope-value check is restricted to the leading segment because it is what distinguishes a genuine value-access chain (e.g. myOahu.Foo.Ctor(), where myOahu really is a value) from a namespace-qualified construction. Once a segment has already been accepted as a namespace-prefix component (i.e. peeling is past the first segment), the chain can no longer be reinterpreted as a value-access chain — there is no value at its head to access .member on — so a later segment coincidentally sharing a name with an unrelated in-scope value (e.g. a field or const declared on the enclosing type, see issue #2419) is not a genuine alternate interpretation and must not stop peeling.
member.param: Whether is the first segment being peeled from the chain (as opposed to a later, already-committed continuation).
member.returns: Whether the segment is a pure namespace/package prefix.

Anywhere else — other methods, after construction, on another instance, or from a derived type's constructor against a base-declared field — the assignment remains a GS0127 error. Static read-only fields keep their existing behavior (assignable only via their initializer, since G# exposes no user-writable static constructor body).

The direct check is needed on its own: a method group with a single, unambiguous candidate is substituted with its natural earlier, while the vector is first built (TryGetSymbolicUserMethodGroupType, before the resolved method — and therefore the refined vector — exists), so RefineSymbolicArgsForMethodGroups sees an already-recovered slot and has nothing left to refine; only an OVERLOADED group (whose arity disambiguation needs the resolved candidate) is ever caught by its own tracking. Every method-group argument needs the same downstream demotion in BuildSymbolicMethodTypeArgs regardless of which of the two steps produced its natural type.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.NilTolerantHandlerTarget(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary:
Issue #3775: e += h / e -= h where h is nil is a silent no-op in C# — add_E forwards to ), which returns the other operand unchanged — so an EventHandler? handler is a legal subscription argument, not a conversion error. Binding the handler against the event's bare (non-nilable) delegate type rejected exactly that shape with GS0155, which is the same defect class as the unguarded using cleanup fixed in #3787: a position where the lowering assumes non-nil while C# defines nil-tolerant behaviour. Here the divergence surfaces at bind time rather than at run time, because the only way to spell the subscription was a !! that throws.
The relaxation is scoped to the subscription argument alone: it widens the conversion target to T? only when the handler expression is already nilable (or the literal nil) and the delegate type's CLR representation is a managed reference. A method group, a lambda, and a non-nilable handler are all unaffected, and nothing about the event's own declared type changes — the backing delegate stays exactly as nilable as it always was.
member.returns: The conversion target for the handler.

member.summary:
Issue #3712: refines a pre-resolution symbolic argument vector once the winning CLR overload is known, replacing each user method-group slot that carries no symbolic function type with the symbolic function type of the candidate whose arity matches the target delegate parameter. The erased CLR vector resolves such a group's return type to object when the return type is a same-compilation user type; without this refinement the generic method is emitted closed over object and the assembly fails IL verification with StackUnexpected.
Issue #3712 follow-up (instance calls): the slot is refined for a SINGLE-candidate group too. A single-candidate group only acquires a natural type when that type is expressible in CLR terms, so a group returning a same-compilation user class reaches this vector as exactly like an overloaded one. The guard below keeps every slot that already carries symbolic information untouched.
member.param: The winning (possibly closed generic) CLR method.
The bound user arguments, in source order.
The pre-resolution symbolic vector, receiver-first when is 1.
Number of leading receiver slots in .
Whether trailing arguments target a params-array element.
Optional resolved source-slot to parameter-position mapping.
member.returns: The refined vector, or when nothing changed.

member.summary: Issue #4133 (hot-core translation guard finding): overload that also reports which slots were refined from a bare method group, so a caller feeding the result into MemberLookup.BuildSymbolicMethodTypeArgs can mark those slots' contribution as method-group-sourced. C#'s own method-type-inference (§12.6.3.7) never makes an INPUT inference from a method group — only an OUTPUT inference from its (eventually resolved) return type, after the other type variables are already fixed. Feeding a method group's own PARAMETER types back in as an ordinary delegate-shaped argument (exactly what this refinement does, for good reason elsewhere — see the type-recovery comment above) lets UnifyForMethodTypeArgs's existing lambda-parameter unification (Issue #1334) treat that parameter type as a genuine contravariant upper bound it is not: Where(pred) over IEnumerable[Item] with pred(x Item?) bool then "raises" TSource from the receiver's true Item to Item?, matching #4133's own mechanism for a case it was never meant to cover.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.ReifiedReceiverClrType(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary:
Follow-up to issue #891: partial-inference fallback for . For each candidate generic method, infers the type parameters reachable from the non-lambda argument CLR types and resolves the closed parameter types of every deferred lambda's delegate (arity-matched to the lambda), even when the delegate's return type remains an un-inferred method type parameter. Builds a per-slot target that carries only the closed parameter types. Candidates must agree on the resulting parameter types; otherwise the fallback declines (preserving the existing GS0304 behaviour) to avoid binding against an ambiguous shape.
Issue #3551: resolves the receiver's REIFIED closed CLR shape for deferred-lambda parameter inference. The cached of a symbolic imported generic can carry an erased or stale closed shape (e.g. IGrouping<string, ValueTuple<string, int>> for the symbolic IGrouping[string?, (string, int32?)], the tuple's Nullable element lost), and a lambda rebound against a target inferred from that shape disagrees with the receiver everywhere else, failing resolution (GS0159). Returns null when no better shape exists.
member.returns: The reified closed CLR type, or null.

through a receiver of that class (this.E += h), as in C#; the event is returned for ordinary binding;

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.SliceResultType(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression,System.Type,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #3907: the static type of a range slice (src[a..b]) over an imported slice shape.
member.param: The slice member's reflected result type.
The slice member's result type, read through the funnel.
member.returns: The slice expression's static type.
member.remarks:
The slice member is discovered by reflecting on the receiver's , and issue #658 erases a type argument that has no CLR representation while binding — so inside class Holder[T] a Span[T] receiver reflects as Span<object> and Slice reports that as its return type. Taking the reflected answer verbatim threw the symbolic T away: destination[1..] produced a Span[object] that no longer converted back into the Span[T] slot it was sliced from.
Every slice shape in the BCL — Span<T>, ReadOnlySpan<T>, Memory<T>, ReadOnlyMemory<T>, string — yields the RECEIVER'S OWN type, so when the reflected result is identical to the receiver's CLR type the symbolic answer is just the receiver's symbolic type, which still carries T. Deliberately guarded on that identity: a slice member returning anything else keeps the reflected answer unchanged, and a receiver whose type argument is already concrete (Span[int32]) gets back the same symbol it had before.

member.summary:
Issue #3880: the indexer-then-invoke reading of X.Member[i](args), attempted only after the generic-method reading the parser committed to has already failed and the member itself turned out not to be callable.
Deliberately narrow. The bracketed item must be a bare identifier — the only shape that is genuinely ambiguous, because anything a type clause can spell but an index expression cannot (T?, []T, List[T], a qualified name) is unambiguously a type argument, and anything an index expression can spell but a type clause cannot (All[0](), All["k"]()) never reached the generic reading in the first place. The index bind is speculative: its diagnostics are rolled back on failure so a genuine "no such generic method" still reports the generic-reading diagnostic the caller would have produced.

Fields are never virtually dispatched, so unlike the method/property base-call paths this needs no non-virtual distinction at emission time: it produces the exact same that an ordinary inherited-CLR-field read already does (see ) — the only "base" semantics needed is resolving the field starting from (the nearest base type) rather than the most-derived receiver type, matching C#'s base.Field shadowing semantics.

member.remarks:
Unlike a binary operator, a compound-assignment operator is an INSTANCE, void-returning method that mutates the receiver in place — the same shape C# 14 uses, so the two languages consume each other's declarations. It is therefore never rewritten to target = target op value; the resolved call IS the assignment.
Resolution is attempted BEFORE the built-in / binary-operator path so a type that declares both operator + and operator += gets the in-place form for +=, matching C#. When the type declares no compound operator this returns null and the caller falls back to the ordinary lhs = lhs op rhs rewrite.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.TryGetUnboundGenericArity(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.TypeClauseSyntax,System.Int32@)
member.summary:
Issue #1989: an unbound-generic typeof(...) target with an EXPLICIT requested arity, spelled with _ placeholder type arguments (G#'s analogue of C#'s comma-count Name<> / Name<,> unbound-generic syntax, since G# generics use Name[T1, T2] brackets rather than angle brackets). Returns true with set to the argument count only when every type argument is a bare _ (no qualifier, nested type arguments, array shape, or nullable suffix) — any real type argument is an ordinary bound generic and is left to .
Issue #2012 (N1): _ is an ordinary identifier in G#'s grammar (it is only special-cased in pattern/discard positions, never reserved as a type-name token), so user code CAN legally declare a real type literally named _ (class _ {}, type _ = ..., or a type parameter named _). If such a type is in scope, treating every _ type argument as the unbound-generic placeholder would silently ignore it and flip Func[_] from "bound to the real type _" to "unbound Func1" — a genuine (if contrived) silent semantic change. So a real type named _ in scope always wins: this method only claims the placeholder reading when no such type is resolvable, deferring to (cref:bindTypeClause) otherwise.

member.summary: Issue #1507: builds the receiver type used to drive DEFERRED untyped arrow-lambda inference over a slice ([]T) or array ([N]T) receiver. Such a receiver's is null for a same-compilation user element (and an array CLR type otherwise), so the extension-method probe in — which is gated on a non-null receiver ClrType — is never reached and the element type is never recovered to target-type the untyped lambda parameter. Normalize to a symbolic constructed IEnumerable[elementType] carrying the element type as a symbolic argument (mirroring the List[T] / sequence[T] shapes), so the LINQ extension Where<TSource>(IEnumerable<TSource>, Func<TSource,bool>) (and every other delegate-taking extension) matches and TSource is recovered as the element type. The constructed ClrType uses the element's erased CLR projection, so a same-compilation user element ([]Item) closes to IEnumerable<object> with the symbolic [Item] argument (the symbolic recovery path re-derives Item), while a primitive/BCL element ([]int32, []string) closes to the concrete IEnumerable<int> / IEnumerable<string> so the CLR inference path recovers the real element type instead of erasing it to object. This mirrors the List[T] behaviour exactly. The IEnumerable<> open definition and closed shape are resolved through the compilation's reference set () so the constructed OpenDefinition is reference-identical to the extension methods' this IEnumerable<TSource> parameter — the symbolic unifier (UnifyForMethodTypeArgs) matches the open definition by reference, which would otherwise fail whenever the reference set is projected through a (its IEnumerable<> is not the runtime typeof). The bound call keeps the original slice/array receiver expression; the emitter already normalizes slice/array receivers to their enumerable surface, so emission is unaffected. Returns false when no normalization applies.
member.param: The normalized symbolic IEnumerable[T] receiver type, on success.
member.returns: true when a normalized receiver type was produced.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.TryNormalizeSymbolicEnumerableReceiver(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol@)
member.summary:
Issue #1320: a sequence[T] / asyncsequence[T] (iterator return types, aliases for IEnumerable<T> / IAsyncEnumerable<T>) or a user-element array receiver over a same-compilation user element type has a null during binding (the element type is not yet emitted). That null ClrType caused instance-method lookup (e.g. GetEnumerator) to dead-end with GS0159, even though the same call resolves on an explicitly-typed IEnumerable[T] parameter (whose ClrType type-erases to IEnumerable<object>) and on a primitive-element sequence[int32] / array. Normalize such a receiver to the equivalent type-erased shape so the shared CLR member-lookup + symbolic return-type recovery path resolves it uniformly:
sequence[T] → a constructed over IEnumerable<> with the symbolic
[T] argument (so the generic GetEnumerator() → IEnumerator[T] overload and its element-typed return are recovered, exactly as for an IEnumerable[T] parameter).
asyncsequence[T] → the IAsyncEnumerable<> counterpart.
user-element array / slice → a plain over the erased array CLR type
(e.g. object[]), reaching parity with a primitive-element array (which finds the non-generic GetEnumerator()).
issue #3311: open map[K, V] (null ClrType) → the symbolic constructed Dictionary[K, V] view,
so the CLR-interop member surface (ContainsKey, TryGetValue, GetEnumerator, …) resolves exactly as on an explicit Dictionary[K, V] receiver. The bound call keeps the original receiver expression; the emitter already normalizes sequence/array receivers (TryNormalizeToSymbolicContainer), so emission is unaffected. Returns false when no normalization applies.
member.param: The normalized receiver type, on success.
member.returns: true when a normalized receiver type was produced.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionBinder.TryNumericTieBreak(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: ADR-0037-style numeric tie-break: when both arms are numeric primitives, pick the wider canonical type using a simple rank. Returns null when either type isn't a recognised primitive.

Issue #2193: overload-resolution tie-break that merges the user-defined extension-function candidate set for (receiver type, name) into a resolved CLR/imported instance-method call and prefers the extension when it is a strictly better match. The defect: a same-named BCL instance method can be applicable to a call only through a lossy delegate-reshaping conversion — e.g. a G# function value (T) -> TResult discarding its result to satisfy the named void delegate parameter of SynchronizationContext.Send(SendOrPostCallback, object). Because the CLR-instance path commits as soon as it resolves, the user extension Send[T, TResult]((T) -> TResult, T) TResult — an exact match — never competed, so the call bound to the void member (GS0124 / GS0151). The fix is deliberately conservative so it does not disturb normal instance-method resolution: the extension is only preferred when (a) the resolved instance method's worst argument conversion is a delegate-reshaping conversion (rank ≥ ), and (b) some applicable user extension matches the same arguments with a strictly better worst-case conversion. An instance method that matches by identity / standard implicit conversion always wins, so a genuine member that is the better match is never shadowed.

member.summary:
Issue #3745: rewrites, IN PLACE, every argument slot holding a user-declared class that erased to System.Object so it carries the implemented imported interface instead. An imported generic method whose type parameter occurs solely inside an interface-typed parameter — e.g. MethodDefinition.DecodeSignature<TType, TGenericContext>( ISignatureTypeProvider<TType, TGenericContext>, TGenericContext) called with a G#-declared NameSignatureProvider : ISignatureTypeProvider[string, object] — gets no bound at all from an object argument, so inference fails and the call reports GS0159 Cannot find function.
This runs ONLY after resolution with the erased shapes has already failed. The object ride-through is load-bearing on its own — it is what makes a parameter whose type is an erased type parameter applicable (issue #2840's Do(ctx T, …) on an imported Jobb[T]) — so a caller must restore the original vector when the retry does not resolve.
member.param: The bound arguments, positionally aligned with .
The CLR argument-type vector, rewritten in place.
member.returns: true when at least one slot was rewritten.

member.summary:
Issue #1423: projects a user-declared class to the implemented CLR interface best suited to drive extension-method receiver matching and generic inference. Prefers an implemented interface that is, or extends, IEnumerable<T> (so LINQ-style extensions whose this self-parameter is IEnumerable<TSource> bind and infer TSource), choosing the most-derived such interface so any methods declared on the richer interface remain reachable. Falls back to the first implemented CLR interface so non-collection extensions can still match an interface receiver.
Issue #3745: the same projection is reused for ORDINARY arguments by , but only after overload resolution has already failed with the erased shapes.
member.param: The user-declared class receiver or argument.
The projected CLR interface type, on success.
member.returns: true when an implemented CLR interface was found.

member.summary: Issue #4287: whether an imported CLR instance method, already selected against a receiver's underlying type, is being called on a receiver somebody STATED is a nilable reference (T?). If so, reports GS0159 ("receiver may be nil"), the same diagnostic a G#-declared method gets on that receiver. This is the call-path twin of CanBindClrInstanceMember, which rejects a stated T? for member reads and writes (#4356/#4390) but was never consulted for calls. The receiver's ClrType is the underlying type's, so without this test this.name.ToUpper() on a string? bound directly and threw a bare NullReferenceException on nil. It runs after selection, so it changes which calls are accepted and never which member is chosen. A name that no instance method matches still falls through to the extension paths, where an extension declared over the nilable type is legal. A value-type T? is not affected: its members live on Nullable itself and are safe to call on nil. A platform T! never reaches here as a ; ADR-0186 §4's attributed check handles it.
member.param: The receiver's syntax, when the caller has it.
The receiver text's start, when it differs from the syntax's.
member.returns: true when GS0159 was reported.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ExpressionTreeRestrictionValidator.ValidateReceiver(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag)
member.summary: ADR-0186 §4: validates a RECEIVER, eliding the platform nil check the binder inserted on it. §4 says the inserted check is redundant where the runtime's own check fires, and names that as a reason to elide it: "The CLR's own check on a callvirt/ldfld receiver makes the inserted check redundant where it fires, which is a reason to elide it as an optimization." Inside an expression-tree lambda gsc emits no IL at all — the access becomes Expression.Property/Field/a call node — and System.Linq.Expressions dereferences the instance when the tree is evaluated, throwing NullReferenceException at exactly the same point. The failure is preserved; only G#'s message is lost. This is the narrow half of a change Copilot review on the flip PR was right to push back on. Removing the rejection wholesale would drop checks §4 genuinely requires — an argument, a store, a return, or a lambda result inside the tree has nothing dereferencing it, and those still report GS0473. What forced the question is that rejecting receivers is a build break on ordinary code: any oblivious reference member touched inside a LINQ-to-IQueryable lambda inserts a receiver check, so .Where(b -> b.Conversion.AccountId == id) stopped compiling the moment the default flipped (Issue2661ExpressionTreeNullablePipelineTests). It is also not a regression: under ADR-0136 that receiver is T?, cs2gs writes an explicit !!, and the same lowering erases it. "The tree dereferences it" is measured, not assumed. Review objected that Expression.Call on a non-virtual method may emit call, which does not reject a null this, so a member that never touches its receiver could complete on a nil — losing the failure entirely rather than merely its message. That is exactly the enumeration ADR-0186 §4 demands (its own receiver exemption was falsified by one), so it was run rather than argued. A compiled tree over a sealed class, through both a field receiver and a property receiver, into both an auto-property and a getter that provably never reads this: shaperesult property receiver → auto-propertyNullReferenceException property receiver → this-free getterNullReferenceException field receiver → auto-propertyNullReferenceException field receiver → this-free getterNullReferenceException All four throw: System.Linq.Expressions' compiler emits the dereferencing form for instance member access regardless of virtuality, exactly as csc does and for the same reason. The objection is well-posed and empirically false for Expression.Compile(); for an IQueryable provider that never compiles the tree, the receiver has no runtime existence at all and no check could be meaningful either way. Adr0186PlatformTypeBindingTests.Section4_AnElidedReceiverCheck_Still_Throws_When_TheTreeRuns keeps that a live assertion rather than a comment. The residual — a receiver failing with the runtime's unattributed message instead of G#'s — is tracked as #4352.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.KnownAttributes.HasAllowNull(System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundAttribute})
member.summary: Returns true when carries (issue #3907).
member.param: The attribute list on a parameter symbol.
member.returns: true when at least one [AllowNull] is present.
member.remarks:
[AllowNull] is the .NET-standard "this INPUT accepts null even though its type is not nullable" annotation. It is the one nullability contract G# cannot spell in a type, because ADR-0155 gives a declaration a single nullability (Kotlin-style) while C# gives it separate input and output contracts. cs2gs widens a REFERENCE-typed [AllowNull] declaration to T? (issue #3694) — the two contracts then agree — but an UNCONSTRAINED type parameter has no such widening, so [AllowNull] T value translates verbatim to @AllowNull value T and only the annotation carries the contract.
Consumed by ConversionClassifier to relax the ARGUMENT conversion at a call site — never the parameter's own type, which is exactly the asymmetry the attribute exists to express: reads inside the body still see a non-nullable T and still require the author's !!.

Reuses every piece of 's plumbing — scope, synthetic function, captured-variable analysis, smart-cast narrowing snapshot — but the body is an expression (or a ) rather than a . The return type is inferred from the bound body's type; a body yields a void return. ADR-0076 / issue #716 extends this in three ways: Optional async modifier — when is set, the body is bound under an async synthetic function and the function- type's return slot is widened to Task / Task[T] exactly as a function-literal would. Block-body return-type inference — the placeholder synthetic function is marked , the return statements inside the block bind without a void or declared- return-type check, and a post-bind pass computes the common type and applies a single conversion to each return expression. Target-typed parameter inference — when is non-null, an omitted parameter type clause is filled in from the corresponding slot of the target. With no target type, a missing parameter type is reported as GS0304.

member.summary:
Issue #4223 follow-up: a NON-generic, zero-capture, ASYNC local function (let/var/const Name = async func (...) ... {...}, no [T, ...] of its own) whose OWN PARAMETER TYPE references an enclosing method/class type parameter still reports GS0468. Every other enclosing-type-parameter shape #4223 enables — the same local's return type or body, the GENERIC-own-type-parameter local/async case, and the sync route entirely — is unaffected and NOT gated here.
Root cause this narrow gate avoids: this specific shape is emitted through the async "erased delegate" adapter (predates issue #2118, used whenever a function-literal's declared type mentions an open type parameter) rather than through ReflectionMetadataEmitter.RegisterStateMachineEnclosingGenerics's reification, which only ever sees the promoted method's OWN (cloned) type parameters and the state-machine class's remap — neither of which the adapter consults. The adapter's parameter-unboxing conversion has a confirmed defect for a value-typed instantiation: confirmed by direct repro, func Outer[U](seed U) U { let Local = async func (x U) U { return x }; return Local(seed).Result } compiles clean and Outer("hi") succeeds, but Outer(42) throws at the first call. The identical crash reproduces on an already-legal CAPTURING async lambda of the same shape (confirmed on this repository's main, predating #4223 entirely), so the adapter defect itself is pre-existing and unrelated to this issue — but relaxing GS0468 for the ZERO-CAPTURE sibling without this gate would newly route a previously-rejected program (this exact shape was unconditionally GS0468 before #4223) through the same broken adapter, trading a compile-time diagnostic for a runtime crash. The issue's own guidance is explicit: "Relax GS0468 only for routes with proven valid emission." This is not such a route yet; fixing the erased-delegate adapter itself is tracked as a separate, pre-existing defect.
Footprint note: this gate must not reject anything that was legal BEFORE #4223. A zero-capture local nested inside a NON-generic user type (class/struct with no type parameters of its own) routes through ClosureEmitter.SynthesizeClosures's display-class path rather than the top-level hoist the erased-delegate adapter belongs to, and the pre-#4223 gate excluded it for exactly that reason — this deliberately mirrors that exclusion rather than widening it. (That display-class path has its own, separately pre-existing instance of the identical adapter defect — confirmed by direct repro on this repository's main, predating #4223 entirely — but it was never covered by GS0468 either before or after this issue, so gating it here would be a new, out-of-scope rejection of previously-legal code.)
member.param: The text location of the declaring let/var/const identifier.

Issue #2027: snapshots the enclosing frame's goto/label state (, , ) and its , then resets all four to a fresh empty state so a nested function-literal body (a lambda OR a local function — both bind through / ) gets its own isolated goto/label namespace and loop-label stack, matching ADR-0070's "label namespace is local to the enclosing function" rule and C#'s prohibition on cross-frame goto flow. Pair with .
Issue #4285: also recomputes for — the nested body has its own goto/label namespace, so whether IT contains a goto/label is a separate question from whether the ENCLOSING function does, and must be answered fresh for the narrowing-lift guard in to apply correctly while the nested body is bound.
member.param: The nested function-literal or arrow-lambda body being entered.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.LambdaBinder.FilterNarrowingsSurvivingClosureCapture(System.Collections.Generic.List{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.NarrowingFrame})
member.summary: ADR-0069 amendment / issue #2442: computes the subset of the enclosing scope's active narrowing frames that may legally survive into a captured closure body (a lambda or local function literal).
member.param: The enclosing scope's narrowing-frame stack at the point the closure literal is entered (a snapshot copy — not mutated by this method).
member.returns: A new frame stack, parallel in shape to , containing only the entries that are sound to keep visible while binding the closure body.
member.remarks: A narrowing entry keyed on p survives into the closure only when p.Root.IsReadOnly is true AND p is a plain variable path (!p.HasMembers). is the binder's own "can never be reassigned" fact — it is exactly the signal already consults to reject any assignment to the variable (a let local, or a by-value / in function parameter), and it is deliberately false for var locals, ref/out parameters, and let ref/var ref aliasing locals (which bind a managed pointer to possibly-external storage — see StatementBinder.Narrowing.cs's ref-local declaration path, which passes isReadOnly: false unconditionally). Because a read-only binding can never be written again anywhere in its scope, the value a nil-guard or is-test proved at the guard site can never change later — no matter when the closure that captured it eventually runs: immediately and synchronously (Task.Run(() => …)), after the enclosing function returns (an escaping/stored delegate), repeatedly (invoked from inside a loop), concurrently on another thread, or after an await suspension point. This is a strictly stronger guarantee than "not reassigned along this particular flow path": it holds for every path, so no additional temporal/flow proof is required. Member-access paths (x.member) are always dropped even when the root is read-only: the ADR-0069 addendum (issue #1180) already treats member reads as fragile because another call or another receiver's assignment could mutate the member through an alias the closure's own narrowing analysis never observes — the same reasoning ) applies at ordinary statement boundaries. Widening that guarantee to "safe forever, even across a closure capture" would be unsound, so this method conservatively keeps the pre-existing behaviour (drop) for every member-bearing key.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.LambdaBinder.FinalizeNestedFrameLabels
member.summary: Issue #2027: reports GS0469 for any goto in the just-bound nested frame that targets a label never declared inside that SAME frame — the equivalent for a lambda / local-function body. Must run before restores the outer label state, so a nested-frame goto is checked only against the nested frame's own labels (never silently satisfied by an outer label of the same name).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.LambdaBinder.ReconcileGenericLocalFunctionGroupCaptures(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundFunctionLiteralExpression})
member.summary: Issue #4221: re-converges a group of consecutive generic local-function declarations' captured-variable sets after every member's body has been bound once in source order. ) (via ) already folds a callee's captures into its caller when the callee was declared — and therefore bound — earlier in the group. That leaves shapes unhandled by a single in-order pass: a call to a sibling declared LATER in the group (forward reference), a call cycle between two members, and — the reason this also walks into each member's body rather than stopping at its top-level literal — a plain or generic local function declared INSIDE a member's own body that itself calls a sibling. That inner literal's own was fixed the moment it was bound, which can be before the callee's capture set has finished converging; leaving it stale would make the enclosing member's own re-walk below (which folds a nested literal's *cached* CapturedVariables via , without re-descending into it) keep missing the transitive capture forever. All of this is legal now that generic local functions may capture at all (#4252 removed the blanket GS0463 rejection); this widens every reachable literal's captured set to a fixed point by recomputing it, in a loop, against the whole group's current best-known sets, until nothing grows. Termination is guaranteed because a set only ever grows and is bounded by the (finite) set of variables in scope; the reachable-literal count is typically small, so the pass count is bounded to be defensive against a bug in the fixed-point logic itself, not because the algorithm needs it.
member.param: Every member of one consecutive run of let Name[T, ...] = func (...) ... { ... } declarations, in source order, after each one's body has been bound.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.MagicCollectionZeroValue.ClassifyForMarker(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #3329: classifies a struct field's shape into the compact tag recorded by the GSharp.MagicCollectionFields cross-assembly metadata marker (see ). A struct's own — where this zero-value synthesis is normally recorded (see DeclarationBinder.Structs.cs) — is unavailable once the struct is referenced from ANOTHER assembly (or, for the REPL, a LATER submission): only the declaring compilation ever binds the struct's own declaration syntax. The marker plus let a struct literal reconstruct the same sound zero value from the field's own reflected CLR shape. Issue #3330 composition: a struct-typed field is tagged "struct" when — and only when — recursing into ITS fields (via the same same-assembly recursion #3330 added) actually finds a magic-collection zero value somewhere in its closure; a struct field with no such need is left unmarked, exactly like every other unaffected field.
member.returns: The marker tag, or null when the type is not a magic-collection or recursively-magic struct shape.

A sibling struct type referenced as a field's type may not have its OWN Fields populated yet at probe time, so the probe must NOT recurse (that would silently under-report via 's empty-by-default field list) — it only asks "is this field's OWN declared type shaped like it might need a zero value," and defers the real (safe-to-recurse) decision to , called later once every struct's fields are fully bound (see the "actual synthesis" call sites that gate on this candidacy).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.MemberLookup.ExcludeNonGenericByRefCandidates(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{System.Reflection.MethodInfo},System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Boolean},System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.String})
member.summary: Issue #3907: removes imported candidates that could only accept a by-ref argument over a same-compilation user REFERENCE type by erasing it — i.e. whose parameter at such a slot is a by-ref over a type that is not generic in the OPEN definition.
member.param: Per-argument flags marking the symbolic by-ref slots; null disables the filter.
Optional source argument names aligned with the arguments.
member.returns: Candidates that can accept the symbolic by-ref argument without erasing it.
member.remarks:
C# requires a ref argument to match its parameter exactly, and no imported signature can name a class this compilation has not emitted yet, so a generic ref T is the only parameter such an argument can legally reach. Without this filter the non-generic Interlocked.Exchange(ref object?, object?) was an exact IDENTITY match for Interlocked.Exchange(&nodeField, nil) — the #658 erasure made ref Node look like ref object — so it beat Exchange<T>(ref T, T), a candidate csc never even considers.
The filter runs on the OPEN candidates on purpose: once a generic candidate is closed over the erasure its ref T has already become ref object and is indistinguishable from the non-generic overload's. Slots are matched positionally and the filter declines to act when the call site uses named arguments, so it can never drop a candidate whose parameter order it has not actually established.

The bound arguments' symbolic types, in source order.
The per-source-index argument names; null entries are positional.
member.returns: The candidates, less any unreachable widening member.
member.remarks:
#4013 took every abstract interface member off a class's own surface but kept two exemptions at candidate COLLECTION, because the compiler still depended on them: a synthesized collection-initializer Add, and a call whose argument carries a same-compilation type. Those exemptions are what left List[int32]{"x"} compiling and throwing ArgumentException, and Dictionary[string, int32]{"a": "x"} with it. The collection lookup is memoized on (Type, name) and cannot see arguments, so the discrimination happens here, at applicability, on the candidate list the call already has — exactly where the issue says it has to.
Two things keep the member, and both are about the CALL rather than the member:
The RECEIVER carries a same-compilation type, so its own members' parameter types are erasure
surrogates and cannot be trusted to judge anything. List[System.Action[Mode]] is built over the flat System.Object placeholder of the generic-CONSTRUCTION path and presents as List<Action<object>>, while the lambda erases the enum and presents as Action<int>; the type's own Add is inapplicable for a reason that has nothing to do with the author's code (Issue2918InlineLambdaErasedReceiverTests). That is #4016's defect one site over, and until it is repaired there the escape hatch has to stay open here.
The receiver's own surface WOULD have taken this call on the arguments' REAL types. A
same-compilation struct has no CLR type while binding, so a []Celsius spread into a List[float64] erases to object and cannot match Add(double) through its user-defined conversion — but the conversion exists, and asking the conversion classifier on the symbolic types finds it (Issue3096CollectionSpreadEmitTests.UserDefinedSpreadConversions…). The receiver has no erasure of its own in this branch, so its members' CLOSED parameter types ARE their real types and no symbolic re-derivation is needed. Issue #4036: keeping the member is only half the answer — the conversion this branch FINDS must also be APPLIED, or the kept member wins on the erased argument and the call throws. asks this same question a second time and names the parameter type to convert to, so the member stays reachable but stops winning.
What is left over is the reported hole and only it: a genuine string at a genuine int32, or a Celsius at an int32 it does not convert to. Neither is an erasure to repair, so the widening member goes and the call reports GS0159 — the same diagnostic the author-written List[int32]().Add("x") already reports since #4013. A GENERIC interface's member is never a target here: on a constructed class receiver it is closed over the receiver's own type arguments and cannot widen, which is why Dictionary[K, V](){ ...pairs } goes on reaching ICollection<KeyValuePair<K, V>>.Add.
An argument with no bound type at all (an un-inferred lambda, a method group) makes the whole judgement unavailable, so the candidates are returned untouched: this filter never removes on ignorance.

member.summary: Issue #4133: picks the fixed type for one type parameter's non-exact bounds, C# fixing style (§12.6.3.13): the candidate set is the union of BOTH and bounds together, not alone when both are present. A contravariant argument (Action<T>, IComparer<T>, ...) contributes an upper bound that must be able to RAISE the fixed type past a lower bound contributed by an ordinary (covariant/invariant) argument — mirroring csc, which lets Action<object> push a T : DisposableBase lower bound up to object. The prior version of this routine only ever considered ONE category as a candidate SOURCE (the caller picked whenever it was non-empty) and used the other category solely to validate that pick afterwards (), so an upper bound could confirm a narrower answer without ever being allowed to win.

Issue #4036: the conversion-APPLICATION half of what decides. When that filter finds the receiver's own surface would have taken the call only through a user-defined implicit conversion, it KEEPS the widening member on purpose — the erasure is genuine and there is a repair for it. This method names the repair: the parameter type, per argument position, that the argument must be converted to for the receiver's own member to be applicable on real types.
member.param: The collected candidates, in candidate order.
The receiver's CLR type; an interface receiver is exempt.
The bound arguments' symbolic types, in source order.
The per-source-index argument names; null entries are positional.
member.returns: Per SOURCE argument position, the type to convert that argument to, or null to leave it alone; default when no repair applies at all. Source-indexed rather than parameter-indexed so the caller can apply it directly to its own argument list, whatever order the author wrote the arguments in.
member.remarks: The defect. A same-compilation struct has no CLR type while binding, so Celsius presents to overload resolution as object. Against List that is an IDENTITY match for System.Collections.IList.Add(object) and no match at all for Add(double), so the widening member wins every betterness ranking and list.Add(someCelsius) compiled to verifiable IL that threw ArgumentException from inside the BCL. The same erasure made list.Contains(someCelsius) answer False and list.IndexOf(someCelsius) answer -1 without any diagnostic at all, and list.Remove(someCelsius) report GS0124 because IList.Remove is void. Why the spread form was already right. List[float64](){ ...someCelsiusSlice } lowers through ExpressionBinder.BindConvertedCollectionAddCall, which types its item placeholder as the collection's ELEMENT type and converts the item to it BEFORE binding Add — so overload resolution never sees the erased argument and picks List.Add(double). That path is collection-shaped: it knows an element type. An ordinary call has no element type, only a candidate set, so the two cannot share one path. They can agree, and this makes them agree — convert first, then bind. Why this is safe. The gate is ' own, verbatim: no widening member in the candidate set means no repair (an ordinary call already ranks user-defined conversions for itself); an erased RECEIVER means nothing here can judge the call; an argument with no bound type means the judgement is unavailable. On top of that, a position is repaired only when the ordinary conversion does NOT exist and the user-defined one does, and only when the own surface offers exactly ONE distinct parameter-type vector — so List.Add(double) and ICollection.Add(double) count as one answer, and a genuinely ambiguous surface is left alone. List[object] is untouched because Celsius -> object is an ordinary boxing conversion, so no position needs repairing. What it deliberately does not do. It does not remove the widening member — #4028 keeps it here on purpose, and that release note stays literally true. The member is still collected and still applicable; it simply stops WINNING, because the repaired argument is a real double and identity beats boxing.

Issue #4133 (review finding): only the STANDARD implicit conversions (identity, reference, boxing, numeric widening) participate in generic-bound elimination/fixing — mirroring ClrOverloadResolution.IsInferenceBoundPromotion's own comment on the CLR side. also admits ADR-0148 structural projection (constructing a new, unrelated user class through its public constructor/member surface), which is a VALUE conversion, not a type relationship, and must never let one bound "satisfy" another — e.g. two structurally-identical but unrelated classes (a homonym Item imported from two different packages) are not implicitly convertible for inference purposes just because a new instance of one could be projected from the other. Using here keeps that projection available for ordinary argument conversions while refusing to let it decide which upper/lower bound wins.
Issue #4133 (Copilot review finding, hot-core translation guard PR): a PURE reference-nullable-annotation difference is treated as mutually satisfying here too, not only inside 's own merge branch. That merge branch only ever runs for a bound pair that both independently pass first — this method IS that gate — so without this check here, a bound PAIR whose only relationship in the "wrong" direction is a nullable annotation (e.g. a nullable LOWER bound against a non-nullable UPPER bound, the mirror image of the shape the merge branch's own comment documents) was eliminated before ever reaching the merge branch that exists to resolve it, silently reporting a symbolic-inference conflict instead.

member.summary: ADR-0193 Phase 2: the known symbolic-projection gap, in one place. and project through here, and so do the symbolic lambda- and delegate-target projections (the binder's TryBuildSymbolicDelegateTarget* and deferred-lambda paths) project a delegate-typed signature position through symbolic type arguments and read the literal's target shape off the result. They need the declaration's [Nullable] merged — a Func<string?, T> parameter's string? lives in the PARAMETER's flags, not Invoke's — but the merge stamps a root ! or ? onto the projected delegate, and every one of those consumers tests the result for without peeling it: exactly the blocker that keeps unmerged. The params-array element projection over symbolic method type arguments (OverloadResolver.ExpandParamsArguments) shares the same blocker. Routing them here, rather than calling the door from several binder files, keeps the gap to one suppressed region that Phase 4 closes by adding the merge in this one member.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.MemberLookup.ReverseInferenceBoundKind(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.MemberLookup.SymbolicInferenceBoundKind)
member.summary: Issue #4133 (Copilot review finding, hot-core translation guard PR): unlike ordinary / , which correctly toggle back and forth as nested generic-argument variance recurses (two contravariant levels cancel out, matching real variance), reversing stays MethodGroupUpper rather than cycling back to . A method group's own parameter type is discarded (never input-inference evidence, §12.6.3.7) at ANY nesting depth beneath its own top-level parameter position, not only at the first level: for M[T](items IEnumerable[T], handler Action[Action[T]]) called with a bare method group Handler(x Action[object]), the outer contravariant position (Action[Action[T]]'s own parameter) demotes once to MethodGroupUpper, and the inner one — Action[T]'s own contravariant type argument — recurses a SECOND time. Cycling back to MethodGroupSource there would fall through to an ordinary bound in — reintroducing the method group's parameter type as genuine evidence through a second contravariant level, exactly the shape this fix demotes at the first level. MethodGroupSource (unreversed) is produced only once, directly by the top-level argument's own bound kind — never by a reversal — so staying sticky here cannot affect the group's own legitimate top-level OUTPUT (return-type) contribution.
