member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.MemberLookup.SafeGetMethodsIncludingSelfAndInterfaces(System.Type,System.String,System.Boolean)
member.summary:
Issue #3679: the variant of ), which also surfaces internal (metadata assembly) instance methods declared by or its base chain. Callers pass true only when the declaring assembly grants this compilation internal access — i.e. when says so for an InternalsVisibleTo friend — mirroring the property/field probes in ExpressionBinder.Access.MemberLookup, which already widen to under that same condition. Without it a friend assembly could reach a referenced assembly's internal fields and properties but never its internal methods.
The result is cached under a distinct key so the public-only and internal-inclusive candidate sets never overwrite one another. Neither set depends on WHICH consumer is asking — only on the members' declared accessibility — so the process-wide cache stays consumer-independent.
member.param: The CLR type (concrete class or interface) to probe.
Whether to also return internal instance methods.
member.returns: The candidate list with self-slot methods first.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.MemberLookup.SafeGetMethodsIncludingSelfAndInterfaces(System.Type,System.String,System.Boolean,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Issue #4013: the variant, which keeps offering an ABSTRACT interface member on a CLASS receiver — i.e. one the class can only have implemented explicitly.
member.param: The CLR type (concrete class or interface) to probe.
Whether to also return internal instance methods.
Whether a class receiver keeps abstract interface members.
member.returns: The candidate list with self-slot methods first.
member.remarks:
The ordinary-call view (every other caller) must not, because an explicitly-implemented member is not on the implementing type's own surface in C# and offering it turned List[int32]().Add("x") into a run-time ArgumentException. The COLLECTION-LITERAL Add probe is a different question and passes true: G#'s spread form (issue #3096) fills a Dictionary[K, V] from KeyValuePair elements through ICollection<KeyValuePair<K, V>>.Add, which Dictionary implements explicitly, and lowering emits that call through the interface — so the member really is reachable there and the literal must keep seeing it. Narrowing this probe as well made Dictionary[string, int32](){ ...pairs } report GS0369 ("no accessible 'Add' method or settable indexer").
Restricting the re-admission to GENERIC interfaces was tried, since the hazard the issue names is specifically a NON-GENERIC sibling (IList.Add(object)) — and it broke Issue3096CollectionSpreadEmitTests.UserDefinedSpreadConversions_ArrayAndCollection_RunAndVerify: spreading a []Celsius into a List[float64] relies on IList.Add(object), because a same-compilation struct has no CLR type while binding and so cannot match Add(double) through its user-defined conversion. The literal path therefore keeps the FULL pre-#4013 view here, and for a while List[int32]{"x"} still bound IList.Add(object) and threw at run time — the same hole as this issue's, reached through a collection literal rather than an author-written call.
Issue #4028 closed that without touching this probe: a lookup memoized on (Type, name) cannot see arguments, so the discrimination is made at APPLICABILITY instead, by , which drops a NON-GENERIC interface's widening member from the collected list unless the call really has an erasure to repair. Both views above are therefore still exactly as #4013 left them.

Returns the original instance, unchanged, when nothing needed stripping, so a caller can tell "no annotation difference here" from a reference comparison alone.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.MemberLookup.TryFindInterfaceOnlyInstanceMethod(System.Type,System.String,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Type},System.Type@)
member.summary: Issue #4013: the interface declaring an abstract instance member named that — a class — implements EXPLICITLY and that is APPLICABLE to this call, in the case where the class exposes no member of that name on its own surface.
member.param: The member name the call site used.
The bound arguments' erased CLR types, in source order.
The interface declaring the applicable member.
member.returns: True when the member is reachable only through an interface-typed receiver.
member.remarks:
The diagnostic companion to the interface-walk rule in ). That rule stops offering such a member as a candidate for an ordinary call; without this helper the resulting failure reads GS0159 Cannot find function Contains, which is what a genuinely misspelled member reports too and does not tell the author that the member exists and how to reach it.
Deliberately UNCACHED and called only from the terminal member-not-found error path, so the memoized candidate lookup on the hot path is untouched. Two conditions gate it. The class surface must be empty for this name — when the class does expose a same-named member the call is an ordinary inapplicable-overload failure and keeps GS0159, exactly as an imported member with no interface sibling already does. And one of the EXCLUDED members must actually be applicable to the bound arguments: a name match alone is not enough, because the advice this diagnostic gives — "reach it through an interface-typed receiver" — is a dead end otherwise. map[string, int32]{}.Contains(1, 2) matches Contains by name, but no unary ICollection<KeyValuePair<K, V>>.Contains can take two arguments, so that call keeps GS0159 (review finding on PR #4031).

The interface path is tried first (fast path, and it is the only path that recovers a same-compilation user element type through the symbolic machinery); the pattern path is the fallback used for CLR wrapper types that implement no interfaces at all, such as System.Runtime.CompilerServices.ConfiguredCancelableAsyncEnumerable<T> (the type produced by IAsyncEnumerable<T>.ConfigureAwait(bool)).
member.param: The bound element type symbol, on success.
member.returns: true when the type implements IAsyncEnumerable<T> or exposes the pattern-based await foreach shape.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.MemberLookup.TryGetClosedMapProjectionView(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #4033: the Dictionary[K, V] view of a CLOSED map[K, V], so a member read through the map spelling projects through the receiver's symbolic arguments exactly as the Dictionary[K, V] spelling of the SAME type does (ADR-0104 says they ARE one type).
member.param: The receiver type a member was reflected through.
member.returns: The symbolic dictionary view, or null.
member.remarks:
is the OPEN twin and deliberately refuses a map with a CLR type, because an open map has no other way to reach the dictionary surface. A closed map does reach it — by reflection off its own ClrType — but arrives as a , which is neither an nor a , so every projector above answered null and the member's type was read straight from declaration metadata. For .Keys/.Values that metadata is a placeholder at the TKey/TValue positions, so for v in m.Values { v.Length } lost the element's property surface for the map spelling alone, after the Dictionary spelling had already been fixed.
The open definition comes from the map's OWN ClrType rather than the host typeof(Dictionary<,>): issue #4023 gave a map over an imported key or value a backing dictionary built inside that key/value's MetadataLoadContext, and a member reflected off a context type must be described by that same context's open definition — mixing the two is what #4023 was about.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.MemberLookup.TryGetClrDictionaryTypes(System.Type,System.Type@,System.Type@)
member.summary:
Probes for a member-mapping shape and returns the key/value type arguments when present. Recognizes the broader read-only mapping family: any interface whose generic type definition is IDictionary<TKey, TValue> or IReadOnlyDictionary<TKey, TValue> — mirroring how the enumerable probe accepts the whole IEnumerable<T> family rather than one concrete type (issue #1483). This lets for k, v in d key/value destructure receivers that surface only through the read-only contract (e.g. immutable dictionaries or user types implementing only IReadOnlyDictionary<,>).
When a type implements BOTH interfaces (e.g. Dictionary<K, V>), the writable IDictionary<,> is preferred. This is enforced with a two-pass probe — the first pass scans for IDictionary<,> and only when none is found does the second pass scan for IReadOnlyDictionary<,> — so enumeration order can never pick the read-only interface over an available writable one (they may even carry different type arguments in pathological types).
member.param: The dictionary's key type, on success.
The dictionary's value type, on success.
member.returns: true when the type implements IDictionary<,> or IReadOnlyDictionary<,>.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.MemberLookup.TryGetOpenMethodOnDeclaringType(System.Type,System.Reflection.MethodInfo)
member.summary: Issue #2375: locates the counterpart of (a method already opened at its OWN generic-method-parameter level, e.g. via MethodInfo.GetGenericMethodDefinition()) on — the receiver's fully open declaring type (all of ITS OWN type parameters unbound too). This matters because GetGenericMethodDefinition() only opens the method's own type parameters; if the method's DECLARING type was already closed (e.g. erased to object by overload resolution), the declaring type's arguments remain closed on the result, silently corrupting any reference to the declaring type's own type parameter inside the method's signature (e.g. a return type like DependentBuilder<TRelated, TEntity> would keep TEntity erased to object even after re-opening TRelated). Match is by metadata token + module, which is stable for methods on a constructed generic type.
member.param: The receiver's open generic type definition.
member.returns: The fully open method, or null when no match is found.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.MemberLookup.TryMapSourceArgumentsToParameters(System.Reflection.MethodInfo,System.Int32,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.String},System.Int32[]@)
member.summary: Issue #4036 (review finding): maps each SOURCE argument index to the parameter position it actually binds to on , so a caller holding arguments in source order can compare them against parameters in declaration order.
member.param: The candidate whose parameter names the argument names bind against.
The per-source-index names; null entries are positional.
The source-index to parameter-position mapping, or null when none is needed.
member.returns: Whether the arguments bind to this candidate's parameters at all.
member.remarks:
This is the exact hazard #4026 hit one inference over (BuildSymbolicMethodTypeArgs zipped open parameters with symbolic arguments positionally, and a named call defeated it), and it is resolved the same way: through ClrOverloadResolution.TryBuildNamedArgumentReordering, the resolver's own mapping, so no second implementation can drift from it.
Three outcomes, and the middle one is the reason this is a helper rather than a call to the reordering directly. true with a null mapping means "nothing to reorder" — the call named no argument, so source order IS parameter order. true with a mapping means the names bound. false means the call DID name an argument and the names do not bind against this candidate, which is not a licence to fall back on positional order — it means this candidate cannot take this call at all.

member.summary:

The canonical case is a generic collection implementing IEnumerable[T] with both the generic GetEnumerator() IEnumerator[T] (satisfying IEnumerable<T>.GetEnumerator) and the non-generic GetEnumerator() IEnumerator (satisfying the inherited IEnumerable.GetEnumerator). member.returns: true when the pair forms a valid covariant interface bridge.

The one comparison behind a gain (ADR-0208 A1): a joined type that fails it is a new or a stronger fact, and a joined type that passes it must never replace the held fact.
| held | joined | adds nothing | | --- | --- | --- | | T | T | yes | | Dog | Animal (reference upcast) | yes | | Animal | Dog | no (stronger) | | IA | IB (unrelated interface) | no (a different test) | | int32 | object, ValueType or an interface it implements (boxing) | yes | | int32 | int32? | yes | | object | int32 | no (stronger) | | int32? | int32 | no (stronger) | | int32 | int64 (numeric widening) | no (a different fact) |

A path that every reachable predecessor holds survives with the incoming type that every other incoming type converts to, else with its declared non-null type . A path that some predecessor lacks is dropped. External-callable facts intersect. Unreachable predecessors are skipped. Callers must not fold this pairwise: the result for Dog, Cat and Animal on x object? is Animal, while a binary fold gives object.
member.param: The incoming states, in source order.

member.summary: The type of one path after a join (ADR-0069 issue #4989 addendum and ADR-0208 amendment A1): the first incoming type that every incoming type converts to without changing representation, else the declared non-null type of the path . Every incoming type is a fact, so the declared type is always sound. The forward-goto join and the shadow join share this one rule.
member.param: The incoming types, in source order.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ObliviousScope.IsInConformanceClause(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.TypeClauseSyntax)
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether is written in a base-type / interface list or a generic constraint — including as a type argument inside one (class Bag : IEnumerable[Item]). These are conformance relations, not slots: they say what a type is, and what an implementing member must match. ADR-0186 open question 13 already records that a conformance relation has no point at which a check could be inserted; making its arguments platform types would add nothing a check could use and would split one interface into two — an oblivious IEnumerable[Item!] and the IEnumerable[Item] every enabled caller and every inherited slot is written against. gsc also emits no nullability metadata for a base list, so another compilation reads the relation exactly as written either way. The members that implement the relation are ordinary declarations and stay oblivious; matching them to the slot reads through their platform wrappers (T! has T's signature).
member.returns: true inside a base list or constraint.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ObliviousScope.IsInNativeInteropSignature(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.TypeClauseSyntax)
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether is written in the signature of a native-interop function (@DllImport / @LibraryImport). Such a signature is exempt from the scope rule: its reference positions describe marshalling, which the P/Invoke binder and emitter classify by the exact written type (a string parameter marshals as a native string, a delegate return is rejected, @MarshalAs is validated against it), and a native signature carries no CLR nullability contract for obliviousness to describe. A nilable native reference is spelled T?, as it is outside an oblivious scope.
member.returns: true inside a native-interop signature.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ObliviousScope.IsInteropAttribute(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.AnnotationSyntax,System.String)
member.summary:
Gets a value indicating whether spells the BCL interop attribute : bare (@DllImport, as a System.Runtime.InteropServices import brings it into scope) or fully qualified (@System.Runtime.InteropServices.DllImport, which the P/Invoke binder recognises by CLR identity — issue #1206). A differently-qualified name (@MyInterop.DllImport) is some other attribute and is not exempt.
This is decided by spelling rather than by the bound attribute because a declaration's type clauses are bound before, and independently of, its attributes. The one spelling it cannot tell apart is a user type named DllImport brought into scope unqualified, shadowing the BCL one; such a function's signature is then left as written.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.ObliviousScope.ScopeMap.TryFind(System.Int32,System.Boolean@)
member.summary: Finds the innermost scope containing . Scopes come from syntax, so any two either nest or are disjoint: among the scopes that contain a position, the innermost is the one that starts last. The scopes are sorted by start, so this binary- searches for the last scope starting at or before the position, then climbs that scope's enclosing chain until one still contains the position. Every scope containing the position encloses that last-starting one (they nest), so the climb cannot skip it, and it never visits an ended sibling.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.OverloadResolution.ClrOverloadResolution.BuildGenuineExplicitTypeArgFlags(System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol})

member.remarks: A type argument is GENUINE when it denotes a type applicability can rank against for real. A same-compilation class, struct or enum, and an in-scope type parameter, have no reference-context CLR type: the binder closes the candidate over an erasure SURROGATE (MemberLookup.TryProjectErasedClrType's imported base, or object) and re-emits the real symbol into the MethodSpec, so those positions must keep their erased-slot exemption. The predicate is the one the ARGUMENT side already uses to decide the same question (ExpressionBinder.IsErasedArgumentApplicabilityMismatch), so a nested surrogate such as M[List[Derived]](...) — whose CLR type is the erased List<object>, not null — is correctly not genuine.

member.summary: Evaluates a single candidate for applicability against the supplied argument types, appending it to when it applies. Factored out of so the per-candidate work can be guarded against reflection load failures (issue #321) without disturbing the surrounding control flow.

Issue #506: evaluates a candidate in expanded form — the trailing params T[] parameter accepts zero or more positional arguments, each assignable to the element type T. Closes open generic candidates (e.g. Bar(params T[] items)) by inferring T from the trailing arguments via the same unification used by . Honours named arguments that bind to a fixed parameter in its natural source position; later positional surplus is packed into the synthesised params array. Mirrors the applicability check in but rewrites the trailing parameter type to the element type for ranking purposes.
Validate receiver witnesses against closed signatures. Upper bounds retain compatible but unenumerable subtypes for later argument inference.

Issue #530: when multiple surviving candidates have the same parameter types but different declaring types (e.g. Task<T>.GetAwaiter() hiding Task.GetAwaiter()), keep only those declared on the most-derived type. This mirrors C#'s method-hiding semantics: a derived class method with the same signature as a base class method hides it.

This mirrors C#'s implicit numeric conversion of a lambda body to an expected delegate return type, and lets a uint32 selector flow into Enumerable.Sum(Func<T,long>). Parameter and return types are compared by name to remain safe across reflection contexts (the literal's natural Func<...> may be a host-runtime constructed type closed over MetadataLoadContext arguments). Only the widening lattice in this file is consulted; narrowing and signed/unsigned same-width mismatches are rejected.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.OverloadResolution.ClrOverloadResolution.IsErasedGenericParameterSlot(System.Reflection.MethodBase,System.Int32,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Boolean})
member.summary: Issue #3982 / #3989: whether the candidate's parameter at could have acquired its closed shape by type-argument erasure rather than by being declared that way.

member.remarks: One question, asked by two gates of opposite polarity: ChannelViewAppliesAtErasedGenericSlot ADDS applicability where the answer is yes, and the #3989 erased-argument check REMOVES it where the answer is no. Both read the candidate's OPEN declaration through ; a slot whose open declaration cannot be located stays "possibly erased", which is the permissive direction for the channel gate and the safe one for #3989's. Issue #4026 narrows the "yes" by one case. "Could have acquired its closed shape by erasure" is false when the call site PINNED the slot's method type parameters itself, with type arguments that have a CLR identity of their own. Probes.CountAny[ImportedBase](List[Derived]) closes CountAny[T](List[T]) over a real ImportedBase, so the parameter really is the INVARIANT List and the argument's List

member.summary: Issue #932: determines whether and are two distinct delegate types with an identical Invoke shape — the same parameter types and the same return type. A func/arrow literal's natural delegate type is a System.Func<...> / System.Action<...>, but a CLR API may type the parameter as a structurally identical, differently named delegate (e.g. System.Predicate<T>, System.Comparison<T>). Parameter and return types are compared by name to remain safe across reflection contexts (the target parameter is typically loaded through a MetadataLoadContext while the literal's natural Func<...> is a live-runtime constructed type). The exact-return-type requirement keeps this distinct from (differing returns) and (void discard), which handle the non-identity return shapes.

Whether this is the bound's outermost position. The relation there is ASSIGNABILITY, not the invariant identity that is correct at an argument position, and that distinction is load-bearing rather than defensive: it was measured, and comparing the two arguments for identity here fails the legal Chain[ChBase, ChDerived] with a false GS0152. Issue #4063: a bare type parameter at the top is therefore routed to , which asks assignability of the symbols, instead of declining to answer at all — declining is what left Chain[ChA, ChB] over two unrelated erased classes accepted.

The printed forms of the shape fragments on the path from the bound's root to this node. Review finding (#4068): the previous form of this method stopped at a fixed depth of eight, which silently turned a legal deeply nested bound into an indeterminate answer and handed it to the erased comparison — the very hole this check exists to close, measured at nine levels. Recursion is bounded by CYCLE detection on this path instead, which terminates on malformed metadata without capping legal signatures: a well-formed shape tree is finite and strictly shrinks at every step.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.OverloadResolution.ClrOverloadResolution.MatchDependentTopOfBound(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)

member.param: The symbol supplied for the BOUNDED parameter.
The symbol supplied for the BOUNDING parameter.

member.remarks: One predicate, two spellings. The G#-declared spelling of this exact bound (func take[TBase, TDerived TBase]()) has been answered by Binder.SatisfiesDependentBound since #4043, and that predicate is deliberately reused here rather than reimplemented: an independent copy would let the imported and G#-declared spellings of the same rule drift apart, and it is the drift — not the relation — that produces a false GS0152. The reference is a call to one pure internal static method in the same assembly; no binder state is reachable from here and none is used. It only ever REJECTS what it can disprove. SatisfiesDependentBound accepts on every indeterminate answer, so a false from it is a definitive "no". A true is mapped to Indeterminate rather than to Matches — it may mean "yes" or "cannot tell", and the CLR comparison this falls back to accepts an erased vector anyway, so the outcome is identical and the label stays honest. An open side declines outright. When either symbol still mentions a type parameter the relation has no closed answer, and the self-substitution SatisfiesDependentBound performs for a self-referential generic interface bound needs the bounded parameter's own symbol, which the imported path does not have. Refusing to answer there keeps the missing symbol from ever mattering.

Among survivors, the standard tie-breakers run in C# order: fewer-parameters (fewer omitted optionals), more-specific parameter types, then non-generic-over-generic. Only open generic method definitions whose arity matches are considered, and they are closed with these exact type arguments instead of inference. Non-generic and mismatched-arity candidates are dropped (matches C#'s rule that explicit type arguments require a matching generic method).

Issue #321: projects an inferred type argument (a live host-runtime taken from a bound argument) onto the reference load context that loaded the candidate methods, so accepts it. Without this projection, closing a generic method such as JsonSerializer.Serialize<TValue> with an inferred System.String throws "was not loaded by the MetadataLoadContext". A flagged argument may, in addition to its natural string type, convert to an IFormattable/FormattableString parameter. null (the default) disables the relaxation, preserving prior behaviour for all other call sites.

Issue #343: optional per-argument names supplied at the call site. Entries are null for positional arguments and the parameter name for named arguments (e.g. F(1, x: 2) → [null, "x"]). Named arguments must follow all positional arguments in source order; the binder pre-validates this layout. When non-null, each candidate's applicability check additionally requires that every named argument maps to a distinct parameter on that candidate, no positional slot is overwritten by a named slot, and every unfilled non-trailing slot is optional. The returned records, for each source argument index, the resolved parameter position so binding can preserve source evaluation order while presenting values in parameter order.

Used so the generic value-type/struct constraint check can see through the object erasure of same-compilation user value types. It is the exact base-class analogue of what #4070 did for the interface half: Probes.NeedsScheme[T]() inside func callIt[T SchemeOptions]() reported GS0159 Cannot find function because the candidate was silently FILTERED out, while class Fwd[T SchemeOptions] : SchemeConstrained[T] bound. csc accepts both.

Extracted from so the SAME walk answers the question on both paths that ask it. #4070 enumerated them: the generic-TYPE construction path (, #4037's GS0580) walked the class chain; the generic-METHOD path (SatisfiesDeclaredConstraints' #2617 arm, since #750/ADR-0088) did not, so Probes.NeedsDisposable[T]() inside func callIt[T DisposableBase]() reported GS0159 Cannot find function while class Forwarded[T DisposableBase] : DisposableConstrained[T] bound. csc accepts both (measured). The leaf ErasedSymbolSatisfiesInterfaceConstraint is deliberately left byte-identical — its type-parameter arm reads only interface bounds, and it has other callers that must keep that meaning.
Issue #4084 CLOSED the dependent-bound gap this once declined: the walk read only ClassConstraint, so [TBase DisposableBase, TDerived TBase] did not forward TBase's IDisposable onto TDerived — GS0159 at a generic method, GS0580 at a generic type, two different wrong answers to one question csc answers yes. The chain is now , #4067's existing symbol walk, which follows as well and terminates on a visited set rather than a depth limit — so one chain serves both paths and the base-class sibling () alike.
The METHOD-path caller additionally guards on the UNSUBSTITUTED constraint mentioning no type parameter, which is the same skip the generic-TYPE path applies (#4031/#4041) — a self-referential bound such as where T : IEquatable<T> cannot be answered on the erased vector. An in-scope generic type parameter (, e.g. the forwarded TEnum of
[TEnum Enum struct]) satisfies only when its own resolves to the same CLR type (transitively, through a chain of forwarded constraints) — a bare struct constraint with no class bound does not prove anything about Enum or any other base.

member.summary: Issue #1213 / #1221: lowers a call through a delegate/function-typed variable to a . When the variable is the implicit backing-field of a field-like event (an ) the callee is loaded as a field read on this (e.g. ldfld Base::Changed) — including a backing field declared on a base class, so an inherited event can be raised from a derived type — rather than a (non-existent) local slot. The null-conditional invocation form Ev?(args) is guarded by a null check (a ) so a null delegate short-circuits, mirroring Ev?.Invoke(args). A void delegate yields a plain no-op; Issue #2798: a value-returning delegate yields the correct optional/null result via the established result-slot lowering instead of NRE-ing (or silently dropping the ? and producing a non-optional result). Issue #2799 follow-up: this guard applies uniformly across every receiver kind reaching this path — implicit field-like event backing field, bare static field or property, and a plain local or parameter — not only the field-like event originally handled. The receiver is evaluated exactly once.

Wraps a null-conditional delegate/event invocation in a that short-circuits when the captured receiver is null. A void-returning invocation leaves no value (a plain no-op null branch); a value-returning invocation adopts the established result-slot lowering — the result type is the nullable wrapping of , and a value-type return additionally allocates a $nres_ slot so the null branch can materialize default(Nullable<T>). Shared by the CLR-delegate call path (OverloadResolver.CallBinding) and the structural path (). The caller must have already incremented binderCtx.NullConditionalCaptureCounter for the capture; this method reuses that same value for the result slot.

member.summary: Issue #1631: classifies the implicit conversion from a user-symbolic argument type to a user-symbolic parameter type using the SAME ranking the CLR-reflection resolver () uses for imported-method overloads, so both resolvers agree on which conversion is "better". Bounded to the conversion shapes the user-symbolic classifier actually distinguishes: identity, nullable-wrap (T -> T?), and numeric widening (via the shared ). Every other implicit conversion (reference upcast, interface satisfaction, boxing, user-defined op_Implicit, …) folds into — the user-symbolic type model does not carry enough structure to rank those sub-kinds separately, but they still rank strictly better than the numeric/ delegate special cases ranked worse below.

Issue #1493: coerces a single trailing argument bound for a G# variadic (...T) element slot to the variadic element type, applying the same implicit conversions a fixed parameter of that type would accept — reference upcast, interface conversion, tuple-element conversions, nullable lifting, implicit constant narrowing, and user-defined implicit conversions. Returns the (possibly conversion-wrapped) argument so the emitter packs the element with the variadic element type rather than the argument's static type; reports GS0154 and sets when no implicit conversion exists. This keeps overload applicability and final coercion in agreement with the non-variadic / array-literal element paths.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.OverloadResolution.OverloadResolver.ComparePlatformArgumentTargets(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)

ADR-0186 §3: for a T! argument, a non-null T parameter beats a T? parameter over the same underlying type.
Scoped as narrowly as the rule is: it fires only when the argument is platform-typed and the two candidate parameters are exactly U and U? over one underlying. Any other pair — including U against an unrelated V, and every pair at all while --nullability=platform-types is off, since nothing constructs a platform type then — is left to the ordinary ranking below.

Returns a negative value when is the better (more-derived) target, positive when is, and 0 when the two targets are unrelated (neither implicitly converts to the other) — preserving genuine ambiguity. Convertibility is probed one-directionally via rather than hand-rolled type checks so user classes, interfaces, and imported/BCL reference types are all handled uniformly.

Different s rank by their declared ordinal (lower is better); same-kind numeric widenings tie-break via the shared "better conversion target" rule (C# §7.5.3.4), reusing the exact CLR-path helper rather than reimplementing the numeric/signed-vs-unsigned lattice a second time.

member.summary: Issue #2403: whether 's unqualified callee name could resolve to a genuine non-constructor callable — a same-compilation free/extension or function-valued local reachable through , or an implicit-this instance/static sibling method (including a private one) on the enclosing struct/class or interface body, or an inherited CLR method on the implicit receiver — checked BEFORE the CLR constructor/conversion fallbacks a few lines below in run. That is intentional: when this returns true, simply skips the CLR early-return paths and falls through to its ordinary implicit-this / symbol-lookup call-binding logic further down, which already performs full overload selection via / / and reports the correct diagnostic (wrong-argument-count, ambiguity, ...) against the genuine user candidate — so no overload-resolution logic is duplicated here. When no such candidate exists, this returns false and the CLR paths run exactly as before, so genuine constructor/conversion calls (e.g. StringBuilder(16)) are unaffected.

Review finding (#3988, Copilot on PR #3999): true when some supplied argument is a nullable REFERENCE that reaches no candidate's corresponding parameter in EITHER form — neither as S? nor as the bare S. Such a call is not a null-safety failure (dropping the annotation would not help) and it is not an ambiguity (nothing is applicable to choose between), so it belongs on the no-applicable-overload path rather than on GS0266's.
member.returns: true when no overload can accept the argument in either form.
member.remarks: Deliberately conservative in three ways, so that only the shape the review raised is diverted. It requires an argument that actually is a nullable reference; it requires EVERY candidate to reject BOTH forms, so a set containing even one overload the bare value could reach keeps its existing diagnostic; and it skips the same candidates skips, so the two agree about what they are looking at.

member.remarks: This was a == test on the two s. Neither nor declares an operator ==, so that is REFERENCE identity — it only ever succeeded when the argument's type symbol was literally the same instance as the parameter's. The []string a carrier is declared with and the string[] read back from CLR metadata denote the same runtime type but are built on different paths, so f(Environment.GetCommandLineArgs()) failed the pass-through test, fell into the element loop, failed string[] -> string, and the candidate was dropped as non-convertible. When EVERY candidate is dropped the caller keeps the unfiltered set and ranks it, so two variadic siblings tie and the call is reported ambiguous (GS0266) instead of binding. Classify the conversion instead: an identity or implicit conversion to the carrier is exactly what "the argument already is the carrier" means, and it is the same test the final argument coercion applies.

In the pack case, every trailing element is first run through (issue #1493) so implicit conversions — numeric widening, interface upcast, nullable lifting, constant narrowing, user-defined implicit conversions — are applied to the element before it lands in the slice, keeping all call paths in agreement (issue #1630: this used to be duplicated by hand at each call site, and two copies had drifted to pack raw, uncoerced elements).

That is deliberately not rendered as an assembly name here, because the only assembly reachable from a is the one declaring T itself — System.Runtime for a string! — which names the wrong thing and would actively mislead. The declaring member is not in reach at the coercion point; naming the type and the boundary is the honest subset, and the file:line that follows locates the rest.

A short phrase naming the boundary the value crossed — "an argument to a non-null parameter", "a member access receiver". It is what turns an NRE into an attributable one, which is §4's entire justification for preferring a call-site check over the CLR's own.

Whether --platform-nil-checks=off may remove this check. True for every check the compiler INSERTS; false for the one the author WROTE (a user !! over a platform operand, which §6 calls the explicit spelling of the same coercion). member.summary: Issue #4265 soundness guard: true when (or its getter) carries [UnscopedRef] (System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.UnscopedRefAttribute). C# accepts the attribute on EITHER the accessor or the property itself — an expression-bodied indexer ([UnscopedRef] public ref int this[int i] => ref _value;) emits it on the property's own metadata row, not get_Item, so both must be checked (confirmed via CustomAttributeData against a real compiled indexer of each shape — checking only the getter missed the expression-bodied spelling entirely). 's BoundClrIndexExpression case treats a byref-like CLR indexer's target as encapsulating a caller-supplied REFERENT (like Span[T]'s backing pointer) — safe to forward through a by-value parameter. That premise fails for an indexer explicitly marked [UnscopedRef]: the CLR author has declared it returns a reference into the RECEIVER'S OWN storage instead (exactly mirroring what @UnscopedRef signals for a native G# member — see Binder.cs's ThisParameter.IsScoped handling), which a by-value receiver cannot safely yield. Real C# enforces the same distinction (CS8166: an [UnscopedRef] member invoked through a by-value parameter is rejected).
member.returns: true when the indexer or its getter carries [UnscopedRef].

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.RefCapabilities.ReceiverContributesRefScope(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression)
member.summary: ADR-0187 / issue #4350 (the C# scoped-this rule): whether the REF-safe-context of contributes to the reference a ref-returning call or property read hands back.
member.param: The ref-returning call or property read.
member.returns: true when the receiver's storage can be the returned reference's source.
member.remarks: Every struct instance member's this is implicitly scoped ref, and the binder already enforces the callee side of that contract: a member that returns a reference into its own receiver must be @UnscopedRef (GS0589). So when the receiver's static type is a concrete struct — the call then names the implementation it dispatches to — a member WITHOUT @UnscopedRef cannot be the source of a reference into the receiver's storage, and C# excludes the receiver from the result's ref-safe-context entirely. Interface implementations are now held to the same one-way slot contract, so they cannot add @UnscopedRef behind an unannotated interface member. This helper still recognizes only direct native struct-member nodes; type-parameter dispatch, imported calls, base calls, and unrecognized nodes keep the conservative answer.

member.summary:

Any ref a member returns into its OWN receiver storage then points at that temp, which dies at function exit — so the binder's ref-safe-scope walk must treat such a forward as function-local (StatementBinder.IsDefensivelyCopiedReceiverForwarding). Before this helper existed the rule lived as three independently drifting copies in the emitter and nowhere at all in the binder, which is exactly how the caller-side dangling-reference hole got in.
Every caller keeps its own value-type/reference-type guard; this helper is deliberately ONLY the shared core, so extracting it left the emitter's behaviour byte-for-byte unchanged.
is structurally false for every native G# member — G# has no readonly func — so it carries information only for CLR metadata members, whose IsReadOnlyAttribute reads.
member.param: Whether the called member is itself a readonly member.
member.returns: true when the receiver is defensively copied before the call.

member.summary: Splits a call's arguments into the two escape-source kinds needs, keeping them in SEPARATE lists (issue #4265) because the caller checks them with different scope semantics: holds the operand each ref/in/out parameter whose effective ref scope can contribute to a return had its address taken of (checked against its own storage scope), and holds each non-scoped by-value byref-like (e.g. Span[T]) argument unchanged (checked against its ENCAPSULATED REFERENT's scope instead — see StatementBinder.HasFunctionLocalReferentScope). Conservative on any shape the caller-side scope walk cannot decompose (a conditional address, a parameter/argument count mismatch, or a ref/in/out argument that was not itself wrapped in a ): the unrecognized argument expression itself is returned unchanged so the recursive HasFunctionLocalRefScope walk's default ("unrecognized shape is function-local, i.e. unsafe") still applies, rather than silently treating an undecomposable argument as safe to escape through.

Issue #4224 (root cause #4) / #4265: decomposes a native ref-returning call or property read into the pieces the caller-side ref-safe-scope computation (HasFunctionLocalRefScope) needs — its instance receiver (whose storage the callee could be returning a reference into), the argument expressions passed to ref/in/ out parameters (any of which the callee could likewise be returning), and — issue #4265 — the argument expressions passed to by-value BYREF-LIKE (ref struct, e.g. Span[T]) parameters, whose ENCAPSULATED REFERENT (not their own storage) the callee could be returning through, e.g. func First(s Span[int32]) ref int32 { return ref s[0] }. These two argument kinds are kept in SEPARATE lists rather than merged, because the caller checks them with different scope semantics (HasFunctionLocalRefScope vs. HasFunctionLocalReferentScope) — conflating them would let a ref argument bound to a byref-like value smuggle a dangling reference through the wrong (too permissive) check. A scoped parameter of any of these three kinds is excluded: the callee's own signature promises not to return that reference, so the caller's argument does not contribute to the result's scope.
member.param: The instance receiver, or null for a static/no-receiver call.
The underlying storage of each non-scoped ref/in/out argument.
Each non-scoped by-value byref-like argument, unchanged.
member.returns: false when is not a native ref-returning call/property (the out parameters are then empty).

Applies one expression's backward transfer to : if the expression is a top-level assignment to an interesting by-ref-like local that is not also read within its own right-hand side (see the self-referential-redefinition note below), that local is a "kill" — its pre-statement liveness does not depend on what's live after. An assignment *through* a native ref-alias local (alias = 42) is never a kill — issue #4222: it writes to the pointee via the alias's stored address, which requires the alias itself to be live at that point (there is no syntax to re-seat an alias to a new address, so every assignment is a use). Otherwise every interesting local read anywhere in the expression is added to live. If the expression contains an await, any currently-live interesting local (other than a pure kill target of this same expression) is reported as unsafe.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.RefStructAsyncLivenessAnalyzer.IsNativeRefAlias(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.VariableSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #4222: true for a native let ref/var ref alias local (tracked via , since its Type stays the pointee type — see ), as opposed to a by-ref-like (ref struct) value local.
The fixed body always runs unconditionally (no branching), and its synthetic pinned/pointer/source locals do not exist before it, so they're excluded from what flows backward past the statement.

A pattern switch, unlike select, can complete having matched no arm when there's no exhaustive default — that "nothing matched" path must also contribute to what's live before the statement (it falls straight through to whatever's live after it).

try/catch/finally: an exception can transfer control from any point in the try body straight into a catch clause or (if uncaught, or on normal/exceptional catch completion) into finally. Modeled as an "ambient live" set — the union of what's live entering every catch clause and the finally block — that is folded into the live-out of every block inside the try body (not just its formal exit), so a local that's read in finally (or a catch) shows up as live at an earlier await inside try, even though normal control flow alone would never reach that read from there.

A branch leaves the local non-null when it either (a) assigns it a statically non-null value (see ), or (b) is entered under a condition that narrows it non-null (x != nil) and never reassigns it to a nullable value. The result is the intersection over the two branch exits, so the local is narrowed only when proven non-null on every path that reaches the join.

member.remarks: Legality mirrors ECMA-335 III.4.24 (and C#'s CS0156 / CS0724): the statement must be lexically inside a catch handler, and no finally clause may sit between it and that handler — by the time a nested finally runs the CLR has already left the catch handler, so rethrow there would be unverifiable IL. member.summary: Issue #4965 (ADR-0202): whether the end of a block whose bound statements are is unreachable, so that a value block ending this way has the bottom (never) type instead of needing a trailing value (GS0277). The last statement must be a return, throw or rethrow, a direct break/continue/goto (bound as a goto, which always leaves the block because the block ends right after it) — also when it sits in the tail of a nested block, an if/else, or a try (which is how a defer or using let prefix wraps the rest of the block) — or a structured statement every branch of which ends in return/throw (see EndsInUnconditionalExit). Gotos inside a switch statement are deliberately not counted: a break in a switch-statement arm targets the switch's own exit label and falls through to the end of the block, so counting it would type a block that completes normally as never (fail-safe; a tail if-else is an if-expression and is typed by its own branches instead).

member.returns: true when control can never reach the block's end.

| member | runs at construction | | --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | | instance field initializer | yes | | primary constructor | yes | | explicit constructor | yes | | shared { init { ... } } block of a class (non-beforefieldinit .cctor, runs at the first newobj) | yes | | shared { init { ... } } block of a value type (a literal or default is initobj, which does not run it) | no | | shared field initializer only (beforefieldinit, runs at the first static field access, which is user code that is classified where it is written) | no | | none of the above | no |

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.StatementBinder.ContainsUserGotoOrLabel(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Syntax.SyntaxNode)
member.summary:
Issue #4285: syntactic (pre-binding) check for whether — a function/lambda/local-function BODY, or any subtree of one — contains any user-written goto statement or non-loop label: declaration, i.e. any construct that participates in this function's own goto/label namespace (see / ). A label: on a loop (ADR-0070, ) is excluded: it only names the loop for break/continue and is never a valid goto target — only populates , and BindLabeledStatement never calls it for a loop label — so a loop label alone cannot create the reachability hazard this check guards against.
Does not descend into a nested function-literal or arrow-lambda body (, ): those get their own fresh goto/label namespace and their own fresh , computed separately by LambdaBinder.EnterNestedFrame when THEIR body is bound, matching ADR-0070's "label namespace is local to the enclosing function" rule.
Likewise does not descend into a or (ADR-0146 "rich" anonymous object literal method/event members, still present as raw syntax inline in the enclosing expression even though Binder.IsRichAnonymousObject binds them via a synthesized struct declaration): those members are bound as their own, independent functions through the ordinary struct-method bind path (one of the Binder.cs call sites that already computes its own ), so a goto/label inside one must not mark the syntactically enclosing OUTER function as goto-bearing too — that would incorrectly over-suppress the outer function's own, otherwise-valid narrowing lifts.
Used to populate once per function-equivalent binding session, which consults to conservatively suppress the early-exit / post-switch narrowing lift for the WHOLE body whenever the function contains any goto/label at all, rather than pinpointing which SPECIFIC lift site a given goto can actually reach. See the comment on for why a more precise CFG-based reachability check is a valid future refinement, not required for this fix.
The consumer rule of ADR-0213 section 7, steps (i) to (vii), for one fact.

Mirrors the BoundDereferenceExpression pointer-parameter case in exactly: a non-scoped by-value parameter's encapsulated reference is caller-supplied (the caller already guaranteed its lifetime by constructing/passing the value), so only a directly-named non-scoped parameter is caller-scoped here; any other shape (a local, a nested call result, ...) conservatively falls back to the function-local-by-default walk, since this compiler does not yet track how a ref-struct LOCAL's own encapsulated reference was constructed (e.g. stackalloc vs. wrapping a heap array) with C#'s full precision.

Issue #2159: intersects two branch-exit non-null maps, keeping a local only when both branches prove it non-null with the same underlying type.

The member's own return ref was validated against ITS receiver, which the caller then substitutes; any reference into the receiver's own storage therefore points at a temp that dies at function exit. Real csc rejects the C# analogue (CS8156).
Deliberately EXCLUDES the Span-shaped CLR indexer branch: that result points into the ENCAPSULATED BUFFER the receiver merely wraps, not into the receiver's own storage, so copying the receiver (its pointer and length) does not disturb the referent at all — issue #4265's premise, still correct. The exclusion lapses exactly when the CLR author marked the indexer [UnscopedRef], which declares the opposite.
The BoundDereferenceExpression arm is load bearing for DIAGNOSTIC SELECTION only, never for soundness: ConversionClassifier.AutoDereferenceRefReturn wraps every imported/CLR ref-returning member read in one, so without it the CLR-indexer case below is still correctly REJECTED (hook A sees the unwrapped node through 's own dereference recursion) but is reported as the generic GS0254 instead of GS0591. Adding it cannot over-reject: this predicate is consulted only after has already said no.

member.summary: Issue #4219 (umbrella remainder): the non-generic counterpart of — same shape, minus the type-parameter list. A generic local function is ALWAYS routed through the directly-callable-symbol path (a CLR delegate cannot close over an unbound generic method, so it has no other option); a non-generic one is not under any such constraint and, standing alone, keeps its existing "delegate-valued variable" representation (see StatementBinder.Narrowing.cs's bindFunctionLiteralWithSelfDeclaration self-recursion path) to avoid silently changing every ordinary let f = func ... in the language. Only a run of TWO OR MORE consecutive non-generic members (see the minimum-run-length gate in ) opts into forward visibility — that plural shape is unambiguously a deliberate group of named local functions, not an ordinary single closure-valued local. An explicit outer type clause (let f (int32) -> int32 = func ...) is also excluded: the direct-call path's signature comes entirely from the LITERAL (its own parameters/return type), so a declared outer type would be silently ignored instead of type-checked/converted against — the old path still validates it via ConversionClassifier.BindConversion.

It ALWAYS routes through the direct-call path, standing alone or not (unlike 's 2-or-more-member gate — one ref-returning literal has no other representation to fall back to), reusing named-function ref-return machinery (issue #4224) for calls, aliasing, and emission. member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.StatementBinder.IsReferenceLikeType(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #1123: whether is a reference-like type, which is what scopes assignment narrowing to shapes whose narrowed read needs no special emit — reference nullability being purely an annotation. User value structs (null ClrType during binding, IsClass == false) and CLR value types / pointers / by-refs stay excluded, because the narrowed-read emit path does not unwrap Nullable<T>.

member.remarks: Issue #3988: this was the FOURTH hand-copy of — its own comment said it mirrored "the reference-likeness rule the conversion classifier uses" — and it had drifted the same way the overload resolver's copy had. It named interfaces, user classes and reference-constrained type parameters but no STRUCTURAL shape, so a slice, array, named delegate, function type or channel whose element leaves its ClrType null did not narrow. That became load-bearing the moment #3988 made a nullable argument at an open non-nullable parameter an ERROR: the diagnostic names narrowing as one of its remedies, and for exactly those shapes s = source did not lift while if s != nil did — measured, var s chan[T]? = nil; s = source; takesOpen[T](s) reported GS0154 with no way to satisfy it. Every shape this adds is a genuine CLR reference, so the narrowed read stays the metadata-only no-op the #2159 arm below already relied on. The copy is gone; this DELEGATES.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.StatementBinder.NestedAssignmentPreservesNarrowing(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #3907: whether — the right-hand side of an assignment — is itself an assignment whose own value proves the outer target non-nil.
member.param: The outer target's underlying non-nullable type.
member.returns: true when the nested assignment narrows the outer target.
member.remarks:
A nested assignment's STATIC type is its own target's DECLARED type, so order = (buffer = [8]int32) types as buffer's []?int32 even though the value it propagates is the definitely non-nil array literal. The outer assignment therefore failed and order stayed nullable, while the identical order = [8]int32 narrowed — an asymmetry with no justification, since the two assign the same value. C# reaches the same conclusion: its flow analysis tracks the assigned value's null-state, not the nested target's annotation.
Sound because the value of an assignment expression IS the value assigned — not a re-read of the target — so x = (y = v) gives x exactly the value v and must narrow on exactly the evidence x = v narrows on. That is why this applies the SAME test to the inner operand rather than a weaker or stronger one: the rule is a look-through, not a new narrowing source.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.StructuralProjectionPlanner.HasErasedTypeArgument(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #4014: true when is a constructed generic carrying a SYMBOLIC type argument that its cannot represent — an argument with no CLR identity of its own while binding (a same-compilation class, struct or enum). The container's ClrType is then an ADR-0004 erasure surrogate rather than the type the source actually denotes, so comparing closed CLR types across such a pair compares surrogates. Recursive, so a nested List[List[Mode]] is caught too.
member.returns: true when an erased argument is present.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.StructuralProjectionPlanner.IsDistinctConstructionOfTheSameClrGeneric(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #4014: true when and are two DIFFERENT closed constructions of the SAME CLR generic definition — e.g. List[int32] and List[string]. The planner's question is "can the target be constructed from the source's public member surface?", and for two constructions of one generic that question answers yes for a reason that has nothing to do with the values involved: the two share a member surface BY CONSTRUCTION, and the members whose types actually differ (the ones mentioning the type argument) are exactly the ones a projection cannot carry. For List the incidental overlap is a parameterless constructor plus a settable Capacity, so the plan built a NEW, EMPTY List and copied a capacity — measured on the parent, let zs List[string] = xs for an xs List[int32] holding one element compiled, IL-verified, and printed 0. The verdict lives HERE rather than in 's projection arm because THREE callers ask the planner directly — , applicability's structural-projection argument check (#4006), and ClrOverloadResolution's argument check — and closing only the conversion arm leaves the other two open, which is literally the #4006 shape. Deliberately scoped to pairs whose CLOSED CLR types are BOTH GENUINE and DIFFER, and — see , which the caller ands with this — whose member surfaces do NOT expose the difference. Two exclusions are load-bearing here, and both were measured rather than assumed: Identical closed types are not touched — that is identity, not a projection. An ADR-0004 ERASURE SURROGATE is not a closed type. A constructed generic over a same-compilation element has no CLR identity while binding, so its ClrType is a surrogate: #2889's List[Mode] over a same-compilation enum presents as List
member.returns: true when the pair must not project.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.StructuralProjectionPlanner.MemberSurfaceCarriesTheDifference(System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary{System.String,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.StructuralProjectionSourceMember},GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #4014, Copilot review on PR #4029: true when the two constructions' public member surfaces THEMSELVES differ — i.e. at least one same-named member has a different type on the two sides, because it mentions the generic definition's type parameter.
member.param: The source's collected public readable members.
The projection target, a sibling construction.
member.returns: true when the difference is visible in the surface.
member.remarks:
This is the discriminator between the two situations the same-definition test alone cannot tell apart, and both were measured on the parent:
An imported Box<T> with a settable T Value EXPOSES the difference: Box[int32] has
Value int32 where Box[string] has Value string. The author can therefore see the incompatible member and SUPPLY it, which is exactly what ADR-0148 §B explicit object spread is for — Box[string]{ ...boxOfInt, Value: "replacement" } compiled on the parent and printed replacement. Refusing that outright was a regression. The ordinary member rules already decide this pair correctly in BOTH directions: without the override, the parent reports (and this branch still reports) GS0490: Source member 'Value' of type 'int32' is not implicitly convertible to 'string', at the spread and at an implicit assignment alike.
List<T> does NOT expose the difference: its projectable surface is Capacity/Count,
identically int32 on both sides, and the elements live in private state. The author cannot supply what they cannot name, so every spelling loses them — measured on the parent, the implicit assignment, the argument position, List[string]{ ...xs } and List[string]{ ...xs, Capacity: 4 } all compiled and all printed 0. That is the case this refuses.
Deliberately NOT expressed as "only refuse strict/implicit projection", which is what the review proposed. Both spread spellings above reach the planner with strict: false (ExpressionBinder.Literals.BindStructuralSpreadLiteral), so gating on that flag would have fixed the reported regression while reopening a measured element loss. The surface test does both.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportAmbiguousImportedType(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String)
member.summary: Issue #2012 (N3): an explicit-arity open-generic typeof(Name[_, ...]) whose base name + requested arity (e.g. Func1) resolves to two or more DIFFERENT CLR types across the imports in scope. Distinct from (cref:ReportUndefinedType) (which means no type matched at all): here at least two imports each contribute a candidate and they disagree, so the previous behavior of reporting "type doesn't exist" was a misleading diagnostic for a genuinely different failure mode (nothing was undefined — too many things were defined). Mirrors the wording of (cref:ReportAmbiguousImportedStaticMember) (#1201) for the analogous ambiguous-import-member case.
member.param: The source location of the ambiguous type reference.
The ambiguous arity-suffixed type name (e.g. Func1).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportChannelBindingTargetCount(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String,System.String,System.Int32)
member.summary: ADR-0174 D3: GS0554 — a channel-receive binding form was given the wrong number of targets.

The canonical spelling of the form, for example let value, ok = <-ch.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportChannelLocalUsedBeforeAssignment(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Issue #3316 / ADR-0159: reports a use of a channel-typed local that some control-flow path can reach without a preceding assignment. A bare chan T slot has no usable zero value (the ADR-0159 carve-out), so — unlike zero-valued locals — declared-without-initializer channel locals are flow-checked by with C#'s CS0165 semantics: declaring is free, using before definite assignment is the error.
member.param: The location of the offending use.
The channel type name (e.g. chan int32), spliced into the suggested make remedy.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportChannelRequiresInitializer(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Issue #3310 / ADR-0159: a bare chan T local, global, or field declared without an initializer has no usable default value (the magic-collection empty-instance zero values deliberately exclude channels — buffer size and ownership are semantic decisions make exists to force), so the declaration must initialize it explicitly.
member.param: The location of the declared identifier.
The channel type name (e.g. chan int32), spliced into the suggested make remedy.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportCircularConstraintDependency(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Issue #4043: reports a circular dependent-constraint chain ([T T], [A B, B A]), mirroring C#'s CS0454.
member.param: The text location of the constraint reference that closes the cycle.
The type parameter the cycle is reported on.
The type parameter its bound names.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportClassInheritanceCycle(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String)
member.summary: Issue #973: reports a class that participates in a transitive base-class inheritance cycle (e.g. class B : C together with class C : B). The two-phase declaration model (#973) declares all type-name shells before binding any base clause, so such mutually forward-referencing cycles can no longer be screened out by declaration order and must be detected explicitly once every base class is resolved. Direct self-inheritance (class A : A) is reported separately by .
member.param: The text location of the base-type clause.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportClassInheritsFromItself(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String)
member.summary: Issue #949: reports a class that directly names itself as its own base class (e.g. class A : A or the generic class A[T] : A[T]), which is an illegal self-inheritance cycle. Note that naming the enclosing type merely as a generic type argument of a base/interface type — the common class Shape : IEquatable[Shape] pattern — is legal and is not reported here.
member.param: The text location of the base-type identifier.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportCloseOperandIsNotChannel(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Reports that the operand of close(ch) is not a channel (Phase 5.4 / ADR-0022).

The actual type of the operand.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportColonEqualsRemoved(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String)
member.summary: ADR-0077 / issue #717: GS0305 — the legacy short variable-declaration operator := has been removed. Every binding site must spell let name = expr (immutable) or var name = expr (mutable). The lexer continues to tokenise := so the parser can emit a single high-quality diagnostic at the offending token rather than cascading parse errors.
member.param: The source location of the offending := token.
A context-specific replacement snippet (e.g. let x = 1 or var x = 1) shown in the message.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportConditionalMethodMustReturnVoid(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String)
member.summary: Reports GS0212 when [Conditional("SYMBOL")] is applied to a function whose return type is not void. The CLR rule (matching C# CS0578) is that conditional-method calls may be elided at the call site, which is incompatible with a non-void result flowing into the surrounding expression. ADR-0047 §6 / issue #176.
member.param: The source location of the function declaration.

The type of the true-branch expression.
The type of the false-branch expression.

The type of the false-branch lvalue.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportConflictingInterfaceDefaults(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.StructSymbol,System.String,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: ADR-0085 / issue #726: GS0318 — an aggregate implements two unrelated interfaces that each provide a default body for the same method signature, and the aggregate does not declare its own override. The implementer must declare a same-name same-signature method to disambiguate (Java-style "explicit override" rule). The message names both interfaces and the disputed method so the fix is immediately apparent.
member.param: The source location of the implementing aggregate identifier.
The name of the first interface providing a default.
The name of the second interface providing a default.

member.summary: Issue #948: a const field must be given an initializer (a compile-time constant value). Reported when a const field declaration omits the = expr initializer.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportConstraintNotInterface(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String)
member.summary: Reports a type used as a type-parameter constraint that is neither an interface, a class, nor another type parameter (issue #1052 generalised the former sealed-interface restriction; issue #1056 additionally permits base-class constraints; issue #4043 additionally permits another type parameter, so this now fires only for value types such as a struct or enum).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportConstructedTypeParameterRequiresNewConstraint(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String)
member.summary: Issue #988: GS0389 — a type parameter is constructed (T()) but it carries no init() default-constructor constraint, so the compiler cannot guarantee an accessible parameterless constructor exists. Mirrors C#'s CS0304. The fix is to add an init() constraint to the type parameter (e.g. [T init()]). (Constraint keyword renamed from new() to init() by issue #997.)
member.param: The source location of the constructing identifier.
The name of the type parameter being constructed.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportDefaultStaticInterfacePropertyNotSupported(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Reports GS0396 — ADR-0089 / issue #1019: a static-virtual interface property declared inside an interface shared { … } block carries an accessor *body* (a default static slot). Default-bodied static interface properties are deferred (interface properties are abstract slots only in this release); declare an abstract slot (prop Name T { get; } / prop Name T;) instead, or expose a default via a static func in the interface shared block.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportDeferOperandHasByRefArgument(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation)
member.summary: Reports that the operand of a defer statement is a call with one or more ref/out/in arguments (issue #1635 NB-1). Eager argument capture spills each argument's evaluated value into a fresh readonly local ahead of the deferred invocation; a by-ref argument's value IS the address of its target storage, which cannot be spilled into an ordinary local without either aliasing an unrelated temp (silently breaking the by-ref contract) or requiring verifiable-IL support for spilled managed pointers that the emitter does not have. Rather than mis-defer the call, defer on such a call is rejected outright.
member.param: The text location of the operand.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportDeferOperandIsNotACall(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation)
member.summary: Reports that the operand of a defer statement is not a call expression (Phase 7.1 / ADR-0030).
member.param: The text location of the operand.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportDeinitMayNotDeclareParameters(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation)
member.summary: ADR-0068 / issue #698: reports a deinit declaration that carries a parameter list. Destructors take no parameters — the CLR invokes Finalize() with no arguments.
member.param: The location of the offending open paren.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportDeinitMayNotDeclareReturnType(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation)
member.summary: ADR-0068 / issue #698: reports a deinit declaration that carries a return type. Destructors always return void — the CLR's Finalize override may not return a value.
member.param: The location of the offending return type token.

member.param: The location of the offending deinit keyword.
The enclosing type's name (may be empty).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportDllImportNotSupported(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String)
member.summary: Reports GS0211. The diagnostic ID is reserved (issue #179 / ADR-0047 §6) for historical reasons — the v1.0 release flagged every use of @DllImport with it. ADR-0086 / issue #727 removed the blanket rejection; well-formed P/Invoke declarations now succeed and the remaining invalid-shape cases route through GS0322–GS0329. This fallback message is retained for callers that still report the old "not supported" path while a follow-up audits every call site; in the current codebase nothing fires it.
member.param: The source location of the annotation.
The attribute name as written in source.

The referenced instance member / parameter name.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportFieldOffsetInvalidOnNonExplicitLayout(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: ADR-0093 / issue #759: GS0348 — a field carries a @FieldOffset annotation but its declaring type is not declared with @StructLayout(LayoutKind.Explicit). Field offsets are only meaningful inside Explicit-layout types.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportFieldOffsetInvalidValue(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String)
member.summary: ADR-0093 / issue #759: GS0350 — the integer argument of @FieldOffset(N) is not a non-negative int32 constant.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportFieldOffsetRequiredOnExplicitLayout(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String,System.String)

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportFixedBufferAlreadyFixed(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String)
member.summary: GS0507 (ADR-0125 amendment, issue #4378): a fixed statement pins a fixed-size buffer field reached through an already-fixed variable (a local, a by-value parameter, or a pointer dereference). Such storage cannot move, so there is nothing to pin — the buffer is used directly as a pointer. Mirrors C#'s CS0213.
member.param: The text location of the pinned source expression.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.DiagnosticBag.ReportFixedBufferElementTypeNotSupported(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Text.TextLocation,System.String)
member.summary: GS0409: a fixed-size buffer element type is not a supported blittable primitive (ADR-0122 §10 / issue #1035).
