member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Emit.UserTokenResolver.TryGetSymbolicSubstitutedImportedCallReturn(System.Reflection.MethodInfo,System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol},GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol@)
member.summary:
Issue #903: when a generic imported (extension) call — e.g. a LINQ Single/First/Last whose open return type is a bare method type parameter TSource — is closed over a same-compilation user element type (List[Check].Single(…) where Check is a struct/class still being compiled), ) encodes a MethodSpec whose type argument is the symbolic Check (via ). The emitted call therefore returns the reprojected element type directly on the stack — a raw Check value for a struct, a Check reference for a class — NOT the type-erased object that the placeholder-closed reports.
Without this guard the body emitter would feed that erased object placeholder into EmitErasedObjectReturnWidening, which for a value-type element emits a spurious unbox.any Check against a stack slot that already holds a Check value (ilverify StackUnexpected/StackObjRef and a runtime crash), and for a reference-type element emits a redundant castclass. Returning the substituted symbolic return lets the caller short-circuit the widening, exactly as the instance-method and property variants above do for symbolic open-generic containers.
member.param: The placeholder-closed generic method selected by overload resolution.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Emit.UserTokenResolver.TryPromoteNonCapturingGenericLambda(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundFunctionLiteralExpression,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundBlockStatement)
member.summary: Issue #2118, extended by #4223: promotes a zero-capture local function/lambda that references one or more ENCLOSING method/class type parameters into a genuine generic method. Clones each referenced enclosing type parameter (with its constraints remapped onto the clone) and appends the clones after the function's own declared type parameters (if any — a plain, non-generic-own local function has none, so the clones become its entire list, exactly the original #2118 shape). Records the enclosing-TP -> own-clone-ordinal remap (so the signature/body encode translates references into the method's own MVar slots) and the ordered originals (used as MethodSpec type arguments both at the delegate-materialization ldftn site and, for the direct-call generic-own-TP shape, at every call site — see ). No-op for a lambda that references no enclosing type parameter.
member.param: The non-capturing lambda literal being hosted as a top-level static method.
The lambda's lowered body (walked for type-parameter references).
member.remarks: Issue #4223 (transitive case): promoting a CALLEE can, in turn, require its CALLER (another zero-capture local in the same pass) to also carry the same enclosing type parameters, purely so the call site has something to pass — a caller whose own signature/body never mentions the parameter directly (e.g. let A = func(x T) int32 { return B(x) } calling let B = func(x T) int32 { return Public() }, where only B mentions the enclosing type via an implicit static-owner call). Confirmed by direct repro: without this, the caller's emitted call site falls back to encoding the extra argument as a dangling VAR slot (silently WRONG at runtime whenever that slot's ordinal coincidentally collides with one of the caller's own — worse than a crash) or an invalid one (System.BadImageFormatException). The caller in turn discovers this need through consulting for every call it makes, so this method must be invoked to a FIXED POINT over every zero-capture literal in a pass (see ReflectionMetadataEmitter.SynthesizeClosuresAndStateMachines) — a callee promoted on a later iteration still reaches its not-yet-reprocessed callers. Each call re-derives the function's full referenced set from scratch (including whatever was already promoted, since a caller's own call sites are re-scanned every pass) rather than computing a delta, which is safe because promotion runs entirely before any metadata is emitted — no push observes an intermediate state.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Emit.WellKnownReferences.TryResolveEmbeddableAttribute(System.String,System.Type@)
member.summary: Issue #3811: resolves a compiler-embeddable attribute — one the C# compiler synthesizes into the emitting assembly when the target framework does not publish it (NullableAttribute, NullableContextAttribute) — and accepts the answer only when it is externally visible. The plain lookup with requireExternalVisibility: false is wrong for this family. Because csc embeds a private copy into every assembly whose target framework lacks the type, practically every netstandard2.0 package assembly carries an internal NullableAttribute of its own, and the first declarer in the reference closure is simply whichever of those the resolver reached first — for src/Sdk/Gsharp.NET.Sdk that was Microsoft.Build.Framework, whose copy exists only in its ref/netstandard2.0 asset. Scoping the TypeRef there emits a cross-assembly reference to a type that is neither public nor present in that package's other assets, so a downstream compilation resolving the same package for a different TFM throws TypeLoadException: Could not find type 'System.Runtime.CompilerServices.NullableAttribute' in assembly '' while reading the referencing assembly's nullability metadata — surfaced as the internal-compiler-error diagnostic GS9998. External visibility is exactly the right discriminator: an embedded copy is always internal, while every targeting pack from .NET 5 onwards declares System.Runtime.CompilerServices.NullableAttribute as a public type of System.Runtime. The resolver's externally-visible overload additionally skips an inaccessible shim and keeps searching for an accessible duplicate (issue #3445), so a closure containing both an embedded copy and the real contract assembly resolves to the contract assembly. When nothing public declares it — a downlevel target such as netstandard2.0 — the accessors bind to an embedded copy declared in this assembly (issue #4922, ); a target on a runtime that cannot embed (no source copy) keeps the old outcome of omitting the attribute. A declaration found only through the host fallback (issue #4921) counts as "nothing public declares it" for a downlevel target .
member.param: The resolved, externally visible attribute type.
member.returns: true when an externally visible declaration was found; otherwise false.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Lowering.Async.AsyncCaptureWalker.ReferenceCollector.RewriteFunctionLiteralExpression(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundFunctionLiteralExpression)
member.summary: Issue #2331 (deferred half): a parameter or local whose only reference anywhere in this async body is inside a nested lambda — including a lambda nested inside that lambda — must still contribute to the hoist set. Otherwise its value does not survive suspension across an intervening await: a resumed MoveNext call is a fresh invocation of the same method, so any variable that was not hoisted into a state-machine field is re-initialized to the CLR default instead of retaining the value it held before suspension.
member.remarks: intentionally treats a function literal as an opaque leaf (its body is a separate lexical scope), so without this override the walk above never reaches a variable read/written only inside a nested lambda body. Blindly descending into node.Body with this walker would be wrong: it would also invoke for locals the lambda itself declares, incorrectly hoisting lambda-owned state into the outer async method's state machine and breaking the lambda's own lexical scope. Instead, this reuses the capture metadata the binder already computed: lists every outer-scope variable the lambda (or any lambda transitively nested within it) needs, because LambdaBinder.CapturedVariableCollector.RewriteFunctionLiteralExpression already propagates a nested literal's own captures up into every enclosing literal's list (issue #503) — the exact mechanism 's own capture walker relies on for the same reason. additionally recurses defensively (mirroring 's walker) using a dedicated helper that itself never records a variable declaration, so a lambda's own locals are still never hoisted even if a future binder change stops fully flattening the capture list.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Lowering.Async.SpillSequenceSpiller.Spiller.RewriteConditionalGotoStatement(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundConditionalGotoStatement,System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundStatement}.Builder)
member.summary: Spills awaits that appear inside a condition. By the time the spiller runs, the Lowerer and the statement binder have already desugared if/while/for/do-while statements into label/goto form, so an await embedded in a branch or loop condition lives here rather than in a (issue #1266). Without this case the condition await leaked un-rewritten to the emitter, which threw GS9998.
member.remarks: The spilled side-effects (including the await suspension points) are emitted immediately before the conditional goto. For loops the binder places the loop's check: label directly ahead of this conditional goto, so the spilled condition computation sits inside the loop and is re-evaluated on every iteration — preserving while/for/do-while re-evaluation semantics. The call also handles short-circuiting &&/|| conditions (see SpillLogicalAnd/ SpillLogicalOr), so a right-operand await only runs when the left operand requires it.

member.summary: Spills a (e.g. an interpolated string lowered to the handler pattern, issue #368) by flattening its statements through the statement rewriter — lifting any awaits to statement level — and then spilling the trailing value expression. The hole pre-evaluation in InterpolatedStringHandlerLowerer guarantees awaits precede the (possibly ByRefLike) handler local, so no handler local is live across a suspension after this flattening.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Lowering.Async.SpillSequenceSpiller.Spiller.SpillConditional(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundConditionalExpression)
member.summary: Spills a ternary/conditional expression (issue #1619). Unlike a plain binary expression, only one of WhenTrue/WhenFalse executes at runtime, so an await in an arm must not run unconditionally. This mirrors the if/else-with-goto expansion used by /: the condition (if it itself has an await) is spilled unconditionally first, then each arm's side effects are guarded behind a label so only the taken arm's await(s) actually run.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Lowering.Async.SpillSequenceSpiller.Spiller.SpillConditionalAddress(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundConditionalAddressExpression)
member.summary:
Spills a conditional address-of expression (ADR-0061; issue #1619 completion). Unlike 's ternary case, the *result* here is a managed pointer (T&), which cannot be carried across the if/else join in a plain spill temp: — the pass that runs immediately after this one — eliminates every T&-typed local by re-deriving its address from a *single* declaration-site template at every use site, since state-machine field hoisting can never hold a managed pointer. A local reassigned differently in each branch (one address in the "then" arm, a different one in the "else" arm) breaks that single-template assumption — the hoister only tracks the last template it walks over lexically, so it would silently rewrite every read to whichever branch's address expression appears last in the statement list, regardless of which branch actually ran (this was caught by Await_In_Conditional_Address_Condition_Selects_Correct_RefBranch failing with the wrong branch's value).
The fix: never store the address itself across the join. Only the (plain-typed, non-byref) sub-expressions that an await could be nested inside — e.g. an indexer's index, a field access's receiver — are spilled, and only inside a guard that runs solely when that operand is the one selected (so its await never fires on the unchosen branch). The two (possibly-rebuilt) lvalue trees are then fed back into a fresh so the existing, unmodified EmitConditionalAddress emitter still performs the actual branch-and-take-address IL — it just re-evaluates the (already spilled, side-effect-free) condition a second time and reads whichever branch's temps were populated.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Lowering.Async.SpillSequenceSpiller.Spiller.SpillExpression(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundExpression)
member.summary: Core spilling: recursively visit an expression, returning a whose Value has no embedded awaits (they've all been lifted out as side-effect statements). If the expression has no awaits, returns a trivial spill sequence.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Lowering.Async.SpillSequenceSpiller.Spiller.SpillNullConditionalAccess(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundNullConditionalAccessExpression)
member.summary: Spills a null-conditional access (?.) expression (issue #1619 completion). Mirrors : the receiver is always evaluated (spilled unconditionally if it has an await), but — and any await inside it — must only run on the non-nil path, so that path is expanded into explicit if/else statements instead of letting the opaque single-expression emission (EmitNullConditionalAccess) own it. The not-null branch reuses the general-purpose conversion emitter (rather than duplicating EmitNullConditionalAccess's bespoke Nullable-wrap IL) to lift a value-typed result into when needed.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Lowering.Async.SpillSequenceSpiller.Spiller.SpillSwitch(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Binding.BoundSwitchExpression)
member.summary: Spills a switch expression (issue #1619 completion). A guard (when clause) containing await stays diagnostic-gated: a false guard must fall through to the next arm's pattern test, and replicating that retry as bound-tree control flow would mean re-implementing the whole pattern-matching decision tree ( and friends) instead of reusing it — a duplication this pass avoids for every other kind. The discriminant and each arm's result value, however, are fully spillable: this method reuses the existing (unmodified) pattern-match dispatch to select which arm matched — by building a second, award-free "index" switch whose arms carry the same patterns/guards but return the arm's ordinal instead of its real result — and only then evaluates the *selected* arm's (possibly awaiting) result, via an if/else-if chain on the stored index. Any locals a pattern binds (e.g. case Point(var x, var y)) are still assigned by the (unmodified, reused) pattern test itself, so they remain visible to the result-evaluation chain.

Spills a target/pointer expression together with a following argument list, preserving the rule that the target is evaluated before any argument (issue #1619). Used for indirect calls, function-pointer invocations, and CLR indexers.

Spills two operands evaluated eagerly, left-to-right (no short circuiting) — mirrors the non-logical path of and . If the second operand has an await, the first is spilled to a stable temp first (unless it's already pure/constant) so its value survives the suspension.

Issue #4965 (ADR-0202): stores a spilled operand in a fresh temp and returns the read of it. An operand of the bottom (never) type — a throw expression, or a block, if or switch every path of which exits — is never stored: it runs as a statement, and the operand becomes the unreachable throw nil trap. Nothing after it runs, so no later operand, await or call is reached; even a state machine's resume edge into the rest of the sequence only reaches a throw. never has no CLR form, so a temp of that type could not be encoded (GS9998).
member.param: The spill locals of the current sequence.
The side effects of the current sequence.
member.returns: The expression that reads the stored operand.

Issue #3730: now belongs to the reference closure's reflection context while may still be a host RuntimeType (every built-in TypeSymbol wraps one), so the argument is projected into the handler's context first. Left unprojected, MakeGenericMethod yields a System.Reflection.Emit.MethodBuilderInstantiation whose GetParameters() answers the unsubstituted T — the same cross-context artefact #3752 hit through MakeGenericType. The projection goes through ClrTypeUtilities.RemapHostCoreTypeToContext, which is the sibling probe that was already right: the user-handler path in InterpolatedStringHandlerInfo has closed its AppendFormatted over a remapped typeof(object) since #368, while the default-handler path here closed over raw host types. Same helper, same question, one of the two arms omitted it. It is best-effort by construction: a type the reference set cannot name falls back to the raw argument rather than failing the compile.

member.remarks:
For each user try { … } finally { … } that contains yield statements, Dispose must run the finally block when invoked while the enumerator is suspended inside that try. The suspension is identified by the current state field value, which equals one of the yield states inside the try.
Nested try-finally with yields produces innermost-first walking so that inner finallies run before their enclosers, matching the normal stack-unwinding semantics on foreach early break.
If the iterator body contains no yields inside any try-finally the body is the trivial state = -1; return; as before.

A call that had one candidate, a property, a field or an event answers that symbol alone. <list type="table"> <item>Imported function or method: the reflected overloads the resolver held, as imported function symbols; derived type first, then its bases; within a type by metadata token.</item> <item>Local function: the function alone (a lexical group has one member).</item> <item>Free source function: the functions of that name in the package, by file path (ordinal), then by start position.</item> <item>Method of a class or struct: the methods of that name declared by the receiver's type, then those of its base classes, and a call through a constructed base or interface keeps the declaring type's signatures.</item> <item>Interface method: the methods of that name of the interface and of its base interfaces; the private helpers only for a query inside the interface.</item> <item>Type parameter with constraints: the methods of that name of each constraint, in constraint order.</item> <item>Partial type: the methods of every part, by file path (ordinal), then by start position.</item> </list> Constructor calls and extension methods dispatched as instance calls are not in the contract. The compilation must have set before its first query; a compilation without it answers an empty array for every node.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.SemanticModel.LookupMembers(System.Int32,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol,System.String,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Returns the members of that a member access at can name, instance and static, as symbols.
member.param: A character offset into this model's tree.
When given, only the members of this name.
Cancels index construction on first use.
member.returns: The members in the order of the table, empty when none matches.
member.remarks: Contract, one row per receiver type. T? and T! first answer for T. <list type="table"> <item>Tuple: the declared element names, then the positional ItemN names, as fields in element order.</item> <item>Struct or class, declared or imported record: fields, properties, events and methods of the type and of its base classes, base classes last (instance members), then the static members of the type itself. A static member of a base class is not a member of the derived type.</item> <item>Struct or class, then (issue #5441): the public instance members of the nearest imported base class (reached through source base classes), or of object when there is none, read at that base, in metadata order. A static or non-public member of the base is not listed. A member that the type or a source base overrides is not listed: the override stands for the slot.</item> <item>Struct or class, then (issue #5441): each default method of an interface the type or one of its base classes implements, interfaces in declaration order and their base interfaces after them, when neither the type nor a base class declares a method of that name (the rule of the call binder). A private helper is listed only where the enclosing declaration may access it.</item> <item>Interface: the properties, events and methods of the interface and of its base interfaces (instance), the static members of the interface itself, then the members of each CLR interface the declared interfaces extend, nearest first.</item> <item>Enum: the enum members, which are static.</item> <item>Any other type that has a CLR type (imported types, arrays, maps, primitives): the public properties without index parameters, fields, methods that are not special names, then events, each in metadata order; instance and static members; types read through the ADR-0193 readers at the receiver. For an interface, the members of the CLR interfaces it extends follow its own (issue #5441), each in the same order, in the order of the guarded transitive interface list .</item> <item>A slice, array, map, channel or sequence with no CLR type, because its element is a source type or a type parameter (issue #5441): the members of the type the call binder uses for the receiver (System.Array, Dictionary, Channel, ChannelReader, ChannelWriter, IEnumerable), with member types read at the receiver's type arguments. The list is the one the same collection of a primitive has, extensions aside.</item> </list> A member that is private or protected is returned only when the enclosing declaration of may access it. Imported members are public ones. With , only members of that name: a method name returns every overload, in declaration order. Extension members (ADR-0212 question 12), last and for every receiver type that is not an error: <list type="table"> <item>Extension function declared in source: each one in scope whose receiver type can take the receiver, found by the rule a call by that name uses, as the function symbol. Order: file path (ordinal), then start position.</item> <item>Extension method of an imported class: each static [Extension] method of the classes in the namespaces the file imports whose first parameter can take the receiver, by the rule of the call binder, as an imported function symbol whose parameters include the receiver. A receiver with no CLR shape (a declared class) is probed as its imported base class, and through the interface it implements when it has none or the base is object. Order: the holder classes in reference order, then metadata order. Generic methods keep their open signature.</item> </list> An extension is listed even where a member of the same name hides it at a call, and the receiver of a static access (a type name) gets the same extensions as an instance.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.SemanticModel.LookupSymbols(System.Int32,System.String,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Returns the symbols a simple name resolves to at in this tree, one symbol per name: the innermost declaration shadows.
member.param: A character offset into this model's tree.
When given, only the symbol of this name.
Cancels index construction on first use.
member.returns: The symbols, empty when none resolves.
member.remarks: Contract, tiers from innermost to outermost; a tier only answers a name no inner tier answered. <list type="table"> <item>Locals (tier 1): a let or var is visible from the end of its declaration (from the start of its initializer when that is a function literal, so it can call itself) to the end of the nearest enclosing block or block expression; an if, for or if let header initializer to the end of its statement; an if let binding from the end of its clause to the end of the then-region (never the else branch); a while let binding from the end of its clause to the end of the body; a guard let binding to the end of the enclosing block; a for, await for or tuple for variable through its body; a catch variable through its when filter and body; a parameter (also a destructured, lambda or function-literal parameter) through its function, constructor, lambda, literal or accessor; the pattern variable of a switch case or arm through that case or arm; any other pattern variable from its declaration to the end of the enclosing block.</item> <item>The implicit ctx of a scope is visible in the scope body.</item> <item>The implicit this parameter of the enclosing instance method, constructor, destructor or accessor follows the locals.</item> <item>Members (tier 2): inside an instance method, constructor or accessor of a struct or class, the members of that type reachable without a receiver, inherited ones included; inside a shared member or a field initializer, the static ones. An instance member wins over a static member of the same name, whatever the depth, as in the binder.</item> <item>Globals (tier 3): the compilation's functions, variables, structs, interfaces, enums and delegates, then those of the prior submissions, newest first, when the compilation is a submission. A type alias is found by its name and answers the type it names; the enumeration does not list it (the symbol would carry the target's name).</item> </list> Order: scope depth innermost first, then declaration order within a scope. The globals are listed in source order across kinds (files by name, then position), and the members of a type by their depth in its hierarchy, so the result is deterministic. Imported (CLR) types are not listed.

member.summary:
Issue #4453: the C# CS1540 receiver rule for protected instance members. Outside its declaring class, a derived class may reach a protected instance member only through a receiver whose static type is that derived class or a class derived from it, because a receiver typed as the base (or a sibling) may be an instance of some other subclass. The CLR enforces the same rule (ILVerify reports MethodAccess/FieldAccess).
This reports only the receiver half: it returns false when already rejects the access, so the caller never reports the same access twice. Static members, which have no receiver, are exempt, as in C#.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ClrNullability.ClassifyFlag(System.Byte)
member.summary: ADR-0186 §2: maps one C# nullable-metadata byte onto what it says. The per-byte half of , kept separate because NullableFlagsBuilder reads bytes out of an already-expanded array and so has no position to classify. Any byte other than 1 or 2 is . That is not leniency: 0 is the oblivious byte, and csc emits no other value, so an unexpected byte can only mean the reader has been handed something it cannot interpret — for which "the declarer said nothing" is the honest reading and the safe one.
member.param: A single C# nullable-metadata byte (0, 1 or 2).
member.returns: What that byte says.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ClrNullability.ClassifyPosition(System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{System.Byte},System.Int32)
member.summary: ADR-0186 §2 — the three-state classifier, and the successor to 's two-valued answer. Maps the DFS position within onto what the declarer actually said about it: shapeResult empty (no [Nullable], no [NullableContext] anywhere) length 1, flags[0] == 0 (oblivious context) length 1, flags[0] == 1 length 1, flags[0] == 2 length > 1, flags[index] == 0 length > 1, flags[index] == 1 length > 1, flags[index] == 2 length > 1, index beyond the array — the declaration supplied no byte for this position, which is the same statement as supplying none at all A scalar/context byte is a genuine statement about every position, so it is classified directly rather than treated as absent.
member.param: The nullable-flags byte array (possibly empty or scalar).
The DFS position index of the reference-type position.
member.returns: What the declaration says about that position.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ClrNullability.CountNullabilityBytes(System.Type)
member.summary: Counts the number of bytes the C# compiler emits for in a [NullableAttribute] byte array. The count follows the CLR DFS pre-order layout: reference and array positions contribute one byte, as does a closed generic value type's leading oblivious placeholder. Nullable<T> is transparent and contributes only T's subtree; generic parameters contribute one slot (forced to 0 for a struct constraint); non-generic value types contribute none.
member.returns: The number of nullability bytes this type occupies.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ClrNullability.DefaultAbsentFill
member.summary: ADR-0186 §2: returns the byte an absent position expands to, which is not a detail but the rule itself written as a value. ADR-0136 says an absent position means T?, so the fill is 2. ADR-0186 says it means T!, so under the fill becomes 0 — the oblivious byte, which then reads as . This must track the mode, and an implementer who leaves it at 2 gets a silent drift rather than a failure: the layout/projection paths ( → ProjectNullableFlags, and NullableFlagsBuilder.MergeDeclarationNullability's declaredFlags) would expand an absent byte to 2 and read the position as T?, while the direct path ( over the raw flags) reads the very same declaration as T!. Two readers disagreeing about one declaration is precisely the #3705 family-2 defect ADR-0136's single-predicate rule exists to prevent, and ADR-0186 explicitly preserves that rule. Platform-types is the default since ADR-0186 step 3, so 0 is the ordinary answer. Under --nullability=enabled this is the literal constant 2 the two-argument overload always used, so that mode keeps ADR-0136's reading unchanged.
member.returns: The fill byte for positions the declaration did not supply.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ClrNullability.ExpandNullableFlags(System.Type,System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{System.Byte})
member.summary: Expands scalar, context-only, or absent nullable metadata to the CLR per-position layout for . Generic value-type placeholders are emitted as oblivious byte 0, while metadata-transparent Nullable<T> recurses directly into T. Struct-constrained generic parameters likewise force a 0 slot. Empty and missing positions use the importer's current reading rule and expand to — byte 0 (oblivious) under ADR-0186's platform-types mode, which is the default since step 3, and byte 2 (nullable-by-default, ADR-0136) under --nullability=enabled.
member.param: Physical nullable flags, possibly scalar or empty.
member.returns: One byte per CLR nullable-metadata position.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ClrNullability.ExpandNullableFlags(System.Type,System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{System.Byte},System.Byte)
member.summary:
Issue #3705 family 2: ) with an explicit fill for positions the declaration did not supply.
The fill the two-argument overload chooses IS the reading rule. Under --nullability=enabled it is 2 — the #1354 rule, "the declarer said nothing, so assume nullable" — and under ADR-0186's platform-types mode, the default since step 3, it is 0 (see ). Either way it is right for a concrete reference position and wrong for an OPEN type-parameter position, whose nullability comes from the substituted argument instead. A caller that must distinguish "the declaration explicitly said 2" from "the declaration was silent and the ADR-0136 reading defaulted it to 2" cannot do it from the default expansion, because both look identical. Passing absentFill: 0 yields the literal reading in either mode.
A scalar or context byte is a genuine statement about every position and is preserved under both fills; only truly absent and beyond-length positions differ.
member.param: Physical nullable flags, possibly scalar or empty.
Byte to use for positions the declaration did not supply.
member.returns: One byte per CLR nullable-metadata position.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ClrNullability.GetNotNullIfNotNullParameters(System.Reflection.MethodInfo)

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ClrNullability.IsFlagNonNull(System.Byte)
member.summary: Issue #1354, issue #3705 family 2 — the predicate that turns one C# nullable-metadata byte into G#'s answer, and the only place in the compiler allowed to decide it. G#'s import rule is the inverse of C#'s. C# reads "nullable iff the byte is 2", so oblivious (0) and absent metadata mean non-null. G# reads "non-null iff the byte is 1", so oblivious and absent both mean T?. Two readers open-coding the two rules is exactly how the #3705 nullability family kept producing member kinds that disagreed about the same declaration, so the rule lives here and and NullableFlagsBuilder.MergeDeclarationNullability both defer to it rather than comparing bytes themselves. ADR-0186 §2 preserves that single-predicate principle and gives it a third value: the byte classifier is now and this predicate is a projection of it. G#'s rule "non-null iff the byte is 1" is unchanged; what changed is that the other two answers are no longer the same answer, because 0/absent means T! and only 2 means T?.
member.param: A single C# nullable-metadata byte (0, 1 or 2).
member.returns: true only for 1 (not-annotated).

member.summary: Issue #1354: applies the "unannotated imported reference types are nullable by default" (Kotlin-style) reading rule to a single reference-type position. Given the nullable-flags array returned by and the DFS position : empty (no [Nullable] and no [NullableContext] anywhere) → nullable (T?). A single scalar/context byte (flags.Length == 1) applies to every position: non-null iff that byte is 1. A per-position array (flags.Length > 1): non-null iff flags[index] == 1. Only an explicit 1 (NotAnnotated) means a non-null reference type; 2 (Annotated), 0 (oblivious) and absent are all NOT non-null. ADR-0186 §2: this predicate is now a projection of , which is the real reader. It survives because "is this position non-null?" is a question several callers genuinely only need a bool for, and its answer is unchanged — but it is no longer sufficient on its own, because false now covers two different declarations (T? and T!). A caller that needs to tell them apart must ask .
member.param: The nullable-flags byte array (possibly empty or scalar).
The DFS position index of the reference-type position.
member.returns: true when the position is explicitly non-null.

member.summary: Returns whether two s refer to the same logical CLR type, regardless of which reflection context produced them. Two types are considered the same when their s match.

member.remarks: Issue #504-reopen: constructed generics, arrays, by-ref, and pointer types are compared structurally (definition + element / type arguments) rather than by raw . The FullName of a constructed generic (e.g. Nullable) embeds the assembly-qualified name of every type argument (System.Boolean, System.Private.CoreLib, …), and those assembly identities differ across reflection contexts — the host runtime's System.Boolean lives in System.Private.CoreLib while the MetadataLoadContext-loaded reference-assembly System.Boolean lives in the System.Runtime facade — so the embedded strings diverge even when the two types denote the same logical CLR shape. Recursing on the type definition plus each leaf type argument keeps the cross-context identity check correct, since leaf non-generic types have an assembly-independent .

member.summary: Issue #338 (generalizing the #321 fix): determines whether an exception thrown while reflecting over a CLR member's signature is a metadata/assembly load failure. Such failures arise when a member's signature (parameter, return, property, field, or event-handler type) references a type that cannot be loaded or projected under the reference — for example a ref-struct type or a type living in a transitive assembly that was not supplied via /r:. Member enumeration sites treat the offending member as absent rather than letting the throw sink the whole member set; any other exception is left to propagate. This is the single shared predicate used by every CLR member enumeration site (overload resolution, property/field/event/constructor enumeration, and the member-access binding path).
member.param: The exception observed while evaluating a member.
member.returns: Whether the exception represents a tolerable load failure.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ClrTypeUtilities.IsRuntimeProvidedType(System.Type)

member.returns: true when the type is a host System.RuntimeType.
member.remarks:
RuntimeType.MakeGenericType answers a real RuntimeType only when EVERY type argument is itself a RuntimeType. Hand it one that is not — a RoType, or an in-flight — and it silently answers a System.Reflection.Emit.TypeBuilderInstantiation instead, a structural placeholder whose GetMethod, GetProperty and GetConstructor all throw . Such a type is non-null and looks usable, so a plain ClrType != null gate lets it through and the failure surfaces much later as a missing member or an internal compiler error.
The same predicate is spelled inline in the emitter (MethodBodyEmitter.IsRuntimeProvidedType, ADR-0174 D12's ChannelElementNeedsSymbolicType); this is the binder-side spelling of it.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ClrTypeUtilities.IsValueTypeSafe(System.Type)
member.summary: Issue #3764: returns whether is a CLR value type, answering correctly for types that reached the compiler from outside the reflection context asking the question. is not a metadata predicate: every implementation answers it by comparing the type's against its own context's System.ValueType. Inside a that identity is the System.ValueType of the context's core assembly, so a type whose base comes from some other assembly compares unequal and the property answers false for a genuine struct — silently, with no exception. That is not hypothetical. Compiling a netstandard2.0 target whose reference closure does not declare DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler, the resolver's fallback assembly loader supplies the host's System.Private.CoreLib definition; the context's core assembly is netstandard, so the handler answers IsValueType == false while simultaneously answering IsByRefLike == true and reporting BaseType == System.ValueType — a contradiction only a value type can produce. Emit decisions keyed on the raw property then chose callvirt plus a by-value receiver for a struct's instance call and produced IL that only ILVerify rejected. The fallback is exact rather than heuristic: in ECMA-335 a value type is precisely a type whose immediate base is System.ValueType (or System.Enum, itself the base of enums). Structs never have deeper hierarchies, so one hop by name settles it. System.Enum is excluded explicitly: it is a class that derives from System.ValueType.
member.returns: true when is a CLR value type.

member.remarks: RoDefinitionType.MakeGenericType accepts only arguments loaded by its own context and throws for any host RuntimeType. Callers that already treat the rejection as "no closure" test this first. A false answer does not promise success: other contexts and constraint violations still throw, and callers keep their catch for those.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ClrTypeUtilities.SafeIsOverride(System.Reflection.MethodInfo)
member.summary: Issue #2291: safely determines whether a property accessor OVERRIDES a base declaration, tolerating a that does not support (it throws unconditionally for every virtual method, not just an unresolvable one). A genuine C# record's EqualityContract property getter is virtual (so a derived record can widen it), which is exactly the shape that first surfaced this: building a semantic aggregate for an imported record under an MLC-backed resolver must not crash just because ONE property happens to be virtual. Falls back to "not an override" on failure — the same conservative default every other MLC-safe query in this file uses.

member.returns: true when the accessor is confirmed to override a base declaration.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.Display.SymbolDisplay.TryFormatWithPlatformArguments(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullabilityAnnotatedTypeSymbol,System.String@)
member.summary: Issue #4361: renders an annotated imported type from its nullability-applied arguments when — and only when — one of them is platform-typed. The annotated wrapper's own name is its base type's, so a nested argument's nullability never reached a diagnostic: Arbitrary[Type!] and Arbitrary[Type] both printed Arbitrary[Type], and a conversion ADR-0186 §3 rule 3 correctly rejects read as "Cannot convert type 'X' to 'X'". Platform-ness is exactly the case where the two sides can differ in nothing else, so it is the case rendered here, consistently with how a top-level T! is already displayed. (A nested ? is left as before on purpose: surfacing it everywhere is a separate display change with a much wider blast radius, and nothing in the conversion rules turns on it alone.)
member.param: The rendered name when this applies.
member.returns: true when a nested argument is platform-typed.

member.summary: Issue #1624 regression fix: appends the identity-key fragment for a type that is neither a type parameter, a function type, nor a same-compilation user type without CLR backing. Such a type either has no ClrType (the true singleton built-ins like void/error, safely shared by name) or carries a live — a built-in primitive (a genuine process-wide singleton) or an projected from a (a distinct instance per compilation even when the simple name matches, e.g. two test compilations that each define a "Holder" class). Keying by the CLR object's identity keeps every true singleton shared while never aliasing two same-named types loaded by different compilations.
member.param: The key builder to append to.
The type whose fallback key fragment to append.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ImportedAssemblySemantics.TryDetectCSharpRecordSemantics(System.Type,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ImportedTypeSemantics@)
member.summary: Issue #2291: recognizes a genuine C# compiler-emitted record / record struct shape when the assembly it lives in was compiled by the C# compiler (not gsc) and therefore never wrote a marker for it. Every C# record synthesizes a PrintMembers method and a copy constructor (.ctor(SameType)); a record class additionally synthesizes a public parameterless <Clone>$ method and a protected/internal EqualityContract property (a record struct has neither — value-type copying makes them unnecessary). Requiring the FULL marker set for the type's value/reference kind keeps this from ever misclassifying a hand-written class/struct that merely happens to declare one of these members incidentally.
member.param: The externally-referenced CLR type to inspect.
member.returns: true when has the full record shape.

member.summary: Gets or creates the imported type symbol for the given CLR type.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ImportedTypeSymbol.GetConstructed(System.Type,System.Type,System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol})
member.summary: #313: gets the generic type constructed over one or more in-scope type parameters (e.g. List[T]). Issue #5158: equal constructions share one instance. Two calls are equal when they pass the same erased closed type object, the same open definition object and the same argument symbol objects in the same order.
member.param: The type-erased closed CLR type (type parameters projected onto object).
The open generic CLR definition (e.g. List<>).
The symbolic type arguments, possibly containing .
member.returns: The constructed .
member.remarks: The table is a chain of weak tables, one level per key part. The symbol at the end of the chain is held through a , not directly: the symbol refers to every key above it, so a strong value under a long-lived last key (a primitive argument) would keep the erased type, and with it the whole reference context, alive. While any caller holds the symbol, equal calls get the same instance; once all callers drop it, a later call builds a new one, which nobody can tell apart. Keys use reference identity, so a symbol from another reference set, another nullability mode (a nullable or platform-type annotation is a different argument object) or another argument identity never answers for this one. A missing deduplication is harmless; an alias would not be. Each symbol is built once under the lock of its entry and published after it is fully built, and an exception while building publishes nothing. No collection is iterated, so the table does not affect ordering or output.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ImportedTypeSymbol.GetWithoutNullability(System.Type,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullabilityFreeReason)
member.summary: ADR-0193 §3: for an audited, nullability-free conversion — the twin of , for callers that need the imported symbol itself rather than 's primitive and tuple mapping. GSA0007 checks it exactly as it checks that door: allowed anywhere, except on a signature accessor.
member.returns: The cached .

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ImportedTypeSymbol.ReifyClosedClrType
member.summary: Issue #2381: recursively reconstructs the TRUE closed CLR type for this constructed generic, recomputing every type argument's CLR type from its CURRENT state rather than trusting the cached (possibly erased) .
member.returns: The reconstructed closed CLR type, or the cached (possibly erased) when reification is not possible.
member.remarks:
A constructed closed over a same-compilation class/struct argument (e.g. List[DiagnosticCheck]) caches an object-erased shape (List<object>) because, at the time ran during binding, the argument's own CLR type (its emitted TypeBuilder) did not exist yet — see . That erased shape is safe for member/index/conversion resolution during binding, but is wrong for final metadata (method signatures, generic builder instantiation, field types) once the argument's real CLR type is available.
This walks + and rebuilds the closed type via using each argument's CURRENT CLR type, recursing into nested constructed generics (e.g. List[List[UserClass]], Dictionary[string, UserClass]) so every level reflects its real closed shape. Value-typed nullable arguments are projected through so they close over Nullable<T> rather than the bare value type.
Falls back to the cached (possibly erased) when reification is not possible: an in-scope type parameter argument () has no concrete CLR type to close over; a nested argument's own CLR type is still unavailable; or legitimately rejects the reconstructed arguments (CLR generic constraints).

A prior version of this method only matched a tuple sitting DIRECTLY at the top of the position being merged (optionally under one Nullable wrapper) — so a named tuple nested one level deeper, e.g. IReadOnlyList[(string Key, string? Value)] reached through an async Task[...] return, was silently left unnamed: this method returned unchanged because the top-level shape () didn't match either pattern, even though (which recurses) correctly said "yes, look deeper" to the caller.

member.summary: ADR-0193 amendment (2026-09-26, #4451, owner decision): an explicit method type argument that closes an open slot the declaration leaves oblivious reads as T!. Ob.WrapList[string](x) over an oblivious List<T> WrapList<T>(T value) binds T = string!: its parameter takes a nil unchecked, as the C# does, and its return is List[string!], so a nil element is checked where it is read. This narrows 's Unchanged only for an explicit reference type argument at an oblivious slot; an annotated or enabled slot, a value-type argument, and an argument that already states its nullability (string?, string!) are unchanged. Inference reaches the same answer on its own (#4459: an oblivious slot keeps the argument's T!).
member.param: What the open declaration says about the slot the type parameter fills.
member.returns: The type the type parameter is bound to.

member.summary: Issue #4403: the direct parameter reader lifts a reference parameter whose default value is null to T?. That is a G#-side inference from the default value, not a classified metadata position, so it is named here rather than passed off as an Annotated state. Only ClrNullability.GetParameterTypeSymbol applies it today; #4403 decides whether the other readers should.
member.returns: The parameter type, stated nullable.

member.summary: The byte-domain applier for an open slot, for the projection reader (ClrNullability.ProjectNullableFlags), which rewrites a flag array rather than building a . The argument is an erased closed CLR type and so states no nullability of its own: every position in it reads as not-annotated, which is how the merge reader reads the same argument after . A Nullable decision annotates the argument's root only — never its inner positions, which belong to the argument, not the slot.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullabilityImportRule.DecideOpenSlot(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ClrNullabilityState,GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeArgumentKind)
member.summary:
ADR-0186 §2's open-type-parameter carve-out plus ADR-0193 owner decision 1: an open slot widens to T? only for an explicit [Nullable(2)], and only when the argument is known to be a reference type. Every other cell leaves the argument to speak for itself. DeclaredReference / Value / Unknown
AnnotatedNullable / Unchanged / Unchanged
NotAnnotatedUnchanged in every column
Oblivious / absentUnchanged in every column
The Annotated × Unknown cell is Unchanged by the owner's 2026-09-24 ruling (ADR-0193 Open question 1). Revisiting it as Platform is #4385, a Phase 3 exit criterion — not this class's call to make on its own.
member.param: What the open declaration says about the slot.
What is known about the substituted argument.
member.returns: The decision.

member.summary: The inverse of , for method type-argument inference: given the argument a call passes to an open slot, the type argument that slot must be closed over. Where widens a Reference argument to T?, a X? argument passed to that slot supplies T := X. This is C#'s rule: Required<T>(T? value) where T : class called with a Type? infers T as Type, so the call returns Type. Every other cell hands the argument back unchanged. A value type int? is its own argument (T := int? for an unconstrained T?), and so is a T! platform value.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullableLifting.IsAnyValueTypeNullable(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullableTypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #1700: unifies (BCL / open struct-constrained type-parameter underlyings, which carry a runtime ClrType) and (same- compilation user struct/enum underlyings, which do not) into a single predicate for emit-side code that must treat every value-type Nullable<T> receiver the same way — e.g. the null- conditional-access receiver probe, which cannot use brtrue directly on a Nullable<T> struct value (ilverify StackUnexpected) regardless of which kind of T it wraps.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullableLifting.IsUserValueTypeNullable(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullableTypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #1572: returns true when wraps a user-declared value type emitted in the current compilation — a value-kind (i.e. !IsClass) or an . Such underlyings have a null CLR during emit, so the ClrType probe misclassifies them as reference nullables. Emit and slot-planning code that must close System.Nullable1 over the emitted TypeDef/TypeSpec (rather than a host Type) uses this symbol-aware predicate to detect them. Both the slot collectors and the corresponding emit arms call it so the two sides stay in exact agreement.
member.returns: true for a user value-type Nullable<T>.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullableLifting.IsValueTypeNullable(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullableTypeSymbol)
member.summary: Issue #504: a whose underlying CLR type is a value type maps to the CLR struct System.Nullable<T> — a distinct CLR value type with its own layout and ctor. over a reference type, by contrast, shares the CLR representation of T (the wrapper is a binder-level annotation; ldnull is a valid value for it). Emit-time conversion logic for value-type Nullable<T> needs a newobj Nullable<T>::.ctor(T) for the lift, an initobj for the default value, and box Nullable<T> for object widening — none of which the reference-type path handles.
member.returns: true when the underlying type has a CLR value-type representation.

member.summary: Returns true when is a constructed System.Nullable<T> (i.e. closed-generic over the open System.Nullable1 definition). The open definition itself and non-generic / unconstructed types return false.
member.returns: true for a constructed Nullable<T>.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullableLifting.RequiresSymbolicNullableGetValue(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.NullableTypeSymbol)
member.summary:
Issue #2333: returns true when wraps an underlying whose Nullable<T>::get_Value() MemberRef cannot be built from a runtime (the emit-side WellKnownReferences.GetNullableGetValueReference helper) because the underlying has no ClrType during emit. Three shapes qualify:
a user-declared value-kind struct or enum (see );
an open type parameter constrained to struct — its Nullable<T> instantiation closes over a
generic-parameter var/mvar signature slot, not a resolvable host Type.
a tuple whose symbolic element annotations prevent a direct ClrType, while its runtime
representation remains System.ValueTuple. All shapes route through the emit-side ReflectionMetadataEmitter.GetNullableGetValueMemberRefForUserValueType helper, which builds the MemberRef symbolically off the emitted/encoded parent TypeSpec instead. Callers that must pick between the ClrType-based and symbolic get_Value paths (EmitUnary's !! arm, the null-conditional receiver probe, and NullableValueTypeUnwrapCollector's slot-planning pass) use this single predicate so all three stay in agreement.
member.returns: true when the symbolic get_Value path is required.

member.summary: ADR-0186 §1 / ADR-0132: the ! follows the same positional rule as 's ?, and it needs a parallel implementation rather than falling out for free. A platform array/slice must render with the ! bound to the array itself ([]!T / [N]!T) so its display name is distinct from a slice of platform elements ([]T! = Slice(Platform(T))) — the exact distinction ADR-0132 draws for []?T versus []T?. A platform function type wraps the whole arrow shape in parentheses (((int32) -> void)!) so the ! applies to the function type and not just its return type. For every other underlying type the marker trails the name (T!).
member.returns: The G# display name for the platform wrapper.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.PlatformTypeSymbol.Get(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary:
Returns the platform type T! over the given underlying type, normalised exactly as is, in the mirror direction (ADR-0193 §2).
Wrapping a is a no-op.
Wrapping a returns it unchanged: an explicit statement always beats the
absence of one (ADR-0186 §3), so T?! is T?. With 's own normalisation, neither T?! nor T!? can be constructed.
Wrapping a value type returns it unchanged: T! is a statement about a reference position, and a
value type has no reference nullability to leave unstated. "Value type" is )'s answer, the same classifier the import rule uses.
member.returns: A cached platform wrapper, or itself when one of the normalisations above applies.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.PlatformTypeSymbol.StripTopLevel(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol)
member.summary: Reads through a top-level platform wrapper: 's underlying type when it is T!, and itself otherwise. For the structural questions the binder and lowerer ask of a declared type — "is this an iterator return type, and of what?", "is this a task, and what does it await?" — T! is T: whether the value itself may be nil says nothing about its shape. ADR-0186 §9 is what makes this routine, because every unadorned reference a G# declaration writes inside an oblivious scope is wrapped, including an iterator's IEnumerable[string] and an async function's Task[string]. Those helpers match on the symbolic shape first (is ImportedTypeSymbol, is SequenceTypeSymbol) and fall back to the erased ClrType, so without this a wrapped IEnumerable[string!] silently answered string — and every yield of an oblivious value was coerced to non-null.
member.returns: The type with any top-level platform wrapper removed.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ReferenceImageSet.TryResolveVisibleName(System.String,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Finds the type definition that a well-known name denotes. With requireCoreLibrary, the definition must live in a core library, the same rule as : a namesake in another assembly never becomes the entry, even when it comes first. The names that the runtime binds specially need it (the tagged types and System.TypedReference). Other framework types, such as System.Collections.Generic.List1, live in several assemblies of a reference set, so the first writer owns them. Among the allowed definitions, the first public one in reference order wins, because a dependency can embed an internal copy of a framework type (#3445, #4233). With no public copy, the first allowed definition stands. No allowed definition gives null, and the table then holds a missing type.
member.remarks: The grant of InternalsVisibleTo to the consumer is not applied here. It belongs to the compilation, not to the set (ADR-0209 section 7c).

member.summary: Attempts to parse the section out of a descriptor's full set of (the section is located by its header and read to end-of-file). This never throws: any structural problem (missing header, bad format version, a malformed or out-of-bounds count, truncation) is reported by returning false so the caller falls back to a cold rebuild. Under-trusting a payload is always safe; mis-reading one would be a correctness bug.
member.param: The parsed index on success; otherwise null.
member.returns: true when a well-formed section was read.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ReferenceMetadataIndex.WriteTextSection(System.IO.TextWriter)
member.summary: Serialises this index as the text section to . The section begins with a short # comment, then formatVersion= and assemblyCount=, then one block per assembly: an assembly= line, a typeNameCount= line, and exactly n newline-delimited type full-names. The traversal order is fixed so identical inputs always produce identical text, which lets the language server hash the section for integrity. The caller must write this section last in the descriptor so the body runs to end-of-file.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ReferenceResolver.IsBclOrRuntimeAssemblyPath(System.String)
member.summary: Returns true when the assembly path looks like a .NET BCL / runtime assembly the user is likely to expect transitively when they pass a single user reference (e.g. System.Runtime, System.Collections, Microsoft.CSharp, mscorlib, netstandard). Non-runtime assemblies (test runners, user libraries, third-party NuGet packages already loaded into the host's AppDomain) are excluded so the user-visible reference set in ) stays scoped to the surface the user actually opted into.
member.param: Absolute path to a candidate assembly (a host TPA entry or a user-supplied reference).
member.returns: true when the path's file-name simple name matches a known BCL / runtime prefix, and — for the ambiguous Microsoft.* prefix — the path also confirms a trusted shared framework or reference-pack location.
member.remarks:
Issue #2345 follow-up: this was previously a pure filename-prefix check, and "Microsoft." is not a reserved runtime prefix — plenty of third-party NuGet packages ship under it (e.g. Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Relational, Microsoft.Extensions.*, Microsoft.Data.Sqlite). When a caller's *only* references happened to be such packages, every one of them was misclassified as "already BCL", so ) skipped augmenting the user-visible reference set with the host's actual BCL assemblies. Core types like System.Int32 were then unresolvable by name (only reachable through the resolver's closure, not the user-visible index), later surfacing as an opaque from ) ("Unable to project CLR type 'System.Int32'").
The unambiguous BCL/runtime prefixes (System.*, mscorlib, netstandard, WindowsBase) are reserved by the runtime and are still recognized by name alone — no third-party package may claim them. Microsoft.*, however, is only trusted as BCL/runtime when the assembly's on-disk path additionally confirms it comes from a shared framework or reference-pack directory (e.g. .../shared/Microsoft.NETCore.App/<version>/Microsoft.CSharp.dll or .../packs/Microsoft.NETCore.App.Ref/<version>/ref/<tfm>/Microsoft.Win32.Primitives.dll) — a layout convention of the dotnet host/SDK install contract that is stable across Windows/Linux/macOS and install locations, unlike a NuGet package's cache path (.../packages/<id>/<version>/lib/<tfm>/...). This preserves real framework assemblies (e.g. Microsoft.CSharp, Microsoft.Win32.Primitives, Microsoft.VisualBasic.Core) as BCL/runtime while excluding same-named-prefix third-party packages.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ReferenceResolver.IsUnderSharedFrameworkOrReferencePackDirectory(System.String)
member.summary: Issue #2345 follow-up: reports whether physically resides under a dotnet shared-framework directory (e.g. dotnet/shared/Microsoft.NETCore.App/<version>/...) or a reference-pack directory (e.g. dotnet/packs/Microsoft.NETCore.App.Ref/<version>/ref/<tfm>/...). Both are well-known, install-location-independent segments of the dotnet SDK/runtime layout contract (present verbatim on Windows, Linux, and macOS regardless of where DOTNET_ROOT points), so matching a literal shared or packs path *segment* — rather than searching for a specific root — reliably distinguishes genuine framework/runtime assemblies from same-named third-party NuGet packages, whose cache layout (packages/<id>/<version>/lib/<tfm>/...) never contains either segment.
member.param: Absolute or relative path to the candidate assembly.
member.returns: true when a shared or packs path segment is present.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ReferenceResolver.MapClrTypeToReferences(System.Type)
member.summary: Projects a CLR that may originate from the gsc host runtime onto the equivalent from this resolver's reference set (its when one is in play). This is required before calling ) on an open generic obtained from ): MakeGenericType demands that every type argument was loaded by the SAME context as the generic definition, otherwise it throws ("was not loaded by the MetadataLoadContext that loaded the generic type or method").
member.param: The CLR type to project; may be null.
member.returns: The projected type, or null when is null.
member.remarks: For the resolver (no ) the host type is already the right identity and is returned unchanged. Arrays, byref types, pointer types and constructed generics are projected element-by-element so nested types (e.g. List[int]) are mapped too. Open generic type/method parameters are passed through, as they are only meaningful relative to their already-projected declaring definition. When a leaf type cannot be resolved by name from the references, an is thrown so the cross-context mismatch surfaces here rather than deep inside a later reflection call.
member.exception: Thrown when a non-null leaf type cannot be projected into the reference set's (it is not resolvable by name and is not a recognised array/byref/pointer/generic shape).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ReferenceResolver.TryGetAssemblyPath(System.Reflection.Assembly,System.String@)
member.summary: Recovers the on-disk path that was originally loaded from. Falls back to the per-process registry that populates whenever an assembly is read into a from in-memory bytes (so MSBuild's CopyRefAssembly task is not blocked — see #853 / #858), which is the case where returns the empty string. Used by AssemblyDocumentationProvider.DiscoverXmlPath to locate the companion XML doc file, and by CrossAssemblyDefinitionResolver to locate the originating sibling project / portable PDB for cross-assembly Go-to-Definition.
member.param: An assembly returned by a resolver.
The original on-disk path on success.
member.returns: true when a non-empty path was recovered.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ReferenceResolver.TryGetMemberLookupType(System.Type,System.Type@)
member.summary: Issue #4924: finds the type whose members binding may see for , that is, its declaration on this compilation's target surface.
member.param: The CLR type of a receiver.
The type to enumerate members on; itself when the method answers false.
member.returns: false when the compilation targets a downlevel framework that does not declare .
member.remarks:
The predefined type symbols (string, object, int32, ...) carry the gsc host's System.Private.CoreLib types, which have every member of the host runtime. Enumerating members on them binds a call to an overload the target framework may not have: s.Split(',') against netstandard2.0 chose the host's Split(char, StringSplitOptions), which .NET Framework does not have (MissingMethodException in Visual Studio's MSBuild), instead of the target's Split(params char[]). Every imported-member lookup on a receiver therefore goes through this method, and a host type is projected onto its reference-set declaration. A type from the reference set keeps its identity: projecting it again by name could pick a same-named type from another assembly (#4381).
For a downlevel target a type the target does not declare has no members binding may use: a host type the reference set cannot project, or a type the host fallback supplied only to resolve a dependency's signature (for example System.DateOnly out of System.Private.CoreLib). The method answers false for it and the caller reports GS0546. On any other target the host fallback is part of the runtime the output runs on, and such a type is used as is, as before. The resolver has no separate target, so it keeps the host type. Loads nothing: projection is the resolver's cached name index.

member.summary: Issue #526: resolves a nested CLR type by name on a containing . Used by the binder to walk a dotted-qualifier type clause (e.g. Outer.Inner.DeepInner) one segment at a time after the outermost type has been resolved. Honors the resolver's by going through ), which stays inside the same load context as .
member.param: The simple name of the nested type to look up.
The resolved nested type on success.
member.returns: true when a public or non-public nested type with the requested name exists; otherwise false.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ReferenceResolver.TryResolvePublishedEmbeddableAttribute(System.String,System.Type@)
member.summary: Issue #4921: resolves a compiler-embeddable attribute (for example System.Runtime.CompilerServices.NullableAttribute) that the target framework itself publishes, that is, an externally visible declaration the emitted assembly can legitimately reference.
member.param: The resolved declaration, if the target publishes one.
member.returns: true when the target publishes the attribute.
member.remarks: The host runtime assemblies are appended to every reference set as a transitive-dependency fallback . Where the target is a downlevel framework , a declaration found only there is the host's System.Private.CoreLib, which does not exist on the runtime that will load the output (.NET Framework), so it does not count as published. Where the target runs on the host's own runtime the fallback is harmless and is kept, as it always was.

member.summary: Tries to resolve a fully-qualified type name across the referenced assemblies, optionally enforcing external visibility.
member.param: When true (the default for user-facing binding), a non-externally- visible type does not satisfy the request. When false, infrastructure callers may resolve internal well-known types by exact name.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ReferenceResolver.TryResolveType(System.String,System.Type@)
member.summary: Tries to resolve a fully-qualified type name across the referenced assemblies.
member.returns: true if a matching type was found; otherwise false.
member.remarks: This user-facing overload enforces external visibility: a metadata type resolves by name only when it is accessible to the compilation (mirroring C# accessibility). Compiler infrastructure (the emitter and lowering) resolves well-known types by exact name — including non-externally-visible attributes such as NullableAttribute/IsReadOnlyAttribute — and must use the ) overload with requireExternalVisibility: false to bypass the gate.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.ReferenceResolver.TryResolveTypeInAssembly(System.String,System.String,System.Type@)
member.summary: Issue #3297: tries to resolve a fully-qualified type name from the specific referenced assembly whose simple name is , rather than across the whole reference set. Interactive submission binding needs this assembly-qualified steering: two REPL cells that redeclare the same package foo emit into distinct submission assemblies (gsi$1, gsi$2) that each define a foo.<Program> container, so the flat name lookup of ) can only ever answer with one of them and the other submission's declarations become unreachable. Resolving against the declaring submission's own assembly keeps every submission's members addressable. Enforces the same external-visibility gate as the user-facing flat lookup.
member.param: The simple name of the declaring assembly (e.g. gsi$3).
member.returns: true if the named assembly defines a matching, externally visible type; otherwise false.

The index is accepted only when its recorded assembly identities match this resolver's freshly-loaded assemblies exactly (same count, same in the same order); Content fingerprints must also match. member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.StructSymbol.ConstructNested(GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.StructSymbol,System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray{GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.TypeSymbol},System.Func{System.Type,System.Type})
member.summary: Issue #1521: constructs a reference to a type declared as a nested type inside a generic enclosing type, closed over the enclosing construction's type arguments (e.g. Box[int32].Tag). The nested type has no own type parameters (the CLR models it as Box1+Tag1, redeclaring the encloser's parameters — ECMA-335 §II.10.3.1); the enclosing arguments are recorded on and the member types that mention an enclosing type parameter are substituted lazily (see ). The emitter threads as the nested type's type-argument vector so a constructed use site encodes Box1+Tag1 instead of the open self-instantiation Box1+Tag1.
member.param: The open nested-type definition (its is used).
The flattened enclosing construction arguments in CLR order (outermost first), aligned with ).
member.returns: A constructed nested reference, or unchanged when no enclosing arguments apply.

member.summary: Issue #1537: constructs a reference to a generic type declared as a nested type inside a generic enclosing type, closed over BOTH the enclosing construction's type arguments and the nested type's own type arguments (e.g. Outer[int32].Middle[string]). The nested type declares its own type parameters, so the CLR models it as Outer1+Middle2 — redeclaring the encloser's parameters first, then its own (ECMA-335 §II.10.3.1). The enclosing arguments are recorded on and the own arguments on ; a member whose type mentions either an enclosing parameter (U) or the nested type's own parameter (T) is substituted through the combined map (see ). The emitter threads the combined vector [enclosing…, own…] so a constructed use site encodes Outer1+Middle2.
member.param: The open nested-type definition (its is used).
The flattened enclosing construction arguments in CLR order (outermost first), aligned with ). May be empty when the enclosing type is open but the nested type carries own arguments.
The nested type's own type arguments.
member.returns: A constructed nested-generic reference, or unchanged when neither vector applies.

Same-compilation user classes have no until emitted, so a naive CLR base-chain walk on this type alone can't see it; this walks the symbol-level chain instead, falling back to the CLR chain only once an is reached.

member.summary:
Issue #3814 / ADR-0149: decides whether two same-signature methods occupy the same slot for the purposes of the hiding rule in ).
Two explicit interface implementations of the SAME member on DIFFERENT instantiations of one generic interface (func (IAsyncEnumerable[int32]) GetAsyncEnumerator(…) and func (IAsyncEnumerable[string]) GetAsyncEnumerator(…)) have identical callable signatures — the interface's type argument only shows up in the RETURN type, which deliberately ignores. Without this guard the second one was dropped from the overload set as if it were an override of the first, and the interface-implementation check then reported the second interface unimplemented (GS0187). They are two distinct CLR slots and must both stay visible.
member.returns: true when both carry the same explicit-interface clause target (including none at all).

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.StructSymbol.GetHierarchy
member.summary: Gets this class and every ancestor along its chain, most-derived first.
member.returns: This class and its ancestors, most-derived first.
member.remarks:
Issue #4162 / #4164: a genuine base-class cycle (e.g. class B : C / class C : B) is normally caught by the post-bind cycle detector (#973), but this walk can run earlier — during declaration binding, before that detector has run — from several independent call sites (an annotation naming a cyclic type via ; an override member whose base-member lookup walks the hierarchy). Without a visited guard, a cyclic chain makes this loop forever, growing the list without bound until the process OOMs. visited.Add returning false on a repeat both detects the cycle and stops the walk; the returned (truncated) hierarchy is still correct for every acyclic caller since it only ever omits nodes that would otherwise repeat.
Internal rather than private: this is the single guarded walk of the symbol-level chain, shared by every caller that used to keep its own unguarded copy (TypeMemberModel, ExternalClrOverrideResolver) so a fix here cannot be independently missed by a sibling copy again.

member.name: M:GSharp.Core.CodeAnalysis.Symbols.StructSymbol.GetUnimplementedAbstractMethods
member.summary:
Issue #987: enumerates the unimplemented abstract methods this class would inherit — i.e. every method in the effective member set (own + inherited, after override resolution) that is still . A concrete (non-open) class with a non-empty result fails to satisfy its abstract base contract.
Issue #1055: when a base is inherited as a CONSTRUCTED generic (e.g. Derived : Base[int32]), an abstract base method whose signature uses the base's type parameters is satisfied by an override whose CONCRETE signature matches the substituted base signature. The substitution is composed across every hop of the inheritance chain so multi-level constructions (Leaf : Mid[int32] : Base[T]) resolve correctly.
member.returns: The set of still-abstract effective methods; empty when none.

member.summary: The emitter's historical primary key: a function's own declaration start (a local function or literal has none and sorts last), or any other symbol's first declaring node.

Issue #1499: clones 1:1 as class-level type parameters whose constraint reference types are remapped from the originals onto the freshly cloned set. Uses a TWO-PASS approach: (1) create every clone (name / ordinal / kind / reference-, value- and default-constructor-constraint flags / optional variance) and build the original → clone substitution map; (2) for each clone substitute that map into the original's , and so a constraint that references an original parameter (self-referential T IComparable[T], cross-referential T IEnumerable[U] / T Base[U], or nested T Base[Dict[T, U]]) instead references the corresponding clone(s). Because all clones exist before any constraint is rebuilt, interdependent constraints across the set resolve correctly. Reuses the symbol layer's so the remap walks generic arguments recursively rather than hand-rolling a partial clone.
member.param: The ordered enclosing type parameters to clone.

Issue #4223: the first clone's ordinal. Non-zero when the clones are appended AFTER a function's own declared type parameters (a generic local function that ALSO references an enclosing type parameter) — the clones must occupy CLR generic-parameter slots past the function's own, not restart at 0 and collide with them.
Existing original-to-shell parameter mappings that appended constraints may reference.
Whether to copy declaration-site variance. Synthesized classes and methods must pass false because CLR variance is valid only on interface and delegate type parameters.
member.returns: The cloned type parameters with remapped constraints.

member.summary: Builds the closed ValueTuple<...> CLR type over .
member.param: The element CLR types, in order.
member.returns: The closed CLR type.
member.remarks: Issue #4591: the G# primitives are host typeof(...) types, but every other imported type comes from the compiler's MetadataLoadContext. Closing the HOST ValueTuple over such an element does not throw: RuntimeType.MakeGenericType silently returns a TypeBuilderInstantiation that throws from GetInterfaces and every member lookup, which surfaced as GS9998 on an array-to- IEnumerable conversion and as a silently lost generic overload candidate. When every such element (or, for a host generic already closed over context types such as a function type's Func<…>, every part of it) provably belongs to one MetadataLoadContext, the tuple is therefore closed in that context, with host types remapped into it. Every other shape — all-host elements, or an element whose context cannot be proven — keeps the previous host construction exactly.

A pre-built Nullable<T> over a MetadataLoadContext struct would itself be a host TypeBuilderInstantiation (the #4035 trap), so the wrapper is built only once the context is known, from that context's own Nullable<>.
